items.title: security(platform): isolate per-account credentials into the user workspace — API keys and connectors share one file
items.body:
## Problem

Every account's API keys and connector credentials live in **two shared JSON
files**, filtered by `accountId` at read time. Signup already provisions an
isolated per-user tree, but credentials do not go into it.

Isolation is therefore logical only: one bad filter, one schema mistake, or one
partial write is a cross-tenant credential exposure, and every account's
authentication contends on the same two files.

## Verified evidence (2026-08-26, at `44e85247`)

Shared collections:

```
apps/www/src/server/api-gateway.mjs:47
  keysFile = <workspaceRoot>/data/platform/collections/api-keys.json
apps/www/src/server/connector-store.mjs:104
  file     = <workspaceRoot>/data/platform/collections/connectors.json
```

Isolation that already exists but is unused for credentials —
`ensureUserWorkspace()`, `apps/www/src/server/platform-store.mjs:120-150`:

```
users/<username>/<business-slug>/{logos,projects,collections,schemas}/
```

Note it already creates a `collections/` directory per business. The per-tenant
destination exists; credentials simply do not use it.

Consequences visible in the current code:

- `verify()` (`api-gateway.mjs:122-135`) loads **every account's keys** and scans
  them on every authenticated `/v1` call, then rewrites the entire collection to
  record `lastUsedAt`. Authentication cost grows with total customers, and every
  call is a full-collection write.
- `connect()` (`connector-store.mjs:157-180`) rewrites the whole connector
  collection to change one record.
- Tenancy depends entirely on the `item.accountId === accountId` predicate. There
  is no filesystem boundary behind it.

Related but distinct: #112 covers operator credentials in shared `/root` config
for coding CLIs. This issue is about bapX's own customer credential storage.

## Cause

The JSON collection store was built for a single-operator workspace and was never
revisited when Platform became multi-account. `internal-docs/cloud-agent-platform-research.md`
§5 already recorded that `platform-store.mjs` "writes whole collections on every
mutation — that is fine for tens of accounts and will not survive thousands".

## Scope

**In scope**
- Move API keys and connector credentials to per-account storage under the
  existing `users/<username>/` tree.
- Key verification must resolve without loading other accounts' records.
- Preserve at-rest encryption exactly as it is: AES-256-GCM for connector
  secrets, SHA-256 hashes for API keys, `timingSafeEqual` comparison, and
  `publicView()` never widening.
- A migration for existing records, with the shared files left intact until the
  migration is verified.
- Confirm the routing surface — agents and `/v1` — resolves credentials only
  within the requesting account's tree.

**Out of scope**
- Replacing JSON with a database. Same layout, per-tenant files.
- Per-account key caps and rate limits (#143).
- Coding-CLI operator config (#112).

## Acceptance checks

1. Two accounts each hold keys and connectors; reading one account's records
   touches only its own files — asserted by a test, e.g. by making the other
   account's file unreadable and confirming the first still resolves.
2. A key issued by account A never verifies for account B, and `verify()` no
   longer loads B's records at all.
3. Recording `lastUsedAt` does not rewrite any other account's data.
4. Connector secrets remain AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest and are still absent
   from every response, including error payloads — existing tests must still pass
   unchanged.
5. Migration moves existing records with no loss, is idempotent, and is proven by
   running it twice.
6. The `/v1` path and an agent run both succeed after migration.
7. `internal-docs/` records the new layout; `map.mmd` updated if ownership moves.

items.title: Staging-first full-site backup and verified restore integration
items.body:
## Goal
Allow ChatGPT to determine if the EXACT authorized WordPress site has a tested, independent full-site restore path before plugin ZIP overwrites, theme updates, database migrations, or Core upgrades. WordPress Core has no portable host-level full backup + restore API; no plaintext archives or DB credentials may enter public GitHub, issue logs or MCP tool returns.

## Required external setup (owner/admin)
- Select approved host or backup-provider integration and a dedicated staging clone, using a private account connection (hosting API/SFTP/WP-CLI only where permitted).
- Confirm encrypted offsite copy of database **and** wp-content/files, retention and per-site tenant boundaries, backup frequency and restore target.
- Perform one full restore to staging, independently compare database tables, media/plugin/theme versions and site/frontend health, record proof without secrets.

## Connector development after authenticated proof
- Introduce a provider-version-bound read-only readiness/status adapter first (provider-reported last completed backup, offsite state, restore test date), with no guess from mere installed-plugin names.
- If provider offers stable documented APIs, implement separately approved backup/restore calls; exact site + environment + recovery checkpoint, idempotency, retries, exclusions and progress verification. No arbitrary SQL/file download endpoint.
- Fail closed on no provider, expired backup, missing restore proof or wrong tenant. Require explicit approval for a destructive restore, never run on production as an automatic prerequisite.

## Acceptance
Staging restore succeeds; provider API authorized; current-site identity and offsite archive remain private; backup/restore smoke and negative auth/tests pass. Until then status = BLOCKED_EXTERNAL_ACCESS, not implemented. See WordPress `wp db export/import` docs and existing `docs/PRIVATE-SITE-REGISTRY-ROADMAP.md`.

items.title: [CRITICAL][RLS] shared OutboxPublisher drains FORCE-RLS outbox on the raw pool — NO service publishes any event under prod NOBYPASSRLS
items.body:
**Found by:** Wave A.1 connector remediation (2026-07-05). Missing from the STATE 2026-07-03 RLS-gap list.

`pkg/database/outbox_publisher.go` drainBatch runs `SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE NOT published ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on the raw pool with no tenant context. The shared `outbox` table is ENABLE+FORCE RLS (document 000001:1279-1297). Under the prod NOBYPASSRLS role the scan fails closed to 0 rows in EVERY service — the transactional-outbox pattern silently publishes nothing in prod: no search indexing, no notifications, no audit events, nothing. Strictly worse than the #69 wedge (which at least logged).

**Fix needs its own design** (touches pkg/database used by all 13 Go services + the Python outbox writers):
- per-tenant drain via tenant enumeration (`database.ForEachTenant`, added in the Wave A.1 connector PR), or
- a deliberate policy carve-out / dedicated publisher role for the outbox table (the drain is the one legitimate cross-tenant reader), or
- partition the outbox per tenant.
Ordering guarantees (stop-on-first-failure per aggregate) must survive whichever shape.

**Repro:** trivial with pkg/testutil.NewProdPostureDB — outbox rows inserted via WithTenantTx are invisible to a raw-pool drain under dms_app.

items.title: Deferred: Operational, compliance & infrastructure concerns

labels.name: phase:3
labels.description: Required before public launch / plugin marketplace

milestone.title: Phase 3 — Scale & Extensibility
milestone.description: Connector marketplace, plugin system, visual workflow builder, AI layer, first sector package. Platform extensible by third parties. See docs/roadmap.md §3.

items.body:
## Purpose

This issue tracks concerns identified in the architecture review that are deliberately deferred — not actionable now but should not be forgotten. Review this list at each phase gate and promote items to their own issues when they become relevant.

---

## Disaster recovery & backup strategy

No backup schedule, PITR targets, RTO/RPO SLAs, or cross-region replication strategy is defined.

**Review at:** Before Phase 2 infrastructure provisioning.
- [ ] Define: backup schedule (minimum daily base + continuous WAL for PITR)
- [ ] Define: RPO target and RTO target
- [ ] Define: failover procedure
- [ ] Test full restore before Phase 2 goes live

---

## Redis single point of failure

BullMQ and cache Redis are on the same instance. An outage halts all background jobs AND invalidates all caches simultaneously.

**Review at:** Phase 2 infrastructure design.
- [ ] Separate BullMQ Redis and cache Redis into distinct instances with independent HA
- [ ] Define graceful degradation: cache miss falls through to DB, job queue drains on reconnect

---

## Plugin marketplace security (Phase 3)

**Reconciled 2026-08-19 against 3B (PR #397, merged 2026-08-13) — see comment below for detail.**

- [x] Module Federation remote entries must include SRI (SHA-384) hashes in the manifest; platform validates before injecting — shipped, `apps/admin-ui/src/lib/plugin-remote-loader.ts`
- [ ] Mirror approved plugin remotes to a platform-controlled CDN — do not load from arbitrary third-party origins — not done; likely moot under 3B v1's first-party-only trust tier (spec §C), but never explicitly waived against this item — tracked as ADR-011 OQ-1
- [ ] `@platform/plugin-sdk` requires a semver-versioned API stability contract; breaking changes need a deprecation period (≥2 minor versions) — only a platform-version *compatibility check* shipped (`version-compat.ts`); no deprecation policy exists and the package is still pinned at 0.0.1 — tracked in #433 (ADR-011 OQ-2)
- [ ] Plugin migrations must be reversible up/down pairs; non-reversible DDL requires platform admin approval — not addressed; `plugin-migration-lint.ts` enforces a different invariant (tenant-isolation RLS on plugin tables, R13), not rollback safety — tracked as ADR-011 OQ-3

**Review at:** Before opening the plugin marketplace to third-party developers.

---

## GDPR erasure mechanism at scale

The tenant deletion lifecycle in [issue #5](https://github.com/TinyPhi/OpenWind/issues/5) covers tenant-level deletion. User-level GDPR erasure (a specific user's PII across all entity instances, workflow event comments, notification logs) is a separate problem.

**Review at:** Phase 2, before handling any EU customer data.
- [ ] Design a GDPR erasure job that pseudonymises or nullifies user-linked PII fields across all tables within 30 days
- [ ] Define the scope: which tables, which fields, what "erased" looks like (null vs. placeholder vs. hash)

---

## Data residency

The single-database model makes per-tenant geographic data residency impossible without significant architecture changes. This is a hard constraint for enterprise customers in regulated regions (EU, India, etc.).

**Review at:** Phase 3 enterprise tier planning.
- [ ] Document this limitation explicitly in the enterprise tier SLA
- [ ] Evaluate a regional cluster strategy — separate Postgres instances per region with a routing layer

---

## Sector-specific compliance

- **HIPAA (Healthcare package):** PHI encryption at field level, BAA requirements, audit log requirements beyond what the standard platform provides. Requires a dedicated ADR before the Healthcare sector package ships.
- **PCI DSS (Financial Services package):** Cardholder data isolation, no storage of raw card data, network segmentation. Requires a dedicated ADR before the Financial Services sector package ships.

**Review at:** Before those sector packages begin implementation.

---

## Metabase / analytics cross-tenant isolation

Tenant analytics data is exposed to Metabase via `analytics_user`. If Metabase is misconfigured (a shared dashboard, a poorly scoped query), it could return cross-tenant data. The `analytics_user` grant scope is tracked in [issue #2](https://github.com/TinyPhi/OpenWind/issues/2) but Metabase-level tenant isolation is a separate concern.

**Review at:** Phase 2, before any tenant-facing analytics are enabled.
- [ ] Confirm that Metabase is configured with per-tenant data source isolation (separate connections or row-level filters per tenant dashboard)

---

## API-level connector data sharing / DPA framework

The connector framework sends tenant data to external systems (Stripe, QuickBooks, etc.). There is no mechanism for tenants to control which fields are shared with each connector, and no documented data processing agreement (DPA) framework. This is a GDPR Article 28 requirement.

**Review at:** Before the connector marketplace opens to third-party connectors.
- [ ] Define which fields each connector is permitted to read
- [ ] Provide tenant-facing consent UI for connector data access scope
- [ ] Document DPA obligations for third-party connector authors

items.title: Tracking: scope stores — a platform-run Durable Object per scope that a vertical reaches through `getScope` (first kind: Ontomate)

labels.name: dibs
labels.description: Claimed for local/manual work — the hourly issue→PR pipeline must not pick this up

labels.name: ontomate
labels.description: Ontomate as a scope store, and the platform work it forces

items.body:
### The gap

A vertical can hold state in four shapes today, and none of them fits a service that has its own runtime and its own storage:

- `runtimeNeeds.stores` are the vertical's own Durable Object classes, exported by its one serving script. The code is the vertical's and is JavaScript.
- A static `d1` binding is one database shared by every tenant.
- `runtimeNeeds.tenantStores` is one platform-minted D1 database per (tenant, vertical, binding), reached with `host.openTenantStore(handle)`.
- `runtimeNeeds.blobStores` is R2 per tenant.

None of the reach paths fit either. Module code has no `fetch`. A connector runs on an event, at least once. `peerClient` calls another vertical. `ADMISSIBLE_BINDING_TYPES` refuses `service`, and a `durable_object_namespace` with a `script_name` is refused on purpose.

### The consumer

Ontomate is a schema and data engine for layered models. It is written in Python, keeps a schema catalog in memory and stores each repository in SQLite. The modeling studio is a vertical in which a project is a scope with exactly one Ontomate repository. Every modeling step (inspect, dry run, apply, review, commit) is a synchronous call whose answer the user waits for inside their own operation.

The ask is generic: any vertical can declare an Ontomate store, and the mechanism admits other store kinds later.

### Proposal

1. **Declaration.** `runtimeNeeds.scopeStores: [{ binding: 'GRAPH', kind: 'ontomate' }]`.
   - There is one object per (tenant, vertical, scope, binding), and it is created on first use.
   - `kind` names a store implementation the platform registers and runs: a script, a class and a version. It is never code the vertical uploads.
   - `binding` follows `tenantStoreNeed.binding`, so a vertical can declare two stores of the same kind.
2. **Reach.** `host.getScope(principal, tenantId, scopeId, { store: 'GRAPH' })` returns a stub with the same shape as `ScopeStub`: `tenantId`, `scopeId`, `subjectKind` and `invoke(operation, input)`.
   - The kind publishes its operation catalog as types, so the stub is `StoreStub<OntomateOperations>`.
   - A new kind adds a catalog, not a method.
   - The (tenant, scope) pair is checked against the directory exactly as today (K-3).
3. **Authority.** A store object does not run the kernel and does not call `ctx.check`. Its authority comes from the operation that precedes the call:
   - The vertical's own operation in the scope checks the caller's permissions and computes what the store call may do. In Ontomate's case that is the session's schema levels, data levels and variables.
   - Harness code then invokes the store stub with that result.
   - This is the same place the check lives for scope operations, since `ctx.check` is the first line of the operation and not something `invoke` does.
   - The principal is recorded in the invocation log and is not evaluated by the store.
4. **Wire.** Substrat defines one envelope and carries it over the object's `fetch`:
   - The request is `{ operation, input }`.
   - The response is `{ result }` or `{ error: { code, status, body } }`.
   - `StoreError` carries the store's own error body.
   - `InvokeOptions` describe scope semantics (`ifMatch`, idempotency), so a store stub either refuses them or takes a narrower option type.
5. **Lifecycle.** Every store object also answers four reserved operations that only the platform may call: `substrat.export`, `substrat.import`, `substrat.size` and `substrat.wipe`.
   - The dump format is `scopeDumpTable` (name, DDL, columns, rows).
   - Snapshot, fork, preview, backup-before-reap, reap and the storage meter use these operations.
   - The code is written once per language. Nothing in it is specific to Ontomate.
   - The store decides what its dump holds. Ontomate's dump is the repository. Open sessions and unsaved drafts are not part of it, so a fork or a restored scope starts without them. `substrat.size` reports the object's whole storage, and `substrat.wipe` removes all of it.
6. **Jurisdiction.** A store object follows its scope's jurisdiction. Every scope is `global` today, and per-jurisdiction DO ids are not built (book ch. 13). When they are, store objects take the same id rule.
7. **Pure adapter (D-14).** The SQLite adapter gets the same contract. For the Ontomate kind, the local runner is an Ontomate process with one repository per scope, reached with the same envelope.

### Why this shape

- It is the scope's own model, one step out. A Durable Object per scope with its own SQLite is what a scope already is. The address follows from (tenant, vertical, scope, binding), so no ledger is needed, and the set of objects a scope has follows from the vertical's declaration.
- It keeps the sandbox rule. The vertical still binds nothing but its own stores. The cross-script `durable_object_namespace` binding is injected by the platform, the same way tenant store bindings are needs rather than declared bindings.
- It is the platform's copy, snapshot and metering story extended to one more SQLite database per scope. It is not a new class of storage.

### Not asked

- No network for module code.
- No new binding type a vertical can declare.
- No Python in the vertical's own script.
- No change to what `ScopeStub.invoke` means for scope operations.
- No permission model inside the store.
- No keep-alive. The store tolerates eviction: an object that wakes reopens its repository, rebuilds its catalog and reloads its sessions from its own storage.
- No placement control. A store object is created where it is first called, which is normally near its scope's own object. `locationHint` is not used for scopes either.

### Open for Markus

- The names: `scopeStores`, `kind`, and `{ store }` in `getScope` options.
- How a store kind is registered and deployed: where its build comes from, how a version is pinned and how an upgrade rolls out (child C).
- Whether subject erasure (#2068, D-45) reaches store objects, and through which reserved operation.
- What the invocation log records for a store call.

### Children

- [ ] #2208 A. contracts: `scopeStoreNeed` in `runtimeNeeds`, and the store-kind registry type
- [ ] #2209 B. kernel and adapter-cloudflare: `getScope(…, { store })`, the store stub, the envelope and `StoreError`
- [ ] #2210 C. Platform-run store kinds: deploying, versioning and upgrading the store script (Python Worker)
- [ ] #2211 D. Scope lifecycle covers scope stores: snapshot, fork, preview, backup, reap
- [ ] #2212 E. Storage meter reads scope stores
- [ ] #2213 F. Pure adapter and contract suites for scope stores

items.title: chore(auth): next-auth runs on a beta channel with no decision on record; decide stay, upgrade or migrate

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

milestone.title: v1.8 — Security & hardening
milestone.description: Security and hardening release right after v1.7 (owner, 2026-10-26). Attack-surface map, then read-only Opus audits per area against OWASP ASVS L2 and the vault's security invariants; local ZAP baseline and Trivy image scans; triage with the owner, then fixes through the normal pipeline.

items.body:
## Problem

Authentication runs on a pre-release channel with no decision on record. `app/package.json` pins `next-auth@^5.0.0-beta.32` (installed: 5.0.0-beta.32, `@auth/core` 0.41.3) with `@auth/drizzle-adapter@^1.11.3`. Checked on npm 2026-11-07: `latest` is 4.24.15, `beta` is 5.0.0-beta.32 (published 2026-07-20), and no stable 5.x exists. The caret admits any later beta and a future 5.0.0, so a plain `npm install` can move the auth layer without a PR saying so.

Eighteen files under `app/src` import from `next-auth` or `@auth/*`, including `proxy.ts` (edge `getToken`), `lib/auth/config.ts`, `lib/auth/tenant-adapter.ts` and `lib/db/schema.ts`. Enterprise SSO (dormant since #1845) sits on the same package and resumes in v1.8.

Raised by the external review of `release/1.7` on 2026-11-07 (`claude_code_docs/plans/improvement-plan-2026-11.md`, WS4).

## Reproduction

1. `npm view next-auth dist-tags` → `latest: 4.24.15`, `beta: 5.0.0-beta.32`.
2. `grep next-auth app/package.json` → `^5.0.0-beta.32`.
3. `grep -rl "from \"next-auth\|@auth/" app/src --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' | grep -v __tests__ | wc -l` → 18.
4. No ADR, vault note or issue records why v5 beta was chosen or when it is revisited.

## Cause

The App Router needs Auth.js v5 (v4 has no App Router support), and v5 has been "beta" for the whole life of the project. The choice was forced at the time and never written down, and the version range was left as a caret like any other dependency.

## Expected

A recorded decision (vault `security/` note, linked from this issue) with one of: stay on the beta pinned exactly and name the revisit trigger; upgrade when a stable 5.x ships; migrate to another library. If "upgrade" or "migrate", a follow-up issue with a full drill (auth is a sensitive surface). Whatever the decision, the version is pinned exactly so a move is always a PR.

## Fix (default; the owner can override in a comment)

- This is a decision, taken with the owner in a `/grill` session, not a refactor. The facts to bring: what the app uses from the package (JWT sessions, `forcePasswordChange`, the Drizzle tenant adapter, the SSO providers under `lib/auth/sso`, the edge `getToken` in `proxy.ts`), the cost of a session-format change to signed-in users, and the state of the alternatives (Auth.js stable, Better Auth, hand-rolled sessions).
- Default recommendation: **stay** on 5.0.0-beta.32 pinned exactly (`"next-auth": "5.0.0-beta.32"`, same for `@auth/drizzle-adapter`) in v1.8, with a Dependabot-style check at every release for a stable 5.x; revisit when that ships or when enterprise SSO work starts, whichever comes first. The beta has carried the app through v1.0–v1.7 and every SSO flow is built on it; a migration before launch buys stability on paper and spends a release.
- Not chosen by default: migrating now. Eighteen import sites plus the session format and the SSO code, on the release that is supposed to harden security, not reshape it.
- Out of scope: any change to session shape, tenancy or credentials. Those need their own drill.

## Required tests

- For the decision itself: none; the deliverable is the note and the exact pin.
- For the exact pin: `npm ci` is reproducible (`package-lock.json` unchanged beyond the two range strings); `npm -w app run test` passes the `lib/auth/__tests__` suites; the E2E `auth.spec.ts` shard passes in CI.
- If the decision becomes "upgrade" or "migrate": the follow-up issue carries its own drill and test plan; this issue closes with the link.

items.title: [Architecture] Future scaling considerations: Multi-tenant platform & self-hosted infrastructure
items.body:
## Overview


**Status:** Future consideration - not for immediate implementation

## Consideration 1: Multi-tenant Platform Architecture

### Vision
Scale from single bot to full SaaS platform:

```
Current:    1 Google Ads Account → 1 Bot → 1 User

Future:     Multiple Clients
                ├── Client A: 3 Google Ads accounts, 50 campaigns
                ├── Client B: 1 account, 10 campaigns  
                └── Client C: 5 accounts, 200 campaigns
                            ↓
                    Your Platform
                            ↓
                Multiple notification channels
```

### Required Components

| Component | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| **Multi-tenant database** | Isolate client data |
| **Job queue** (Redis/Celery) | Handle many API calls async |
| **OAuth flow** | Clients connect their own ad accounts |
| **Rate limiting** | Respect Google Ads API quotas |
| **Web dashboard** | Clients manage their own alerts |
| **NotificationService abstraction** | Support multiple channels |
| **Billing system** | If monetized |

### Proposed Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PLATFORM                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  │
│  │ Google Ads  │  │ Meta Ads    │  │ TikTok Ads  │  │
│  │ Connector   │  │ Connector   │  │ Connector   │  │
│  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  │
│         └────────────────┼───────────────-┘         │
│                          ▼                          │
│              ┌───────────────────┐                  │
│              │   Data Pipeline   │                  │
│              │   (Queue/Workers) │                  │
│              └─────────┬─────────┘                  │
│                        ▼                            │
│              ┌───────────────────┐                  │
│              │     Database      │                  │
│              │  (Multi-tenant)   │                  │
│              └─────────┬─────────┘                  │
│                        ▼                            │
│         ┌──────────────────────────────┐            │
│         │      Alert Engine            │            │
│         │  (Rules per client/campaign) │            │
│         └──────────────┬───────────────┘            │
│                        ▼                            │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐     │
│  │ Telegram │  Email   │ Webhook  │ Your App │     │
│  └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Dashboard / Web App / API for clients              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Recommended Next Steps (When Ready)

1. **Short term:** Create `NotificationService` interface to abstract Telegram
2. **Medium term:** Add support for multiple Google Ads accounts
3. **Long term:** Build web dashboard and multi-tenant infrastructure

---

## Related Decisions

- [ ] Define trigger point for scaling (# of users/accounts)
- [ ] Choose between self-hosted vs managed services
- [ ] Determine monetization model (if any)

---

*This issue is for tracking and discussion. Implementation details will be broken into separate issues when the time comes.*

items.title: Show and set the instance's per-tenant database connection and query limits
items.body:
The instance now limits database connections and queries per tenant. The defaults are 10 connections and 200 queries, and a platform operator can set other values per tenant.

**Published**
- `GET /api/v1/database-connectors/instance` returns `limits.connections` and `limits.queries`, each with `limit`, `current`, `source` (`platform` or `tenant`) and `platform_limit`.
- `/meta/capabilities` lists `database_connections_per_tenant` and `database_queries_per_tenant` while the connector is on, as operator entries.
  - Unlike the run cap, they carry only `tenant_change` and no `change`.
  - `limits set --tenant` needs to handle that case.
- `PATCH /api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/limits` (`limits.manage`) takes `max_database_connections` and `max_database_queries`. `null` returns the tenant to the default, and the tenant detail carries the same two fields. A tenant's Owner cannot raise their own limit.

**Refusals**
- One more connection or query than the limit, created directly, by a personal access token or by a package import, is refused with `409`.
- The codes are `database_connection_limit_reached` and `database_query_limit_reached`, both in `/meta/error-catalog`.
- The detail is `{code, message, limit, current}`.
- An import preview names `database_query_limit_reached` as one blocker. Imports that only change existing queries don't count.
- Rows already over a lowered limit keep working and can still be changed or deleted.
- A token's query create is refused before the person is asked to confirm it.

**Suggested kit work**
- Show both limits and counts in `db instance` and `limits`.
- Explain the two codes, and let `limits set --tenant` set them for operators.

items.title: [Enterprise Gap] Define GA deployment profiles, tenant isolation, SSO, and lifecycle provisioning

labels.name: area: auth
labels.description: Authentication, authorization, identity, or tenant isolation

labels.name: area: security
labels.description: Security boundary, hardening, or vulnerability prevention

labels.name: area: ci-cd
labels.description: CI, GitHub Actions, checks, release, or supply chain

labels.name: scope: commercial-readiness
labels.description: Production, enterprise, release, or commercial readiness

labels.name: status: triaged
labels.description: Open issue has an organization taxonomy assignment

items.body:
## Buyer-visible problem

pg-erd-cloud has project membership, OIDC token verification, API keys, encrypted DSNs, and public share links. Those are necessary controls, but they do not by themselves prove that a shared hosted service is multi-tenant safe. Current work such as PR #855 improves OIDC organization binding while explicitly leaving broader multi-tenant isolation and lifecycle provisioning unresolved.

A complete product must make a truthful deployment claim:

- either a **single-tenant/self-hosted GA profile** with explicit boundaries; or
- a **multi-tenant SaaS profile** with enforced tenant ownership on every persisted and cached object.

It must never imply multi-tenancy merely because projects have members.

## Required product decision

Publish and implement two explicit deployment profiles behind the same modular product contracts.

### Profile A — `single_tenant_managed`

- one customer organization per deployment/database;
- Keyverse or external OIDC issuer with organization binding;
- project RBAC within that organization;
- Compose/Podman and production ingress profile;
- customer-owned backup, restore, secret, and network policies;
- no cross-customer claim.

This is the minimum viable GA profile if proven end to end.

### Profile B — `multi_tenant_saas`

Do not mark this profile GA until all requirements below pass.

1. Add normalized tenant authority:

```text
tenant_account
tenant_domain
tenant_membership
tenant_role_assignment
identity_link_record
provisioning_request
provisioning_receipt
data_residency_policy
tenant_audit_event
```

2. Every authority-bearing object must carry or derive one immutable `tenant_account_uuid`, including projects, members, connections, snapshots, snapshot data, jobs, views, annotations, share links, API keys, migration plans/runs, connector artifacts, audit events, caches, object-storage keys, metrics labels, and queue signals.
3. Enforce tenant ownership in PostgreSQL with tenant-qualified foreign keys and RLS or an equivalently strong repository layer plus database tests. Application filters alone are not sufficient evidence.
4. Prevent cross-tenant references before insert/update and reject ambiguous legacy rows during migration.
5. Bind OIDC issuer/audience/organization claims to a tenant through reviewed mapping; never merge accounts by email alone.
6. Add SCIM 2.0 provisioning/deprovisioning through Keyverse or a dedicated adapter. Removing employment/access must revoke sessions, API keys, connector grants, and future project access without rewriting audit history.
7. Provide tenant-scoped encryption context and rotation. A tenant compromise must not expose other tenants' DSNs or connector secrets.
8. Partition/cache/queue keys must include tenant authority and resist hot-tenant starvation.
9. Share links are tenant-owned, project-scoped, expiring/revocable, rate-limited, and auditable; public access must never infer another tenant's existence.
10. Define data residency, export, deletion, legal hold, backup, and restore semantics per profile.
11. OTel traces/metrics/logs must avoid raw DSNs, comments, schema values, tokens, and high-cardinality tenant PII while preserving authorized auditability.

## Required authorization matrix

At minimum:

| Action | Viewer | Editor | Project owner | Tenant admin | Deployer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Read approved snapshot | yes | yes | yes | policy | policy |
| Create connection/snapshot | no | policy | yes | policy | policy |
| Edit view/annotation | no | yes | yes | policy | no |
| Create/revoke share link | no | no | yes | policy | no |
| Create/revoke API key | self/policy | self/policy | self/policy | policy | policy |
| Approve/apply migration | no | no | no | policy | yes + maker-checker |
| Export/delete tenant data | no | no | no | governed | no |

The final matrix may be more granular, but every API, worker command, connector, and UI action must derive from one versioned policy source.

## Adversarial and lifecycle tests

- same UUID/object name in two tenants;
- cross-tenant FK, URL, share link, API key, cache key, queue signal, export, and connector reference;
- issuer/audience/org claim confusion;
- email reuse across issuers;
- tenant-admin demotion, user deprovisioning, session expiry, and API-key revocation;
- restore one tenant without exposing or overwriting another;
- hot-tenant workload fairness;
- RLS bypass attempts through owner/service roles;
- multi-tenant migration from current rows with fail-closed ambiguity handling;
- production statement/branch coverage 100% and public API docstrings 100%.

## Acceptance evidence

- ADR selecting the initial GA profile and defining the non-GA claim boundary;
- PRD/TRD/data model/threat model/UML/operability and privacy/retention docs;
- Keyverse OIDC/SCIM contract tests and standalone fallback behavior;
- clean-install and upgrade rehearsal on real PostgreSQL;
- exact-current-head CI/security/tenant-isolation/browser tests and independent review;
- `docs/product-technical-gap-baseline.md`, README deployment claims, SECURITY, and CHANGELOG updated.

## References — APA 7th

Internet Engineering Task Force. (2015). *System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Protocol* (RFC 7644). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644

OpenID Foundation. (2025). *OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0 final specification*. https://openid.net/specs/openid-caep-1_0-final.html

National Institute of Standards and Technology. (2020). *Zero trust architecture* (NIST Special Publication 800-207). https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207

items.title: Epic: shared-infrastructure multi-tenancy (SaaS) — awaiting business decision

labels.name: epic
labels.description: Tracking issue for a feature area

items.body:
# Epic: shared-infrastructure multi-tenancy (SaaS)

> **Status: proposal awaiting a business decision — do not start implementation.** This epic exists so the architecture, prerequisite graph, and effort shape are sitting in the tracker when the call is made. If the product ships as customer-managed single-tenant instances (Tier A) plus in-org workspaces (Tier B), this epic stays closed-not-planned and nothing below is wasted — every prerequisite is independently valuable and already tracked.

## The three tenancy tiers (decision frame)

- **Tier A — instance per customer**: ready today modulo the *Platform hardening* milestone (#23 migrations, #24 DSN encryption, secrets ops). The compose stack is the unit; customer data and DSN credentials never leave their infrastructure. This is the default enterprise DQ deployment model.
- **Tier B — workspaces within one org**: #26 PR2 (grants) + the "Scope all global surfaces to connection grants" issue complete it.
- **Tier C — this epic**: multiple customer orgs on shared infrastructure with strict isolation. Only justified if the business model is self-serve SaaS.

## Current readiness: zero tenant awareness, favorable architecture

No `tenant_id` exists on any of the ~15 models; `Connection.name` and user emails are globally unique; JWTs carry no tenant claim; one worker claims all checks; all config (`get_settings()`) is process-global — one LLM key, one encryption key for everyone. **But** the codebase concentrates enforcement into few choke points (auth deps in `security.py`, source access via `connector_for` + `guard_sql`, LLM via `providers.py`, exceptions filters in `_filtered`), which is what makes Tier C a large refactor rather than a rewrite.

The crown-jewel risk to design around: `exception_records.row_data` holds samples of customer data in the shared app DB.

## Prerequisite graph (all already tracked — they ARE the runway)

```
#23 Alembic ──────────────► every schema change below ships as migrations
#26 SSO + grants + tokens ─► identity/membership machinery, resource-scoped authz patterns
   └─ grants-scoping issue ► Phase 0: the choke-point inventory tenant filters will reuse
#24 DSN encryption (enc:v1:) ► versioned prefix is the hook for per-tenant keys (enc:v2:<tenant>)
#25 job-queue worker ───────► where per-tenant fairness/quotas attach
#30 audit log ──────────────► gains a tenant dimension
```

## Phases (each becomes its own issue when/if the decision lands)

### Phase 1 — tenant model & identity
`tenants` table (id, slug, name, status active|suspended, created_at). `tenant_id` FK on `users` and `connections`, **denormalized onto the hot tables** (`datasets`, `checks`, `check_runs`, `exception_records`, `rca_sessions`, `chat_sessions`, `custom_dashboards`, `saved_queries`, `audit_log`) — joins alone are not defense-in-depth. JWT gains a `tenant` claim; OIDC (#26) maps IdP → tenant by issuer/domain. Re-scope uniqueness: `(tenant_id, name)` for connections; **decision required**: emails unique per-tenant (allows one person in two tenants via separate accounts — recommended, simpler) vs global users with memberships. Tenant provisioning API (platform-admin role above `admin`).

### Phase 2 — enforcement: app filters + Postgres RLS
App layer: tenant predicate added to the same choke points the grants-scoping issue inventoried. Database layer: **row-level security policies on every tenant-owned table** keyed to `current_setting('app.tenant_id')`, with the session variable set in `get_db()`/`session_factory()` per request from the JWT claim — so one missed application-side filter is a blank result, not a cross-customer breach. SQLite dev mode: app-layer only (RLS is the prod Postgres net); CI runs the RLS suite against Postgres.

### Phase 3 — per-tenant configuration
Per-tenant rows for: LLM provider/model/key (or "LLM disabled" — heuristics-only tenants are a selling point), data-encryption key (envelope: master key wraps per-tenant keys; `enc:v2:` prefix), notification/digest targets, feature flags. `providers.py` resolution becomes per-call with tenant config — it is already the single choke point, which is why this is tractable.

### Phase 4 — fairness, quotas, accounting
Scheduler: per-tenant concurrency caps and fair claiming on #25's jobs table (round-robin across tenants with due work, not global FIFO). Quotas: checks count, profile rows, LLM tokens/month, exception-row storage; enforced at creation/runtime with clear 402-style errors. Metrics gain a `tenant` label ONLY on low-cardinality counters (requests, runs, LLM) — bounded by tenant count; per-tenant usage endpoint for billing export.

### Phase 5 — source-access isolation
SaaS mode config flag that: forbids path-based DSNs (`sqlite:///`, `duckdb:///` on shared hosts = cross-tenant file reads); applies an egress policy per tenant (allowlist of hosts/CIDRs a tenant's connections may reach — SSRF defense for internal services); runs connectors with per-tenant network identity where the platform supports it. This phase is the hardest operationally and the most SaaS-specific.

### Phase 6 — tenant lifecycle
Provision (seeded admin per tenant), suspend (auth refused, workers skip), export (full tenant data dump — datasets/checks/exceptions/knowledge as JSON; the offboarding promise enterprise buyers ask about on day one), delete (cascading, audited, with grace period), per-tenant backup/restore story.

## Explicit non-goals (even in Tier C)

Schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant on shared compute (operationally heavier than RLS for this app's shape; DB-per-tenant IS Tier A); cross-tenant sharing features; tenant-customizable code execution.

## Decision checklist (answer before opening Phase 1)

1. Is self-serve SaaS actually the GTM, or is "managed single-tenant" (Tier A + automation) the real ask?
2. Emails per-tenant vs global memberships (Phase 1 fork).
3. Compliance target (SOC 2 / ISO) — drives how much of #30/#48/#24 must precede launch.
4. Will any tenant require "no external LLM"? (Phase 3 scope confirmation.)

## Effort shape

Phases 1–2 are the structural core (~the size of the whole workbench epic); 3–4 medium; 5 hard-ops; 6 medium. Prerequisites (#23/#24/#25/#26/#30 + grants scoping) are all current-roadmap items — start nothing else until they're done regardless of this decision.

items.title: Add durable Cloud Run-compatible store for hosted tenant deployments
items.body:
## Goal

Make AgentBBS deployable as a durable, isolated Cloud Run service for a commercial tenant. This is required by cognitum-one/comms ADR-0002 and ADR-0005.

## Current blocker

agentbbs-web currently creates MemoryStore in crates/agentbbs-web/src/main.rs. Cloud Run local filesystem is ephemeral, so a tenant BBS would lose boards/messages on instance replacement.

agentbbs-core has a durable RedbStore behind the native feature, but it is an embedded file store. It is not sufficient for Cloud Run unless a supported durable mounted filesystem is selected and its concurrency/locking semantics are proven.

## Required outcome

Add a production-grade durable Store implementation and runtime selection path for agentbbs-web.

Recommended direction: Cloud SQL PostgreSQL.

- Preserve Store semantics:
  - put_board/get_board/list_boards
  - idempotent put_message by content-addressed MessageId
  - get_message/list_messages ordered oldest-first with newest-limit window
  - message_count
- Do not alter anonymous browser-held Ed25519 participant identities.
- Do not introduce Firebase Auth into AgentBBS protocol/API paths.
- Keep MemoryStore as the default for tests/local demos.
- Make persistent backend selection explicit through environment/config; production mode must fail closed if persistence is not configured.
- Document Cloud Run connection requirements and per-tenant database/schema isolation.
- Add migration SQL, integration tests against Postgres, and a restart-persistence test.
- Add health/readiness behavior that reports configured store backend without leaking credentials.

## Comms contract

Comms provisions one isolated agentbbs-web Cloud Run service per tenant and links to it. Comms must not fork or own AgentBBS persistence. The commercial control plane will only mark a tenant active after the service uses the durable store and passes health/readiness.

## Acceptance

1. A message and board survive process restart.
2. Concurrent duplicate federated put_message calls remain idempotent.
3. Tenant deployment cannot start in production with MemoryStore.
4. Local MemoryStore tests still pass.
5. Cloud Run deployment/runbook is documented, including Cloud SQL connector/service-account least privilege.

References:
- https://github.com/cognitum-one/comms
- comms ADR-0002 and ADR-0005

items.title: 🔧 [chore] plan shared multi-environment module workflow
items.body:
## Problem
Module development must work consistently through ChatGPT + Remote Desktop Commander, Codex Cloud, and ChatGPT + GitHub, including five independent module chats. Current instructions and runtime assumptions are local-first; GitHub CI also has a clean-checkout build-order failure.

## Owner requirements recorded 2026-11-10
- Before every module build, give the owner a plain-English overview of 10–15 sentences explaining the result, scope and approach; wait for approval.
- Owner chooses the execution environment for that module.
- Use Super Build for every module; retain the installed skills and honest capability reporting.
- Plan each module so another chat/agent can resume from GitHub without hidden conversation history.
- Support five concurrent chats on independent modules, with GitHub tracking throughout.
- Every completed module produces a PR; owner reviews and explicitly instructs merge.

## Proposed setup (awaiting overview approval)
1. Put the mandatory approval/dispatch rules in the shared root AGENTS.md and reconcile conflicting instructions in AI_CODING_INSTRUCTIONS.md and CLAUDE.md without deleting business rules.
2. Extend the existing GitHub issue contract with overview, approved plan revision, chosen environment, assigned chat/session identifier, branch, base SHA, dependencies, allowed files, shared-contract/migration ownership, acceptance criteria, verification commands and handoff evidence.
3. Before implementation, record which chat owns each approved module. Five chats may run independent branches/worktrees and disposable databases; shared files/contracts or dependency chains are sequenced by the coordinator. An assignee alone is insufficient when all chats use the same account; use distinct session identifiers. Do not claim comments provide an atomic distributed lock.
4. Use one coordinator for dispatch and integration; module chats operate only on their assigned issue and never drain the whole Ready queue or run crash-recovery sweeps over other active chats. Every merge remains owner-directed and serial.
5. Adapt the installed Super Build lane to the selected issue and environment, preserving upstream tooling. A GitHub connector cannot execute a shell runner: it must hand off to a verified authorized execution environment, or explicitly report blocked. Do not call a manual source edit an executed headless Super Build run.
6. Prepare repository-owned setup and verification instructions for Codex Cloud and GitHub CI, resolve clean-checkout declaration build order in a separate coherent change, and prove runtime/package-manager choices rather than copying machine-specific paths.
7. Configure the actual Codex Cloud environment using the owner's connected account, repository, isolated development database and required network access. Repository files alone do not constitute an activated cloud environment. If account setup is unavailable, record the exact remaining activation step.
8. Keep requirements in canonical docs and workflow records in GitHub issues/PRs. Avoid competing permanent module specifications; approved issue plans reference the canonical SRS.

## Approval and safety boundaries
This issue is a planning record, not permission to start product modules. Existing test restrictions remain until the owner explicitly changes them. Planning/overview approval permits only the named module and chosen environment; it never grants merge, production deployment, production-data use or destructive migrations. Material plan changes require a revised overview and fresh scope approval. Never execute work from a stale chat without reconciling GitHub state.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Owner approves the 10–15 sentence setup overview before implementation.
- [ ] Shared instructions unambiguously require overview approval, selected environment, scoped Super Build, GitHub records and review-before-merge.
- [ ] Each module has a reproducible execution contract and a distinct owner session, branch/worktree and isolated database.
- [ ] Five module plans demonstrate independent scopes or explicit serialization of shared contracts/migrations; no chat can silently claim another module.
- [ ] Remote, cloud and GitHub execution capabilities are checked separately and reported honestly, including the GitHub-only runner limitation.
- [ ] Codex Cloud activation and setup verification have actual evidence, or a named account/access blocker.
- [ ] Draft PRs contain actual command results, source SHA, remaining blockers and handoff steps; nothing auto-merges.

## Risk
Medium: cross-chat coordination and execution readiness. Approval and source ownership must remain explicit; instruction-only rules cannot guarantee perfect agent behavior.

## Blocked by
- None.

Status: owner approved the 13-sentence overview on 2026-11-10; scoped implementation authorized.


## Approved BUILD lane execution contract
- Owner approval: current conversation, message "Approved", following the 13-sentence overview recorded in this issue. Method: ChatGPT orchestrator + Remote Desktop Commander for repository preparation.
- Assigned session: root/workflow_setup; coordinator root owns Codex Cloud UI activation and separate CI workflow repair.
- This BUILD lane implements shared instructions, issue contract, and minimal repository-owned cloud setup/verification instructions/scripts only. No actual account activation or CI edits in this lane.
- Allowed files: AGENTS.md, AI_CODING_INSTRUCTIONS.md, CLAUDE.md, docs/agents/issue-tracker.md, existing canonical docs/CURRENT_STATE.md, docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/AI_HANDOFF.md, docs/NEXT_TASKS.md, SRS_AND_BUILD_GUIDE.md; minimal scripts under scripts/dev/ and optional existing .codex configuration pointers. No new business specification documents.
- Read AI_CODING_INSTRUCTIONS.md in full before implementation. Preserve domain/UI rules. Latest owner-approved setup reconciles always-start-local-server requirements for read-only/connector-only modes: runtime startup remains required when actually verifying an interactive module; report unavailable runtime honestly instead of pretending startup.
- Cloud setup uses repository Node20 manifest/pnpm9.15.9 without changing runtime versions, global installations, database migrations or secrets. The recorded local Node24 compatibility probe is not cloud readiness proof.
- Explicitly retain current no-test-suite/no-new-test policy. Owner-approved operational setup/check scripts are infrastructure tools, not test suites. Shell syntax and real static gates may run; do not run pnpm test.
- Keep implementation under400 changed lines. If it grows, keep a coherent scoped draft PR and record remaining scope on this issue. No merge, close, production action or unrelated cleanup.
- Required handoff evidence: actual command exits, reviewed changed paths, which environment pieces are prepared versus proven/activated, and draft PR URL.
Skills: verification-before-completion

items.title: MCP server package: per-tenant addressing, two transports, discovery
items.body:
**Source:** `deltat/docs/MCP.md` §3 (MCP-A1, MCP-A2, MCP-A3). Node-side counterpart: open-deltat/deltat#26.

This is the `@open-deltat/mcp` package: a thin skin over deltat's HTTP/JSON adapter, living in `packages/mcp` alongside `@open-deltat/client`.

### MCP-A1: per-tenant canonical URI
```
https://mcp.delt.at/t/{tenant}/mcp
https://mcp.delt.at/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/t/{tenant}/mcp
```
Tenancy must be in the URI. RFC 8707 requires the client to send `resource=<canonical URI>` and requires the server to reject tokens whose audience is a different resource, so if tenancy is not in the URI then every tenant shares one audience and one stolen token opens all of them. A tenant taken from a header repeats deltat's `wire.rs` `metadata['database']` mistake one layer up.

- [ ] Per-tenant canonical URI on a path (subdomains are the v2 move, they need wildcard DNS and per-tenant cert ops)
- [ ] RFC 9728 protected resource metadata served per tenant
- [ ] Token audience validated against the canonical URI on every request
- [ ] The tenant is whatever the validated token says it is, and the path must agree, or 403

### MCP-A2: one policy module, two transports
- [ ] Hosted (Streamable HTTP, OAuth) and self-host (stdio, single tenant, API key) share one policy module. If policy forks, the self-hosted path becomes the vulnerable one
- [ ] Policy module has no transport imports, proven by the dependency graph
- [ ] Protocol adapter is one thin module pinned to spec floor 2026-07-28, and spec types never leak into policy. MCP went from stateful sessions to a stateless core in about a year, so churn is the base rate

### MCP-A3: discovery
- [ ] `llms.txt` with a machine-readable quickstart
- [ ] `/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json` per SEP-1649
- [ ] Listed in the official MCP registry
- [ ] Submitted to the Claude connector directory and the ChatGPT plugin directory (both consume remote MCP over HTTPS, ChatGPT has never supported stdio)

### Boundary
The bearer stops here and must never reach deltat's `Command` (PROTO-AUTH-06). deltat verifies a node-audienced capability at commit; this package validates the OAuth token and exchanges it. Identity data stays in Tier 3, never in the kernel (NOT-02).

### Test discipline (PRIN-12)
- [ ] Red test first: a token whose audience names a different tenant is rejected with 403 by the path handler, and the test goes red if the audience comparison is removed

**Depends on:** deltat#26 (the HTTP/JSON adapter this wraps) and deltat#23 (principal-bound tenancy, the hard gate on any multi-tenant ring).

items.title: Multi-tenancy and dynamic schema selection
items.body:
Recently, several people asked about implementing dynamic schema selection to enable schema-base multi-tenancy, where tenant isolation is achieved via DDL Schemas. (If you are not familiar with DDL schemas then you can learn the basics e.g. in [PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-schemas.html)).

I am opening this Epic to do discuss possible solutions, implement necessary improvements and document how to implement multi-tenancy, possibly including an example app.

Related discussions:
- Loopback 4, Model, PostgresDB schema name https://github.com/strongloop/loopback-next/issues/5055
- StackOverflow question: [Schema based Multi tenancy in Loopback 4](https://stackoverflow.com/q/60680275/69868)
- StackOverflow answer: [How to attach a single model (e.g. Product) to multiple datasources]( https://stackoverflow.com/a/28327323/69868) (LB3)
- StackOverflow anwser: [How to prefix model name with tenant id](https://stackoverflow.com/a/53229733/69868) (LB3)

Aspects to consider:
- CLI should recognize dynamic repository/datasource in commands like `lb4 datasource`
- How to boot custom artifacts - we can improve `@loopback/boot` (if needed) or move the registration to a different place (e.g. from a datasource file to a boot script)
- How to migrate/update database tables for all tenants when the model shape changes
- How to onboard a new tenant (create the new schema & all tables)

items.title: [P0] Audit en handhaaf 100% portaalinvoer, externe-data-doorwerking en tenant-readback
items.body:
# Doel
**Werkelijke 100% formulier- en externe-brondekking** in het bestaande klantportaal aantoonbaar maken. Geen parallelle Brain, Heartbeat of scheduler. Gaat verder dan de nu ingediende lossless causal-impact reparatie in PR #4214.

## Traceerbare verplichtingen

1. Inventariseer alle routes/pages uit `portal-v2/page-registry.js`, `portal-v2/page-shell.js`, `portal-next`, legacy en dynamische/integratieformulieren. Verzamel in een automatisch gevalideerde matrix: pagina, veld-ID, eigenaar, tenantcontext, write-endpoint, readback, sourceRevision, Brain-ACK en afhankelijke modellen. Markeer read-only en admin-only apart.
2. Sluit iedere customer write aan op één bestaande canonieke state/BusinessInput writeflow of bewijs een andere authoritative servermutatie met precieze Brain lineage. Verbied parallelle browserstores en orphan inputs.
3. Externe provider-/regulerings-/marktdata: op nieuwe observation via bestaande Source Universe + Company Graph per tenant impact herbeoordelen; alleen daadwerkelijk gewijzigde dependency subgraph, met provenance en freshness. Externe refresh mag customer input niet overschrijven; tenant-impact is nooit globale signaaldata.
4. Voor finance, AI/cloud, governance, proces, marketing, mensen, risico, juridische kaders en CSRD geldt: bij relevante change de juiste modellen herberekenen of expliciet REVIEW_REQUIRED als gegevens/regeldragende bron ontbreken. Geen gefingeerde €-impact/emissies/compliance.
5. Complete durability: transactioneel idempotente outbox/split-batch van >750 KB, restarts/offline, foutretries zonder dubbele Brain-records, monotone versiecontrole en per-batch consumer-ACK.
6. Klant ziet in dezelfde portalweergave: wijziging, bron, tijd, vorige/nieuwe waarde waar geautoriseerd, betrokken pagina's/modellen, actueel/stale/review/pending/applied, reden, voorgestelde actie en readback; alleen eigen tenantinformatie. De bestaande impactmap uit PR #4214 is de eerste UI-draaglaag.
7. CI-contract: auto-gegenereerde route/form-dekking op iedere PR; browser E2E met twee geïsoleerde tenants, 200 velden, 1000 signalen, gelijktijdige writes, fake provider failure, conflict, revocation, GDPR/minimisatie, backfill en bijbehorende evidence.
8. Afsluiten alleen na exact-main Required+CodeQL, Supabase runtime/projection readback, Netlify deployment & authenticated browser readback, en bewezen terugkoppeling naar ONE BRAIN/Heartbeat/Powerhouse. Admin-control-center toont per keten onafhankelijk bewijs, geen kunstmatige green.

## Huidige realiteit
Het bestaande impact engine-contract registreert alle **geregistreerde page IDs**, niet het daadwerkelijke gebruik van iedere DOM-input. PR #4214 sluit enkele bewezen causal-loss/race-gaten en voegt klantzichtbaarheid toe. Dit issue mag niet automatisch sluiten op basis van PR #4214 alleen. Laat eerdere gekoppelde verplichtingen bestaan tot eindbewijs.

## Borgingsconsolidatie — 20 oktober 2026

Fingerprint: `borging-consolidatie-20261020-v1`. Op expliciet verzoek zijn negen bestaande Notion-pagina's bijgewerkt en teruggelezen; drie betrokken database-records hebben daarnaast actuele samenvattende properties gekregen. Geen nieuwe parallelle registers.

- [Master Build, Borging & Go-Live Register](https://app.notion.com/p/3c3da36aac8a81dda3fec4fc12bba5df): geconsolideerde statusmatrix en bronbewijs.
- [Canonical System Map](https://app.notion.com/p/3dcda36aac8a8152be3dedbb32b06239): samenhang en bewijsgrenzen.
- [Error Register & Release Gates](https://app.notion.com/p/3c6da36aac8a81cc9731ea9355881230): bewezen herstel versus open resultaten.
- [Menselijk Handboek](https://app.notion.com/p/3dcda36aac8a81acaad1c88751e9e814): uitleg borging en ondernemerbetekenis.

items.title: Implement data model v1 with tenant_id on every table

labels.name: Unified Data Model
labels.description: ORGANIZE: schema for entities, relationships, historical states

labels.name: user-story
labels.description: Feature described from the user's point of view

labels.name: must
labels.description: MUST priority in the proposal MVP boundary

labels.name: team: data-ai
labels.description: Owned by the data and AI team

items.body:
**Parent epic:** #5 (ORGANIZE: Unified Data Model & Entity Profiles)
**Iteration:** Iteration 3 (due Nov 3, 2026) · part of Release 1 (Iteration 4, due Nov 17, 2026)
**Story points:** 8
**Ideal time:** 22 h
**Risk:** Medium. Every other story builds on this schema, so a design mistake spreads everywhere.

## User story
**As a** PULSE developer,
**I want** one agreed, tenant-scoped schema for sources, sync runs, raw and normalized records, organizations, matches and changes,
**so that** every connector lands data in the same structure with its provenance and history preserved.

## Context
Data model v1 separates what sources say (source records) from what PULSE believes (canonical organizations), keeps every version of a record, and records every match decision so it stays explainable and reversible. Decision D5 makes `tenant_id` mandatory on every table from the first migration, because retrofitting it later is expensive and it is the Law 25 boundary between clients. Postgres is the single source of truth.

| Table | Purpose | Key fields |
|---|---|---|
| `tenant` | One Omerlo client | id, name, omerlo_media_id |
| `source` | A connected source per tenant | id, tenant_id, kind (omerlo, csv, mock), config, watermark_updated_at |
| `sync_run` | One connector execution, the snapshot | id, tenant_id, source_id, started_at, finished_at, status, counts |
| `raw_record` | Archived payload pointer | id, tenant_id, sync_run_id, external_id, entity_kind, payload_uri, payload_hash |
| `source_record` | Normalized record, versioned | id, tenant_id, source_id, external_id, kind, name_normalized, domain, linkedin, external_ids (json), attributes (json), valid_from, valid_to, first_seen_run, last_seen_run |
| `organization` | Canonical organization | id, tenant_id, display_name, primary_domain |
| `org_link` | Source record to organization | organization_id, source_record_id, method, confidence, decided_by, decided_at |
| `match_candidate` | Uncertain match for review | id, tenant_id, left_record_id, right_record_id, score, matched_fields, status |
| `record_change` | Diff output between runs | id, tenant_id, sync_run_id, source_record_id, change_type (added, modified, removed), changed_fields (json) |

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] All nine tables above created through versioned migrations that run from an empty database and can be rolled back
- [ ] `tenant_id` is non-null with a foreign key on every table except `tenant`; tables referencing each other cannot point across tenants (composite keys or checks)
- [ ] At most one current version per record: a partial unique index on (tenant_id, source_id, external_id) where `valid_to` is null
- [ ] Indexes on `name_normalized`, `domain`, `linkedin`, and on source and sync run foreign keys, with the reason for each documented
- [ ] ORM models match the migrations (checked in CI by #18)
- [ ] Seed command creates two tenants with one `mock` source each, for local development against the mock server (#51)
- [ ] Integration tests run the migrations up and down against Postgres
- [ ] Schema documented on the "Domain Model" wiki page (#29)

## Tasks
- [ ] Set up the migration tool (2 h)
- [ ] Write the models and the first migration (8 h)
- [ ] Add constraints and indexes and document why (4 h)
- [ ] Write the seed command (3 h)
- [ ] Write the tests (5 h)

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by:** #15 Select tech stack and justify frameworks and libraries, #29 Create the domain model diagram
- **Blocks:** #56 Archive raw payloads before transformation, #57 Map Omerlo payloads to normalized source records, #58 Store source records as versions without overwriting history, #59 Enforce tenant scoping in data access and prove it in CI

## Out of scope
- Activity signals, relationships, scores, status history and watches: added once the product direction is validated
- The tenant-scoped data access layer (#59)
- One database per tenant (future upgrade path)

## Rubric coverage
`PA-2 Modelling` · `Code: Performance considerations` · `Code: Using best practices for framework`

## Definition of done
- [ ] Acceptance criteria met
- [ ] PR reviewed by at least one teammate and linked with `Closes #<this issue>`
- [ ] CI green (lint, tests, coverage)
- [ ] Wiki updated

items.body:
Part 2 of #428. Depends on #454.

A new console project, `Axis.Scenarios`, runs the **test scenarios** of an application folder. Each scenario runs against its own temporary **tenant** database. This issue runs record actions without `expect`, and `expectRecord`. It touches test scenarios, tenants, **entities**, **seed data**, **roles and policies** and activation.

## What changes

- `dotnet run --project src/Axis.Scenarios -- <folder> --server <connection string>`.
- For each scenario it creates an `axis_scenario_<uuid>` database and migrates it. It compiles and activates the folder, applies the seed data and runs the steps. It drops the database afterwards, whether the scenario passed or failed.
- `createRecord`, `updateRecord` and `deleteRecord` run through the record command (#454), as the step's user with that user's roles. Without `expect`, they must succeed.
- `expectRecord` compares the named values of the saved record.
- The runner writes a JUnit file to `artifacts/test-results/` with one test case per scenario. It exits non-zero when a scenario fails.
- The runner uses no extension packages and no deployment bindings yet.

## Acceptance criteria

- Integration test: a scenario that creates and updates a record and expects its values passes, and its database is dropped.
- Integration test: a scenario whose `expectRecord` does not match fails and names the step, the field, the expected value and the actual value.
- Integration test: the JUnit file and the exit code match the results of a folder with one passing and one failing scenario.

Docs: [test scenarios](https://github.com/phuongnse/axis/blob/main/docs/reference/configuration.md#test-scenarios), [D32](https://github.com/phuongnse/axis/blob/main/docs/decisions.md#d32-test-scenarios--agreed), [testing](https://github.com/phuongnse/axis/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#testing).

items.title: Deploy veodiagram on GCP — Cloud Run for API + Cloud Run Jobs for analyzers, Cloud SQL, Memorystore, GCS
items.body:
## Shared deployment template (applies to GCP and AWS tracks)

The two cloud tracks (#70 GCP, #71 AWS) target the same architecture, instantiated against each platform's managed primitives. Mapping a third cloud (Azure, OCI, DO) later is a matter of filling in the same six rows.

| Component | Current (Docker Compose) | Target shape | Why this shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| Web SPA | `web` container (Vite-served) | Static bucket + CDN | Pre-built artifacts; no compute needed |
| API (sync HTTP) | `api` container (Fastify) | Container-based serverless (Cloud Run / App Runner) | Fastify stays as-is; supports WS; scales to zero |
| Analyzer workers | `api` container (BullMQ workers in-process) | Container-based serverless jobs (Cloud Run Jobs / Fargate Tasks) | Long-running, memory-heavy (8GB heap), filesystem-bound (git clone) — exceeds Lambda / Cloud Functions limits |
| Postgres | `postgres` container | Managed Postgres (Cloud SQL / Aurora Serverless v2) | Managed backups, point-in-time recovery, auth-proxy / RDS-Proxy for connection pooling |
| Redis | `redis` container | Managed Redis (Memorystore / ElastiCache) | Keeps BullMQ unchanged; same queue semantics, no rewrite |
| Object storage | `minio` container | Native S3-compatible (GCS / S3) | We already use `@aws-sdk/client-s3` — swap endpoint + creds |

### What stays identical between platforms

- Prisma schema + migrations (`pnpm prisma migrate deploy` on the migrate job).
- BullMQ queues + worker code.
- API code (no framework rewrite — Fastify runs unmodified on Cloud Run / App Runner).
- The S3 SDK calls (only endpoint + credentials change).
- The web SPA build artifact.

### What's platform-specific (lives in the per-cloud issue)

- IaC dialect (Terraform / Pulumi / CDK).
- CI/CD identity federation (Workload Identity Federation vs OIDC role assumption).
- Networking model (VPC connector vs VPC + RDS Proxy).
- Cost knobs (min-instance count, idle scaling).
- Secret store (Secret Manager vs AWS Secrets Manager).

This shared scaffold also informs an eventual third cloud — Azure has the same six slots (App Service / Container Apps + ACI Jobs + Flexible Server + Azure Cache for Redis + Blob Storage), as does any major provider.

---

> Reference architecture lives in the private tracker at mudit70/veodiagram#733. This issue is the public implementation plan with concrete phases and acceptance criteria.

## Goal

Deploy veodiagram to GCP using container-based serverless primitives. The Fastify API and BullMQ analyzer workers move to Cloud Run / Cloud Run Jobs unmodified. Persistence moves to Cloud SQL + Memorystore + GCS. Static frontend moves to Cloud Storage + Cloud CDN.

## Why Cloud Run, not Cloud Functions

The analyzer routinely needs 4–8 GB RAM, filesystem-resident git clones, and minutes of wall time. Cloud Functions Gen2 caps at 16 GB / 60 min in principle but is sized for short request handlers, not BullMQ workers maintaining queue connections. Cloud Run runs our existing container as-is, scales to zero, supports WebSockets, and Cloud Run Jobs handle the analyzer's long-running shape cleanly.

## Component mapping

| Current | Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `web` container | Cloud Storage bucket + Cloud CDN | Vite build → `gsutil rsync` to bucket; CDN serves SPA |
| `api` container | Cloud Run service | Min instances ≥ 1 in production (warm); concurrency 80 |
| BullMQ workers (currently in `api`) | Cloud Run Jobs **or** separate Cloud Run service with `--no-cpu-throttling` | Jobs for one-shot analysis runs; long-lived workers for the screen-name refine queue |
| `postgres` | Cloud SQL Postgres 16 | Private IP, serverless VPC connector, Cloud SQL Auth Proxy sidecar in Cloud Run |
| `redis` | Memorystore for Redis | Standard tier in prod; basic tier acceptable for staging |
| `minio` | Cloud Storage (separate bucket from web) | `@aws-sdk/client-s3` with GCS interop endpoint; or migrate to `@google-cloud/storage` |
| `migrate` job | Cloud Run Job (one-off) | Runs `prisma migrate deploy` before each API revision goes live |
| Secrets (`.env`) | Secret Manager | Mounted as files on Cloud Run; rotation possible without redeploy |
| Observability | Cloud Logging + Cloud Monitoring | Structured logs from pino; uptime checks on `/api/health` |

## Phased implementation

### Phase 1 — Foundations (1–2 days)

1. Create `gcp` Terraform module under `infra/gcp/` (project, VPC, service account, secret manager scaffolding).
2. Bake `apps/api/Dockerfile` and `apps/web/Dockerfile` to Artifact Registry. Tag with git SHA.
3. Stand up Cloud SQL (Postgres 16) + Memorystore (Redis 7) in a dev project. Empty Cloud Storage buckets for `veodiagram-uploads` and `veodiagram-web`.
4. Workload Identity Federation between GitHub Actions and the GCP project — no static service-account JSON keys.

### Phase 2 — Dev environment cutover (2–3 days)

5. Deploy API to Cloud Run dev service, wired through serverless VPC connector to Cloud SQL + Memorystore. Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as sidecar.
6. Deploy `migrate` as a Cloud Run Job; run on every deploy via Cloud Build trigger.
7. Wire static web bucket + CDN; deploy SPA build on every push to main.
8. Smoke test: existing dev smoke spec (the one we ran today) against the new Cloud Run URL.

### Phase 3 — Analyzer workers (2 days)

9. Decide per-queue: Cloud Run Job for one-off `analyze` runs (triggered by Cloud Tasks from the API), Cloud Run service with min-instances for the persistent `screenNameRefine` worker.
10. Cloud Tasks queue replaces the in-process trigger for analyze jobs; BullMQ stays as the worker-side primitive.
11. Smoke: trigger an analysis through the dev API; verify the analyzer Job picks it up, completes, and writes diagram rows.

### Phase 4 — Production environment (1–2 days)

12. Replicate the dev terraform module to a prod project; tighten IAM + network.
13. Custom domain mapping for `veodiagram.confiserve.com` (or wherever the public hostname lives) onto Cloud Run via Cloud DNS + managed cert.
14. Cutover: data dump from Hetzner Postgres → Cloud SQL via `pg_dump` / `pg_restore`. DNS flip after smoke green.

## Acceptance criteria

- Pushing to `main` deploys the API, web, and analyzer to GCP within 10 minutes via GitHub Actions, no manual steps.
- Smoke spec (the 8 tests run against `veodiagram-dev.confiserve.com` today) passes against the GCP dev URL.
- An end-to-end analyze of `rallly` (one of the cross-repo baselines) completes on the GCP analyzer with diagram outputs matching the baseline within ±5%.
- Cold start of the API is < 3s on warm path, < 10s on truly cold; documented in the deploy README.
- API scales to zero on idle dev project; analyzer Jobs scale to zero when queue is empty.
- Hetzner deploy keeps working unchanged — both targets coexist until cutover is complete.

## Cost / scaling notes (rough)

- Dev project at idle: Cloud SQL `db-f1-micro` (~$10/mo) + Memorystore basic 1GB (~$30/mo) + Cloud Run min-zero (~$0) + storage egress (~$5). Estimate <$50/mo idle.
- Prod with light traffic: bump Cloud SQL to `db-g1-small`, Memorystore standard tier, Cloud Run min-instances = 1 for warm path. Estimate $150–250/mo at the current scale.
- Analyzer cost is linear in analyses: a 5-minute analysis on Cloud Run Jobs (4 vCPU, 8 GB) is ~$0.06.

## Out of scope

- Multi-region active/active (single region for v1).
- Per-tenant database isolation (kept as application-layer per #731's analysis).
- Migration to gRPC / pub/sub for service-to-service traffic (HTTP for v1).
- Cost-optimization knobs beyond min-instances (Spot VMs, sustained-use discounts).

## Related

- #71 (this repo) — AWS deployment track. Cross-platform comparison is informative; choosing one cloud doesn't preclude the other.
- mudit70/veodiagram#733 — full GCP architecture write-up + comparison to Cloudflare (#731).
- mudit70/veodiagram#956 — stale GCP refs in old deploy.yml + DEPLOYMENT.md need cleanup before / during this work; their presence today is informational, not load-bearing.
- #1009 (private repo, closed) — pre-merge CI gate is already wired and is reused here for the new deploy pipeline.

items.body:
