# XIV AI GLOBAL OFFLINE SUPER BRAIN — MASTER CURSOR EXECUTION PROMPT — 62L-CP

## Mission
Continue GLOBAL OPERATIONS BRAIN as the XIV Superbrain root by building a GLOBAL KNOWLEDGE SUPPLY CHAIN, a GOVERNED PLUGIN/TOOL FOUNDRY, AGENT-BUILT AI SERVICES, REGIONAL DATA REFINERY NODES, an INTERNATIONAL INSTITUTIONAL MEMORY GRAPH, and a MULTI-CLOUD KNOWLEDGE DISTRIBUTION NETWORK.

This phase should let XIV agents keep expanding the platform through bounded, testable tools and plugins instead of hard-coding every new capability into the core. Agents should be able to identify a missing capability, propose/build a plugin or small AI service in an isolated development environment, test it, benchmark it, register it in an internal catalog, and make it available to other eligible agents only after policy and human review. Existing third-party plugins/connectors should be usable through explicit configuration, scopes, provider capability contracts, terms/licensing metadata and revocation controls. No plugin may grant itself authority, credentials, external accounts, billing, production deployment or broader data access.

Interpretation rules:
- 'Plugin' = a governed adapter/tool/service package with a manifest, version, capability contract, permissions, data classes, runtime requirements, tests, provenance, owner and lifecycle state. Registration does not imply execution permission.
- 'AI agent keeps building more AI tools' = bounded software-factory workcells that create candidate tools/plugins/apps/services from approved requirements, with tests, static/security checks, benchmarks, code review and promotion gates. No uncontrolled recursive self-replication or idea-to-production automation.
- 'Utilize other plugins' = discover/configure explicitly approved existing plugins/connectors/providers and route tasks to them only when scopes, data classification, terms and runtime evidence allow.
- 'Knowledge supply chain' = lawful intake -> validation -> transformation -> evidence -> indexing -> distribution of public/open/licensed/customer-owned/partner-authorized knowledge.
- 'Regional refinery nodes' = small isolated data-processing/indexing cells on explicitly configured local/cloud/edge infrastructure; candidate infrastructure only.
- 'Institutional memory graph' = evidence-backed temporal graph of companies, universities, governments, standards bodies, research institutions, markets, infrastructure operators and public organizations from lawful sources; no private unauthorized dossiers.
- 'Multi-cloud knowledge distribution' = signed/versioned/revocable distribution of approved derived knowledge, indexes, plugin packages, schemas, skills and eval deltas to explicitly configured nodes; no raw-private global pooling.

Target cycle:
AUTHORIZED OBJECTIVE -> CAPABILITY GAP -> REUSE EXISTING APPROVED PLUGIN? -> PLUGIN RIGHTS/SCOPE/CLASSIFICATION CHECK -> IF NEEDED BUILD SANDBOX TOOL/PLUGIN CANDIDATE -> UNIT/INTEGRATION/SECURITY/EVAL TEST -> HUMAN/POLICY REVIEW -> INTERNAL CATALOG REGISTRATION -> ELIGIBLE AGENT ASSIGNMENT -> KNOWLEDGE/REFINERY/DISTRIBUTION WORKFLOW -> BENCHMARK -> ROOT GRAPH + SKILL LEDGER + FOUNDER BRIEF.

## Mandatory Preflight
Read reports through 62L-CO and inspect actual worktree/runtime. Reuse Universe Package Manager, Local App Marketplace, Plugin Ecosystem, Software Factory, Agent Academy/University, Provider Fabric, Multi-Model Federation, Knowledge Exchange OS, Regional Micro-Cloud Fabric, Archive Discovery, Data Refinery, Storage/Index Compiler, Workforce Ledger, local command runner, decision gates, context vault, Guardian/RLS policy controls and benchmark/evidence systems.

Before broad edits produce:
1. truthful agent/workcell census and RUNNING_VERIFIED count from current heartbeat/runtime evidence,
2. current plugin/tool/service registry and package-manager capability map,
3. current configured third-party connector/provider/plugin matrix with AVAILABLE/UNAVAILABLE/UNKNOWN states,
4. current permission/data-class scope model for tools/connectors,
5. current agent software-factory/build/test/eval capability map,
6. current regional refinery/cloud/server/database/edge capability matrix,
7. current knowledge distribution/package/signature capability map,
8. active-diff ownership map; if Cursor churn remains high, restrict implementation to isolated modules/tests/report.

## Governance
L4_AUTONOMY_ENABLED=false. No production deploy/merge/migrations, self-granted permissions, Guardian/RLS weakening, uncontrolled plugin/agent replication, automatic external account creation, autonomous purchases/billing/subscriptions, arbitrary internet/LAN/server/database/device discovery, credential harvesting, offensive cyber, stealth installation/persistence, unauthorized scraping/data mining, raw-private cross-tenant pooling, unauthorized private healthcare/person data, covert tracking, autonomous external publishing, autonomous legal/financial commitments, unsafe physical control, hidden chain-of-thought storage, or unsupported consciousness/quantum/all-world claims.

A plugin/tool/package may NEVER infer authority from installation or registration. Unknown/unconfigured plugin/provider/runtime/node/source/license/connector = UNAVAILABLE / WAITING_DATA / UNKNOWN / DENIED as appropriate. Most restrictive policy wins.

## 30 User Stories
CP1 Plugin/Tool Foundry Contract — define package identity, owner, purpose, capabilities, input/output schemas, data classes, permissions, runtime, dependencies, network needs, tests, version, license, provenance, tenant/Universe scope and lifecycle.
CP2 Internal Plugin Catalog — searchable registry of XIV-built and approved third-party plugins with DOCUMENTED/IMPLEMENTED/VERIFIED/AVAILABLE/DEGRADED/UNAVAILABLE/DENIED states.
CP3 Plugin Capability Manifest — machine-readable declared actions/resources/data classes with deny-by-default permissions.
CP4 Plugin Permission Firewall — per-call authorization for tenant/Universe, classification, network, filesystem, database, connector and consequence scope.
CP5 Plugin Secrets Reference Contract — secret IDs/references only, never secret values in logs/prompts/manifests; explicit owner/revocation/expiry.
CP6 Plugin Dependency/SBOM Ledger — packages, versions, licenses, hashes, vulnerabilities, runtime support and provenance.
CP7 Third-Party Plugin Intake Gate — verify publisher/source, terms/license, scopes, network behavior, privacy/data classes, runtime and rollback before approval.
CP8 Plugin Compatibility Adapter Layer — normalize different plugin/connectors/tools into XIV-owned capability envelopes while preserving provider-specific limits.
CP9 Plugin Health/Availability Ledger — configured != available; current runtime/connector evidence required for AVAILABLE/RUNNING_VERIFIED.
CP10 Plugin Circuit Breaker/Revocation — disable degraded, unauthorized, expired or compromised plugins immediately and surface reason codes.
CP11 Agent Tool-Build Project Contract — requirement, capability gap, owner, sandbox, budget, target users/agents, data classes, acceptance criteria, tests and stop conditions.
CP12 Tool Reuse-First Planner — search existing internal/approved external capabilities before authoring a new tool.
CP13 Agent Tool Scaffold Generator — produce isolated candidate plugin/service skeletons from approved interfaces without granting authority.
CP14 Agent Coding Workcell — bounded architect/coder/tester/security/reviewer roles; persist structured decisions/results, not hidden CoT.
CP15 Automated Unit/Integration Contract Test Lab — deterministic tests for schemas, permissions, error states, timeouts, resource caps and offline behavior.
CP16 Plugin Security Review Lab — static/dependency/secret/path/network/permission checks on owned candidate code; defensive only.
CP17 Tool Benchmark Arena — correctness, evidence quality, reliability, latency, resource/energy proxy, offline performance and regression metrics.
CP18 Plugin Promotion Gate — IDEA -> SCAFFOLDED -> IMPLEMENTED -> TESTED -> SECURITY_REVIEWED -> BENCHMARKED -> HUMAN_REVIEWED -> VERIFIED_CANDIDATE -> NOT_DEPLOYED.
CP19 Agent Skill-to-Plugin Mapper — map eligible roles/skills/tasks to verified plugin capabilities without permission inheritance.
CP20 Tool Usage Evidence Ledger — record tool ID/version, task, policy decision, result status, evidence refs, latency/resource use and failures.
CP21 Regional Data Refinery Node Contract — region, tenant/Universe, data classes, source rights, service roles, residency, quotas, trust and revocation.
CP22 Refinery Plugin Pipeline — compose approved extraction/validation/translation/dedup/entity-resolution/indexing/compression plugins into governed pipelines.
CP23 Institutional Memory Graph Contract — institution, time, geography, type, relationships, evidence, source rights, confidence and contradiction states.
CP24 Global Institutional Research Pack — lawful public/open/licensed knowledge on companies, universities, standards bodies, research institutions, governments/public agencies, markets and infrastructure operators.
CP25 Institutional Pathway Miner — identify evidence-backed collaborations, technology diffusion, trade/infrastructure links and historical evolution while separating correlation from causation.
CP26 Multi-Cloud Knowledge Distribution Contract — source/destination/object/version/classification/residency/tenant/Universe/hash/signature/expiry/revocation.
CP27 Plugin/Knowledge Package Distribution Planner — signed candidate package placement to explicitly configured local/cloud/edge nodes; no stealth install or auto-deploy.
CP28 Package Integrity/Compatibility Gate — hash/signature/SBOM/runtime/version/OS/hardware/policy checks before any eligible installation candidate.
CP29 Plugin/AgentTool/Refinery/Institution/Distribution Benchmark Suite — permission isolation, reuse rate, build quality, security, package integrity, knowledge provenance, distribution safety and recovery.
CP30 Founder Plugin & AI Tool Foundry Brief — exact workforce census, plugin catalog states, approved third-party integrations, agent-built tool candidates, test/security/benchmark status, refinery-node readiness, institutional graph growth, package distribution health, blockers and next safe stories.

## Required Verification
- RUNNING_VERIFIED requires current heartbeat/runtime evidence.
- Plugin registration/installation does not grant permission or authority.
- No plugin may silently broaden scopes or access another tenant/Universe.
- Secret values are never persisted in plugin manifests/logs/prompts.
- Third-party plugin terms/license/source/scope are recorded.
- Unknown/unconfigured plugins remain UNAVAILABLE.
- Agent-built tools remain sandbox candidates until reproducible tests/security/benchmarks/human review pass.
- No recursive idea->build->deploy production loop.
- Tool builders cannot grant themselves new tools, permissions, credentials or external accounts.

items.title: cache: elasticache serverless support (username, key prefix, cluster client)
items.body:
## Problem

A GoBricks service cannot connect to an Amazon ElastiCache Serverless (Valkey/Redis) cache with an RBAC user, and two services sharing one cache endpoint have no protection against overwriting each other's keys.

Today's `cache.redis` surface (`cache/redis/config.go`) carries `host`, `port`, `password`, `database`, pool/timeout knobs and `tls.*`. Three gaps against ElastiCache Serverless:

1. **No `username`.** `buildRedisOptions` (`cache/redis/client.go`) sets `redis.Options.Password` only, so the client sends `AUTH <password>` as the `default` user. ElastiCache RBAC user groups require `AUTH <username> <password>` (Redis ACL). There is no way to reach a serverless cache that has RBAC enabled.
2. **Single-node client.** The connector calls `redis.NewClient`. ElastiCache Serverless exposes one endpoint that speaks the cluster protocol; multi-slot traffic through a single-node client surfaces `MOVED` errors. Needs a `redis.NewClusterClient` / `NewUniversalClient` path (or a verified statement that the serverless proxy tolerates a single-node client for this workload).
3. **No key namespace.** `Get`/`Set`/`Delete`/`GetOrSet` send the caller's key verbatim. The only isolation the framework offers is per-tenant Redis `database` numbers (wiki/cache.md "Multi-Tenant Isolation"), which ElastiCache Serverless does not support (db 0 only). Two services writing `user:42` silently overwrite each other; a same-shape CBOR payload decodes fine, so the collision is invisible.

TLS is already covered (#1591): `cache.redis.tls.enabled: true` verifies against system roots.

## Proposal

Additive config on `cache.redis` (and the per-tenant mirror under `multitenant.tenants.<id>.cache.redis`):

- `username` (env `CACHE_REDIS_USERNAME`) wired to `redis.Options.Username`. Empty keeps today's default-user behaviour.
- `keyprefix` prepended by the client to every key on every operation. Default to `app.name` so collisions are impossible unless two deployments share a service name; empty string opts out explicitly.
- Cluster/universal client mode so a serverless endpoint works without `MOVED` errors. Exact shape (a `cluster: true` flag vs. auto-detect via `NewUniversalClient`) is open.

Recommended deployment posture: one ElastiCache RBAC user per service with an access string scoped to that service's prefix (`~orders:* +@all`), so the server rejects any write outside the namespace and the framework prefix keeps handler code unaware of it. The two features are independent but only enforce isolation together.

## Open questions (for grilling before implementation)

- Should `keyprefix` default to `app.name` (safe by default, but changes every existing deployment's key layout on upgrade) or default empty (no surprise, no protection)?
- Prefix separator and whether the prefix participates in the multi-tenant `database` scheme when both are in play.
- Cluster mode: explicit flag or `NewUniversalClient` auto-detection? How does the readiness `PING` / `INFO` version check behave against the serverless proxy?
- IAM authentication for ElastiCache (`CredentialsProviderContext` token refresh) — same gap, separate issue or part of this one?
- Does the `database` validation (0–15) need a serverless-aware error message when a non-zero value is configured against a cluster endpoint?

## Acceptance

- A service configured with `username` + `password` + `tls.enabled` connects to an ElastiCache Serverless cache with an RBAC user group.
- Two services with different `app.name` values (or explicit `keyprefix`) share one endpoint without key collisions; a test proves the prefix is applied on every operation, including `GetOrSet` and `Delete`.
- wiki/cache.md documents the ElastiCache Serverless posture (username, prefix, cluster mode, db 0 only) and corrects the "separate Redis database per tenant" isolation claim for managed endpoints that do not support `SELECT`.

items.body:
## For people — new commercial offering (2026-11-13)
Build **HandleIT AI Websites + Managed Hosting** as a repeatable customer service, linked from both handleit.online (services) and peasantware.com (software/tools), with **one shared customer account and billing portal**. Use existing IONOS/GitHub/Square platforms rather than building replacements. This issue is the canonical implementation work order for the service, not authorization to charge customers, transfer domains or launch a portal without review. See [Peasantware commercialization audit #21](https://github.com/Mavaebrook/peasantware-website/issues/21).

### Target customer experience
1. Customer signs up once to the *shared* Peasantware/HandleIT customer portal; can manage profile, organization/team, contracts, websites, domain/DNS details, GitHub connection, projects, support and invoices. Do not reuse the single-owner **Peasant Command** login or dashboard as a multi-tenant customer portal.
2. Chooses website package (site build, optional hosting/maintenance), provides branding/content brief, hosting preference, and connects/authorizes GitHub repo through limited-scope GitHub App/OAuth; customer retains code and domain ownership by default.
3. AI-assisted site builder generates a branch/PR via existing Peasant Runtime → Gateway authorized GitHub capability. It does not push AI-generated content unreviewed to production.
4. GitHub Actions runs CI and creates staging preview (prefer **IONOS Deploy Now** for static/SPA/PHP sites; IONOS VPS for supported server apps). Customer reviews preview and explicitly approves a *versioned revision*. Owner/operator approves production release if policy requires it.
5. After approved PR merge to protected main, **GitHub Actions/IONOS Deploy Now automatically publishes**; verify URL/health and show deployment history/rollback in portal. Auto-deploy of reviewed changes, **not auto-publish of unapproved AI output**.
6. Client views order, invoices, recurring plan, status and support; external payment screens are Square-hosted. Billing changes/cancellation must be authenticated and auditable. Owner sees operational/approval summaries in Command via a read-only projection, not a copy of billing data.

### External capabilities verified (2026-11-13)
- IONOS Deploy Now: GitHub App integration, staging previews, GitHub Actions automatic deployments and custom domains. https://www.ionos.com/hosting/deploy-now
- IONOS Hosting APIs cover DNS/domains/SSL management; API access must be enabled on merchant account; do **not** assume public API can provision every Deploy Now plan/hosting contract. https://developer.hosting.ionos.com/docs/getstarted
- IONOS Agency Partner Portal can manage client projects/contracts and delegated permissions; consider before implementing redundant IONOS customer administration. https://www.ionos.com/agency-partner
- Square Checkout API hosted payment links, Square Catalog/Subscriptions/Invoices APIs support one-time and recurring plans. https://developer.squareup.com/docs/checkout-api and https://developer.squareup.com/reference/square/subscriptions-api . Merchant account active/payment-processing eligibility NOT verified (past email notifications are not proof).
- Square webhook: validate x-square-hmacsha256-signature using *raw* request body + exact notification URL, constant-time compare, dedupe event_id, reconcile by Square API before entitlement/provisioning. https://developer.squareup.com/docs/webhooks/step3validate
- No Square/IONOS connector presently available in ChatGPT for active-account inspection. Tokens must be provisioned out-of-band into owning service's Vault/secrets store, never chat/GitHub/browser.
- Avoid creating a Stripe integration merely because the prior packaging audit suggested it; reuse Square **if confirmed active**.

### Ownership & architecture (Global Policy Ledger GPL-001–010)
- **Commerce/account service** (new independently deployable backend only after existing capability audit, e.g. *HandleIT customer portal*): customer identity, organization membership/RBAC, contract IDs, customer-site mapping, support, entitlements/provisioning state, idempotent webhook handling; stores *references*, not card details/IONOS passwords/GitHub PATs.
- **Square**: authoritative charges, checkout, invoices, subscription/payment state and card vaulting; linked via seller-side app credential. Portal uses Square IDs plus verified events and periodic reconciliation, never equates checkout redirect to paid status.
- **GitHub**: authoritative repo/source/PR/CI and deploy revision. Customer repos isolated via installation-specific GitHub App permissions; one repo/site; no global PAT. Preserve staging, manual approval, ownership handoff and rollback.
- **IONOS**: authoritative hosting accounts/products/domains/DNS/SSL. For agency-controlled hosting use consent and scoped API access; distinguish owner-operated infrastructure from customer-owned hosting contracts. No purchase/renewal without explicit agreement.
- **Peasant Runtime/Gateway**: existing agent execution/permissions for draft generation and review; Gateway Vault holds API credentials. **Peasant Command**: internal operator approvals and telemetry, *not* customer identity nor billing database.
- **Public sites**: handleit.online sells AI websites, setup, maintenance, managed hosting; peasantware.com sells portable products and links to same accounts/checkout backend. Cross-domain sessions use redirect/OIDC, not shared cookies across .com/.online. Proposed customer portal origin: portal.peasantware.com, subject to approval and DNS.

### Minimum customer portal
- Sign up/sign in with passkey or vetted OIDC, email verified, session security and per-organization access controls.
- Projects/sites with current status, preview/production URL, GitHub repo, last deploy, rollback history, open requests, client approval.
- Orders, invoices, subscription management (cancel/upgrade per policy), support tickets, account export/delete.
- Customer-access audit, data retention/privacy statement, invoices/taxes/refunds and terms. No payment card numbers stored.
- Admin diagnostics and error states when Square, IONOS or GitHub disconnected. No silent fallback to fabricated data.

### Milestones & acceptance gates
- [ ] P0 — Confirm current Square seller merchant account/payment eligibility, production/sandbox app, Location, webhook and catalog permissions **privately**; confirm IONOS API access and whether Agency Partner or Deploy Now appropriate. Record provider account/status without secrets.
- [ ] P1 — Draft proposed service SKUs and pricing, included hosting costs, maintenance responsibility, domain ownership/migration and customer terms; owner approval **before public price or checkout**.
- [ ] P2 — Host public service-intake page on handleit.online with same existing enquiry flow; link proposed offer from peasantware.com; PR, approval and GitHub CI/deploy only.

items.title: Heart-rate and step-count ids are tenant-free SHA-1 hashes on a global primary key, so a second tenant's record is dropped silently

labels.name: effort:M
labels.description: Crosses a layer, or adds a migration, or touches a shared component

items.body:
> *This was generated by AI during a hostile review in the 2026-10-27 performance sweep (#2901). Found by reading, not reproduced in a running instance; the converted `ActivityWatermarkSourceScopeTests` showed the symptom under a shared database.*

## Summary

`HeartRateMapper` and `StepCountMapper` set `Id = MapperHelpers.ParseIdToGuid(model.Id)`, a SHA-1 of the client's id string with no tenant in it. The primary key on `heart_rates` and `step_counts` is `id` alone. The revive-by-id lookup in `SimpleEntityService.CreateManyAsync` is tenant-filtered (and RLS applies on top), so when tenant B publishes a record whose non-GUID id tenant A already used, B cannot see A's row, inserts, and fails on the primary key. `MetadataPublisher` swallows the exception (`catch (Exception)` around its heart-rate, step-count and related publishes), so B's data is dropped silently. The failure is also a cross-tenant existence oracle.

Two tenants fed from the same upstream (one person's Nightscout mirrored into two tenants, or any connector with deterministic ids) hit this.

## Fix

One mechanism wherever `ParseIdToGuid` feeds a global primary key: derive the deterministic id from `(tenant_id, client id)`, or make the hashed id unique per tenant (composite key). Grep every `ParseIdToGuid` caller; `ActivityDecomposer` and others likely share the pattern. Stop swallowing the insert failure in `MetadataPublisher`, or at least log it at a level an operator sees.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two tenants publishing a heart-rate or step-count record with the same client id both store their row.
- [ ] No publish path in `MetadataPublisher` drops a record on an unlogged exception.
- [ ] `ActivityWatermarkSourceScopeTests` runs on one class-fixture database with a fresh tenant per test, like its siblings, and stays green (it is the regression test for this).

## Out of scope

- The state-span latest-by-source change (#2901) that surfaced this.

## Summary

Investigate migrating Manage2Soar tenant web applications from the current GKE-based deployment model to **Google Cloud Run**.

Manage2Soar tenants generally have low and intermittent traffic. Much of the time, a tenant receives no requests at all, yet the current Kubernetes infrastructure must remain running continuously.

Cloud Run's ability to **scale a service to zero instances when idle and automatically start an instance when a request arrives** appears particularly well suited to the Manage2Soar workload.

The goal of this investigation is to determine whether Cloud Run could substantially reduce hosting costs and operational complexity while preserving the current tenant-isolation model.

## Current Architecture

Conceptually, the current architecture is approximately:

```text
Internet
   |
Google Cloud Load Balancer
   |
GKE
   |
Manage2Soar Django containers
   |
PostgreSQL VM
```

Each Manage2Soar club is currently deployed as an independent tenant with its own configuration and PostgreSQL database.

Persistent media/static resources are already being moved outside the application containers where appropriate.

The primary concern is that Kubernetes compute resources remain allocated even when the applications are receiving little or no traffic.

## Proposed Architecture

Investigate an architecture similar to:

```text
                         +--> Cloud Run: SSC ------> SSC DB
                         |
Internet --> Cloud Run --+--> Cloud Run: MASA -----> MASA DB
                         |
                         +--> Cloud Run: Tenant C --> Tenant C DB
                         |
                         +--> Cloud Run: Tenant D --> Tenant D DB
                         |
                         +--> Cloud Run: Tenant E --> Tenant E DB

                                      |
                                      v
                              PostgreSQL Server
```

Each tenant would continue to run the same Manage2Soar container image but receive tenant-specific configuration through environment variables and/or Google Secret Manager.

This preserves the existing isolation model:

- One application deployment per club
- One PostgreSQL database per club
- Tenant-specific domain
- Tenant-specific secrets
- Tenant-specific OAuth configuration
- Tenant-specific storage/configuration where required

## Primary Benefit to Investigate: Scale to Zero

Cloud Run can be configured with:

```text
Minimum instances: 0
Maximum instances: small tenant-specific value
```

An idle tenant could therefore have:

```text
Cloud Run instances = 0
```

When a request arrives:

1. Cloud Run receives the HTTP request.
2. Cloud Run starts a Manage2Soar container.
3. Django initializes.
4. Django connects to PostgreSQL.
5. The request is processed.
6. The instance remains available while traffic continues.
7. After the tenant becomes idle, Cloud Run eventually scales the service back to zero.

This potentially eliminates paying continuously for application compute for tenants that may receive only a handful of requests during much of the day.

For a small soaring club, occasional cold-start latency may be an acceptable tradeoff for substantially lower hosting costs.

## Proof of Concept

Use a non-production tenant such as `tenant-demo` for the initial experiment.

### Phase 1 - Basic Deployment

- [ ] Identify the existing Manage2Soar container image used by GKE.
- [ ] Deploy the image as a Cloud Run service.
- [ ] Configure tenant-specific environment variables.
- [ ] Configure secrets using Secret Manager or equivalent.
- [ ] Connect the Cloud Run service to a test PostgreSQL database.
- [ ] Confirm Django starts correctly.
- [ ] Confirm database migrations are compatible.
- [ ] Confirm static files work.
- [ ] Confirm uploaded/media files work.
- [ ] Confirm authentication works.
- [ ] Confirm Google OAuth works.
- [ ] Confirm outbound email works.

### Phase 2 - Scale-to-Zero Testing

Configure initially with approximately:

```text
Minimum instances: 0
Maximum instances: 1
```

Test:

- [ ] Allow service to scale completely to zero.
- [ ] Make a request after an extended idle period.
- [ ] Measure cold-start latency.
- [ ] Measure normal request latency.
- [ ] Determine how long Cloud Run keeps an idle instance alive.
- [ ] Verify subsequent requests reuse the running instance.
- [ ] Verify service reliably returns to zero instances.
- [ ] Test multiple simultaneous requests during cold start.

The important measurement is the **actual user-visible cold-start penalty for Manage2Soar**, rather than theoretical Cloud Run startup numbers.

## PostgreSQL Connection Management

This requires particular attention.

Cloud Run can automatically create multiple application instances. Each Django instance can create one or more PostgreSQL connections.

Unrestricted autoscaling could therefore exhaust PostgreSQL connection limits.

Investigate:

- [ ] Django `CONN_MAX_AGE` behavior under Cloud Run.
- [ ] Number of database connections created per Cloud Run instance.
- [ ] Gunicorn worker count.
- [ ] Cloud Run request concurrency.
- [ ] Appropriate Cloud Run maximum instance count.
- [ ] PostgreSQL `max_connections`.
- [ ] Whether connection pooling is desirable.
- [ ] Whether PgBouncer would provide meaningful benefit.

Initial production limits should probably be deliberately conservative, for example:

```text
Small tenant:
    min instances: 0
    max instances: 1-2

Larger tenant:
    min instances: 0
    max instances: 2-3
```

These numbers should be based on testing rather than assumed.

## Background and Scheduled Tasks

Inventory anything currently dependent on:

- cron
- Kubernetes CronJobs
- Django management commands
- long-running processes
- asynchronous/background jobs

Determine whether these workloads should use:

- Cloud Run Jobs
- Cloud Scheduler
- another existing GCP service

Potential examples include:

- roster generation
- scheduled email
- billing operations
- cleanup jobs
- periodic maintenance
- database migrations during deployment

## Deployment and Migrations

Determine the desired deployment workflow.

Potential model:

```text
GitHub
   |
   v
Container build
   |
   v
Artifact Registry
   |
   v
Cloud Run revision
   |
   v
Tenant service
```

Investigate how database migrations should be handled safely.

Do **not** simply run migrations automatically from every web container startup, since multiple instances may start simultaneously.

Potential approaches:

- dedicated Cloud Run Job for migrations
- CI/CD migration step
- controlled management command before traffic moves to the new revision

## Tenant Provisioning

Determine whether creating a new Manage2Soar club can eventually become something similar to:

```text
create database
create secrets
create storage
deploy Cloud Run service
configure domain
configure OAuth
initialize tenant data
```

This may fit well with the existing Ansible-based tenant provisioning work.

Investigate whether Terraform, `gcloud`, Ansible, or some combination provides the cleanest mechanism.

The desired result should ideally make a tenant reproducible from configuration rather than requiring significant manual setup in the GCP console.

## Networking

Investigate:

- [ ] Connectivity from Cloud Run to the existing PostgreSQL VM.
- [ ] Whether Direct VPC egress is appropriate.
- [ ] Whether a Serverless VPC Access connector is required.
- [ ] Firewall changes.
- [ ] IPv4/IPv6 considerations.
- [ ] Whether PostgreSQL remains inaccessible from the public Internet.
- [ ] Cloud Run custom domains.
- [ ] TLS certificate handling.
- [ ] Whether the existing Google Cloud Load Balancer remains necessary.

Removing the existing load balancer and/or Kubernetes networking infrastructure may represent additional cost and complexity savings.

## Observability

Determine Cloud Run equivalents for current operational troubleshooting.

Test:

- [ ] Application stdout/stderr logging.
- [ ] Django exception logging.
- [ ] Cloud Logging integration.
- [ ] Request logs.
- [ ] Container startup failures.
- [ ] Revision deployment failures.
- [ ] CPU/memory utilization.
- [ ] Instance counts.
- [ ] Cold-start visibility.
- [ ] Alerts.
- [ ] Ability to quickly identify which tenant is failing.

## Failure and Rollback Testing

Cloud Run revisions may provide a simpler rollback model than the current Kubernetes deployment.

Test:

1. Deploy known-good revision A.
2. Deploy intentionally broken revision B.
3. Observe failure behavior.
4. Roll back traffic to revision A.
5. Measure recovery time.

Document the resulting production rollback procedure.

## Cost Analysis

The ultimate question is:

> **How much of the current Manage2Soar GCP bill can disappear if application compute scales to zero?**

Capture the existing monthly costs for:

- GKE nodes
- GKE-related charges
- load balancer
- persistent disks
- PostgreSQL VM
- Cloud Storage
- network traffic
- logging/monitoring
- other supporting infrastructure

Then compare against the projected Cloud Run architecture:

```text
Cloud Run compute
PostgreSQL VM
Cloud Storage
Artifact Registry
Secret Manager
networking
logging
scheduled jobs
```

Run the proof-of-concept long enough to obtain actual billing data rather than relying entirely on the pricing calculator.

## Success Criteria

Cloud Run should be considered a viable replacement for the existing GKE application hosting if:

- [ ] Manage2Soar runs without significant architectural changes.
- [ ] Idle tenants reliably scale to zero.
- [ ] Cold-start latency is acceptable.
- [ ] PostgreSQL connections remain controlled.
- [ ] Authentication/OAuth works correctly.
- [ ] Email works correctly.
- [ ] Media/static storage works correctly.
- [ ] Scheduled/background workloads have a reasonable replacement.
- [ ] Deployment is simpler than the current GKE process.
- [ ] Rollback is straightforward.
- [ ] Tenant provisioning can be automated.
- [ ] Operational visibility is adequate.
- [ ] Security is equivalent or improved.
- [ ] Monthly operating cost is meaningfully reduced.

## Non-Goal

This investigation is **not** intended to redesign Manage2Soar as a shared multi-tenant Django application.

The existing isolation model of independent club deployments and independent club databases should initially remain unchanged.

The question is whether **Cloud Run can provide a cheaper and simpler execution environment for the existing architecture**.

## Initial Recommendation

Do not migrate production tenants initially.

Deploy `tenant-demo` to Cloud Run using the existing Manage2Soar container and PostgreSQL architecture.

Set:

```text
min instances = 0
max instances = 1
```

Then measure:

1. How difficult deployment actually is.
2. Cold-start time.
3. Normal response time.
4. PostgreSQL connection behavior.
5. Operational/debugging experience.
6. Scale-to-zero behavior.
7. Actual Cloud Run cost.

If the experiment is successful, migrate one low-traffic real tenant before considering migration of the remaining Manage2Soar deployments.

items.body:
## Outcome

Approve one authorization and storage model that supports a hosted Hormuz service and customer-controlled deployments without retrofitting tenant isolation later.

## Recommended direction

Make tenant, workspace, project/repository, team, actor, and service account first-class identifiers in every authorization decision and persisted event. Use PostgreSQL migrations for the hosted control plane, with database-enforced tenant scoping and a dedicated-database option for enterprise deployments. Retain SQLite only for local development.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An ADR defines tenant, workspace, project/repository, team, human actor, and workload/service-account relationships.
- [ ] Roles and permissions distinguish usage visibility, policy administration, memory read, memory promotion, connector administration, and audit access.
- [ ] Historical events snapshot tenant/team membership at event time.
- [ ] The ADR chooses shared-schema, schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant, or a documented hybrid and explains isolation, backup, restore, residency, and operating cost.
- [ ] Every repository query and mutation has a tenant-scope invariant with cross-tenant negative tests.
- [ ] Migration, rollback, and local-development topology are specified.
- [ ] Product-owner approval is recorded before storage schemas are treated as stable.

## Decision boundary

Schema implementation may prototype behind an interface, but no enterprise migration contract closes before this topology is approved.

items.title: Knowledge retention and central storage: copy what we do not control, and detect a vanished source first

labels.name: needs-structure
labels.description: Missing goal milestone, matching phase label or native parent (#19522)

milestone.title: v0.9-umbrellas
milestone.description: Containers, not work. An umbrella is delivered by its children; it can never close on its own, so it must not occupy a slot in a numbered chunk. Three of these do not declare themselves in the title.

items.body:
## Owner reasoning (2026-09-26), which specifies this precisely

> original document stays in original place — do we need to retain artifact, after it is vectorised
> **if the source is gone we can't use it any more**
> **if we want to retain some knowledge we have to copy to our controlled location — this is where central storage comes in**

That resolves retention into a policy rather than a yes/no, and it scopes central storage to a **retention tier**, not a store-everything layer.

## The policy this implies

| Source | Who controls it | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Watch folder on our own fileserver | us | **pointer + content hash** — copying would duplicate and drift |
| Connector to third-party SaaS (Confluence, Notion, Slack, Jira, GDrive…) | them | pointer **can die** → copy to controlled storage |
| Crawled web page | nobody | **will** die → copy |
| Upload | no durable origin at all — the file was on someone's laptop | copy, or accept that re-extraction means re-upload |

Copying everything is the `store_authority` rule-2 defect (a second original that drifts). Copying nothing loses the ability to ever re-extract. **Copying what we do not control is the only position that is neither.**

## What is lost today when a source disappears — narrower than it sounds

The extracted **text is already retained** — that is the fact content, and it stays in the vector store and graph. What dies with the source is the ability to **re-extract**: better OCR later, fixed table parsing, a corrected extractor. So the exposure is *"permanently stuck with the extraction quality we had on ingest day"*, not *"the knowledge is gone"*.

That is a real cost — #13884 exists because scanned PDFs currently extract to nothing — but it is bounded, and it is what makes the copy tier worth scoping rather than skipping.

## The prior gap: disappearance is not detectable

**Nothing detects a vanished source.** `services/kb_folder_watcher.py` has no deletion handling — one `"removed successfully"` string at `:277`, no `on_delete`, no unlink path. A deleted watched file, a deleted Confluence page and a 404'd URL all leave the fact in place pointing at a locator that no longer resolves, and **no query can identify which facts have lost their evidence**.

So the retention policy cannot currently be sized: nobody can measure how much of the KB has a dead source.

## What exists to build on: nothing

- No MinIO, S3-compatible store, NFS or shared volume in the fleet deployment.
- `integrations/cloud_integration.py` is an outbound **agent tool** (`list_s3_buckets` against a user's own AWS), not storage infrastructure.
- Redis and Postgres are already networked. **ChromaDB supports both** `HttpClient` (central) and `PersistentClient` (per-node disk), with the selection in `knowledge/backends/async_chromadb_adapter.py:199` (#369) — but `codebase_analytics` runs its own `PersistentClient` concurrently with the KB's, so at least part of the vector store is node-local.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Detect first.** Source-liveness checking and watch-folder deletion handling, with a `source_state` on the fact. Cheap, and it makes the problem measurable.
- [ ] **Measure second.** How many existing facts have an unresolvable source. That number decides how much retention is worth before anything is built.
- [ ] **Then storage.** A node-shared, content-addressed store for retained copies — reachable from every fleet node, hash-keyed so the same document arriving twice is stored once. S3-compatible self-hosted (MinIO) is the obvious shape for this fleet; that is a recommendation, not a decision.
- [ ] Retention is **per source class**, per the table above — not global, not per-file-opt-in.
- [ ] The `DOCUMENT` entity from #17526 carries **one of two locator kinds**: an external URI for sources we do not copy, or an internal object key for retained copies. One entity type, two resolutions.
- [x] **Settle the deployment fact:** is ChromaDB running central (`HttpClient`) or per-node (`PersistentClient`) in the fleet today? Readable only from the running system, not the repo. If per-node, a document ingested on one node is invisible to the others, which is a larger problem than retention.

## Why this is ordered detect → measure → build

The retention tier is the expensive part and its size depends entirely on how often sources actually vanish. Building the store first means guessing that number. The detection work is small, independently useful, and turns the guess into a measurement.

Related: #17526 (`DOCUMENT` entity / provenance), #17527 (intake), #17537 (roadmap), #13884 (scanned PDFs extract to nothing — the concrete re-extraction case).

items.title: [ATC-539-01][PROPOSED][READ-ONLY] Effective authority and evidence baseline E1–E6
items.body:
<!-- JSCC-WP-574-ADMIN-PARK -->
> **CURRENT ADMINISTRATIVE DISPOSITION — 2026-10-25:** **PARKED_BY_OWNER** in [WP #574](https://github.com/Shosetzel69/job-search-command-center/issues/574); future work and execution are ON HOLD indefinitely until explicit owner reactivation. Previous issue status: TASK_CONTRACT_PROPOSED. This administrative hold does **not** waive pre-existing IAM/security/CI/Nile/release fail-closed gates or grant TEST/PROD authority. Historical approvals/reviews/evidence and technical scope remain unchanged.
>
Process: AGENTFLOW
Phase: TASK_CONTRACT
Status: TASK_CONTRACT_PROPOSED
Execution authorized: NO
Parent Development Analysis: #541
Parent Architecture Gate: #539
ATC stable ref: ATC-539-01
Scope: authorized READ-ONLY inventory and evidence collection only
Decision baseline: Architecture v1.1; D1–D9, K1/K3/K4, K2=A (TEST blocked)


## STRICT 1-VERSION RISK & REMEDIATION GATE (2026-10-20)

**Owner restriction:** 1 existing DB secret resource and exactly current immutable v1 in DEV; same in TEST. **No new secret objects OR versions.** Prior v2 proposals are void. Google Secret Manager cannot modify an existing secret-version payload: https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/edit-secrets .

**Independent consequence:** no secure supported mechanism currently proven to deliver a second persistent Nile DB password while retaining existing URL-only v1; and **credential rotation/revocation under strict v1 immutability lacks an approved recovery path**. Nile two DB credentials may share one PostgreSQL role (ADR-004); a second password alone is not SQL least privilege. Do not substitute plaintext Cloud Run settings/job arguments, CI logs or out-of-band untracked material. Documented gate/evidence: [#543](https://github.com/Shosetzel69/job-search-command-center/issues/543#issuecomment-6277575878).

**Safe next engineering option** is read-only reviewed source-level migration guardrails proposed in #541, NOT credential provisioning. No security PASS, no TEST GO, no GCP/DB mutations.


## FINAL OWNER CONSTRAINT — ONE VERSION PER ENVIRONMENT (2026-10-20)

**Supersedes ALL previous Nile dual-credential proposals that prescribe v2, pinned dual secret versions, or adding another Secret Manager resource.** Owner's strict constraint: **DEV has exactly ONE existing `NILE_DATABASE_URL` Secret Manager resource with exactly ONE version (currently v1); TEST likewise exactly ONE secret resource and ONE version (currently v1)**. **No new Secret Manager resources AND no new secret versions, including temporary versions, are authorized or included in the proposed implementation.** Desired outcome remains two distinct Nile-issued DB credentials per environment (application vs migration) **only if a compatible and secure technical delivery method is demonstrated**. Current v1 is a single raw PostgreSQL connection URL; existing code expects that format.

**Provider fact:** Google Cloud Secret Manager secret-version payloads are immutable. Google requires **adding a new version** to change the secret's value: https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/edit-secrets . Consequently the prior `v1 APP + v2 MIGRATION` design **CONFLICTS** with the owner's restriction. Nor can existing v1 become a JSON pair in place. A one-version/two-credential plan would require a separate explicitly designed secure credential-delivery mechanism (not silently using environment plaintext, GitHub, logs or new unmanaged secrets). **No such mechanism has been verified or approved.**

**Binding status of `ATC-541-NILE-CREDENTIAL-DEV-01`: `TASK_CONTRACT_CHANGES_REQUIRED` (design superseded); DO NOT APPROVE/EXECUTE the old ATC wording.** Retain its discovery evidence, but withdraw implementation sequence that creates v2. If no secure compatible architecture satisfies one existing immutable version, issue a scoped `ARCHITECTURE_BLOCKED` decision without GCP/Nile writes rather than interpreting 'continue' as a waiver. #539 K2=A TEST STOP; #531 accepted DEV SHA unchanged; `SECURITY_PASS=NO`. Documentation updates only.


Source baseline rechecked: `main@a7cc2e2f1037eaf3cd9c636ae76cd092c45eb693`

## Owner constraint — ONE existing secret per environment (2026-10-19)

**Rule:** Exactly one existing Google Secret Manager secret resource for the database in DEV, and one existing resource in TEST. No new secret resources. Two proposed Nile credentials per environment, API and migration. No assumption that two versions are required: one-version dual-credential payload versus two numeric versions must be reviewed before ATC approval, including access-control trade-offs. **No version creation, credential generation, IAM or deployment change approved.** Earlier design text suggesting a second secret resource or mandatory version 2 is superseded. TEST STOP; DEV acceptance preserved.


## CANONICAL DECISION — ONE SECRET PER DATABASE, TWO NILE CREDENTIALS (2026-10-19)

**Current binding architecture:** exactly ONE existing `NILE_DATABASE_URL` Secret Manager resource per Nile database (DEV and TEST), TWO distinct Nile DB credentials per database (APP and MIGRATION). TOTAL 2 secret resources + 4 Nile credentials. Prefer pinning separate existing-secret versions to API (`NILE_DATABASE_URL`) and migration job (`NILE_MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL`), after independently validating effective version-specific IAM access and separate GCP workload SAs. No new `NILE_MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL` Secret Manager resource. Additional active versions may be billed; no direct IAM fee. The previous two-Secret-per-database proposal is **SUPERSEDED**. Provider SQL least-privilege capability remains unproven/unsupported for `CREATE ROLE`, and TEST restore + authorization gates remain STOP. **No implementation authorized.**

See the separately appended authoritative same-date decision comment in this issue.


## NILE PROVIDER COMPATIBILITY — VERIFIED (2026-10-19)

**Implementation gate, correcting earlier design assumption:** [Official Nile PostgreSQL compatibility](https://www.thenile.dev/docs/postgres/postgres-compatibility) explicitly lists `CREATE ROLE` and `CREATE POLICY` unsupported. [Nile credential API](https://www.thenile.dev/docs/api-reference/databases/create-a-database-credential) issues DB login credentials but does not support selecting custom SQL permissions. [Nile pricing](https://www.thenile.dev/pricing) labels DB/tenant backups and branching "Coming soon". Do **not** assume SQL role segregation or full-fidelity backup/restore is available, nor that upgrading Nile resolves it. Detailed technical/vendor-feasibility questions: [analysis comment](https://github.com/Shosetzel69/job-search-command-center/issues/543#issuecomment-6276663582).

**Approved-cost boundary:** GCP IAM service accounts have no direct IAM fee; reuse current Cloud Run resources. Do not provision a paid identity service, duplicate database secrets, change Nile plan, create SQL roles, modify DB/IAM, or run TEST migration without separately approved proof. GCP service-account separation is *partial* hardening, not independent DB least privilege. `NILE_SQL_ROLE_GATE=BLOCKED_BY_PROVIDER_CAPABILITY`, `BACKUP_RESTORE_GATE=UNVERIFIED`, `TEST=STOP`, `SECURITY_PASS=NO`.



## Objective
Establish an independently recheckable, minimally sensitive **identity→permission→resource→environment→authorized gate** inventory, verify live effective policies and allowlist/deny evidence **E1–E6**, and produce a safe least-privilege remediation order for subsequent ATCs. No technical enforcement or data changes.

## Entry / evidence prerequisites
1. Owner approval of architecture decisions is represented in chat, but trusted/non-delegated owner decision record is still outstanding in parent #539. This issue does NOT self-authorize.
2. Before **executing** this ATC under AgentFlow: explicit `APPROVE_TASK_CONTRACT ATC-539-01`, given through an accepted owner authorization channel, and a **read-only access path with independently attributable identity**. The issue body is a proposal, not an authorization.
3. No GCP IAM/Build/AR/Cloud Run APIs or #537 operations plugin are exposed in this ChatGPT tool session. **Do not call unapproved Google identity, Cloud Shell, Work browser, remote executor, or create credentials** as a workaround. The owner must separately authorize whichever bounded read-only route is used.
4. No secrets or personal data in public issues; timestamps and sanitized permission/resource identifiers only. Evidence containing sensitive policy memberships or token metadata stays in owner-controlled private evidence, with redacted summary here.

## Exact read-only work
- **E1 IAM:** read effective project + service-account IAM policies across `jscc-shared`, `jscc-dev`, `jscc-test`, `jscc-prod`; `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`, build/create/approve, trigger editor, deploy, registry writers, runtime/evidence bucket writers, privilege inheritance, human/AI impersonation and recovery.
- **E2 Cloud Build:** enumerate triggers, regions, source revision selection, control-plane config refs, approval requirements, substitution override permissions, trigger service-account identity, effective build origin, build-approval actor, command/API bypass paths. READ ONLY; never trigger a build.
- **E3 AR:** enumerate `jscc` registry settings, tag immutability, writer grants, image SHA/digest metadata, native provenance and trusted builder for Job and Service artifacts; do not pull images/data to public logs.
- **E4 GitHub:** current ruleset 24524377, source-status provider, installed app permission scopes (particularly `contents`, `workflows`, `checks`, `statuses`, `issues`), alternate owner-account automation, branch merge actor, permitted non-admin operations. Read-only admin/security metadata if available; no config changes.
- **E5 legacy credentials:** inventory secret names, scopes, last use and dependency mapping across GH/Cloudflare; never read/print secret material or rotate/revoke yet. Identify which obsolete paths are still accessible.
- **E6 audit:** confirm actual enabled Cloud Audit Logs & filtered events, alert routing/recipient, pricing for data-access logs and at least one denied-action record *from existing logs only*; determine Github audit visibility/cadence. No generation of real denied operations in TEST/PROD.

## Contract outputs (required)
- `evidence-index`: {E1..E6: VERIFIED | PARTIAL | NOT_VERIFIED, provider, timestamp, object/ref, reviewer, redaction statement}.
- `effective-authority-matrix`: principal, trust role (AI / human / builder / DEV deploy / TEST deploy / reviewer / QA / attestor / runtime), project, privilege, grant source, whether ability is direct or via `actAs`, actual expected gate, bypass exposure; no token values.
- `candidate-source-and-control-plane`: head SHA, build trigger refs, native image provenance availability, deployment digest references; never assume YAML serviceAccount equals actual trigger identity.
- `current-vs-target-gap`: F1–F13 mapped to protected enforcement point and corresponding proposed ATC.
- `execution-order`: K3 account recovery before revocations, source-status check active before hardening, evidence issuers before TEST gate, reversible migration/deny-tests plan; estimated cost vs ADR-006.
- `Evidence Bundle` with all redacted primary identifiers, not self-attested PASS. Independent reviewer verifies completeness prior to readiness.

## Acceptance criteria / adversarial plan
- AC-01 all six evidence families inspected from actual provider, with timestamp + identity and independently accessible proof; if any inaccessible: `NOT_VERIFIED`, not fabricated.
- AC-02 effective GCP IAM map identifies all principals that can override trigger/build/release approval across each project, including impersonation edges.
- AC-03 effective GitHub app scopes and ruleset observed; any AI `contents:write`/`workflows:write` conflict explicitly flagged against K1.
- AC-04 source SHA, image digests/provenance and Cloud Build trigger control ref analyzed as distinct trust anchors.
- AC-05 deny-test **specification only** for forged SHA, self-issued QA, owner-session impersonation, cross-env deploy, legacy GH dispatch, branch/admin bypass; **no live mutations or probes performed** in this ATC.
- AC-06 cost / owner lockout / rollback dependencies defined before enforcement. K2=A TEST hold documented.
- AC-07 no raw IAM policies with sensitive member personal identities, no provider tokens/secret values, no user data posted in public Issues.

## Explicitly out of scope
Implementation, privileged test execution, custom shell, GCP service-account keys, IAM/ruleset edits, GitHub workflow dispatch, Cloud Build builds, deployments, QA verdicts, TEST/PROD use, synthetic PASS attestation, bridge/#537 functional expansion, ADR edits, closing parent finding.

## Retries and stops
- Retry each failed read-only provider call at most once if transient, without switching to a higher-privilege identity. Invalid permission/no connected tool => STOP **for owner access-path decision**; never ask for password/token or improvise insecure connector.
- If collected evidence shows additional architecture/security delta or nonzero operating cost not already owner-approved => STOP for scoped owner decision.
- If any E family remains NOT VERIFIED => mark `EVIDENCE_INCOMPLETE` and block affected enforcement ATCs, but finish all independent portions of the audit first.
- After each GitHub workflow/API operation, run Gmail failure notifications check per AgentFlow §9.2 and cross-check against exact run/SHA; old failures aren't current claims.

## Current preparation note
GitHub-read-only findings G1–G8 and E4/E5 partial status are documented in [#541 comment](https://github.com/Shosetzel69/job-search-command-center/issues/541#issuecomment-6107934936). The contract is ready as a *draft proposal*, not as a runnable authorized tool action. Production changes remain frozen until future separately approved ATCs.

### Canonical outcome before owner action
`Status: TASK_CONTRACT_PROPOSED`.
`Execution authorized: NO`.
`E1–E3/E6: NOT VERIFIED; E4/E5: PARTIAL`.
`TEST: BLOCKED (K2=A)`.

---

items.title: M05-PR16: Expose requester-scoped case progress

milestone.title: M05 - Adaptive Resolution Experience
milestone.description: Deliver the requester canvas and resolver console over the shared case APIs.

items.body:
**Milestone:** M05 - Adaptive Resolution Experience

## Goal
Deliver M05-PR16: authenticated requester-scoped case progress without disclosing resolver evidence or treating approval authority as case ownership.

## Scope
- Add an explicit immutable tenant/case/requester binding, consumed immediately by the protected read.
- GET /bff/v1/tenants/{tenantId}/requester-cases/{caseId}/progress returns only case ID, goal, lifecycle status, openedAt and updatedAt.
- Resolve the actor exclusively from the requester OIDC session. Unowned, foreign-owned, cross-tenant and absent cases share the same 404 response.
- Keep the route unavailable to workbench clients; preserve disabled-mode and no-store contracts.
- Include additive migration, real PostgreSQL integrity/upgrade and HTTP tests, ADR and operator documentation.

## Design decisions
Ownership is separate from REQUESTER/RESOLVER approval evidence and never grants execution or approval authority. Legacy cases receive no inferred owner or automatic backfill. Until authenticated intake (M05-PR23), trusted database operators may bootstrap a reviewed binding with a bounded provenance reference; no browser or legacy API accepts actor IDs or ownership claims. One immutable initial requester per case; no reassignment/delegation is introduced. A single tenant/actor/case-constrained SQL statement provides one snapshot and selects only the public projection. OPEN is not a run/claim state; VERIFIED_RESOLVED remains the existing accepted-proof case state. No dependency or new authority algebra.

## Acceptance criteria
- Correct registered requester can read only an explicitly bound case, including cases without approval attestations.
- Other requesters, approval-only/resolver-only identities, tenant crossover and unbound/absent cases disclose no case fields and use indistinguishable 404 problems.
- No raw observations, connector/provider identifiers, notes, ownership actor IDs, contract/run/approval data or proof payloads enter responses.
- Session/client checks and no-store remain enforced; reads neither mutate state nor acquire authority/control.
- Database enforces one immutable binding per case, tenant-safe actor/case references and bounded nonblank provenance.
- Empty-chain and previous-version upgrades preserve existing cases as unowned; migration order and rollout/rollback costs are documented.
- Focused policy/static/security tests and complete Maven verification are recorded accurately.

## Out of scope
Requester discovery/list pagination, UI/user guide (M05-PR17), authenticated intake (PR23), browser ownership assignment, historical backfill, ownership transfer/revocation, requester approvals/consent, information forms, notifications and live IdP/two-origin acceptance.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Current state

Issue #190 is OPEN and unblocked. Issue #141 is CLOSED, and its documentation and code pull requests #192 and #193 are merged. The connector-template path is therefore available to #190.

Issue #190 has no linked implementation pull request or issue-specific CI result. It does not carry `ready-for-agent`. Removing the stale blocker does not claim that the per-tenant signal design is implemented or verified.

## Proven

- The current `main` branch includes the prerequisite #141 work.
- Pull requests #192 and #193 are merged.
- No open blocking issue is declared for #190.

## Unknown

The per-tenant signal topics, per-tenant signal groups, Kafka ACL changes, generator changes, and two-tenant recovery test remain unimplemented or unverified. These acceptance items must still pass before #190 can close.

## Historical evidence

The previous issue body is retained verbatim below. Its checked #141 dependency and related sentences describe the earlier planning state. They are historical and must not be read as a current blocker after #141 merged.

## Authorized scope amendment (2026-08-28)

Hari authorized issue #190 to correct the public artifacts that would otherwise retain the removed shared signal topic. Issue #190 now also owns:

- `tests/Lexfield.Connect.Tests/Snapshots/README.md`
- `docs/diagrams/incremental-snapshot-channels.drawio`

Hari further authorized PR #271 to include the blueprint correction on 2026-08-28. Hari then supplied two review corrections for the diagram and connector-test wording. The repository correction ratchet requires the general rules behind those corrections to land in `docs/agents/writing-style.md` in this open PR. The change adds current-state notes beside protected historical text; it does not edit or delete human-authored blueprint lines. Issue #250 retains its separate `docs/specs/11-infra-disposable.md` follow-up.

Issue #258 already has a blocking edge from #190 and owns the snapshot README as follow-up documentation. That edge makes the overlap explicit. Issue #190 will update the README with the behavior so the implementation does not merge with false operator guidance; #258 remains open for Hari to reconcile after the linked pull requests exist.

The updated contract-documentation forecast is 11 files and at most 470 changed lines: the two existing specification files, the snapshot README, two Draw.io sources, and four committed renders. The implementation forecast remains 10 files and at most 500 changed lines.

<details>
<summary>Previous issue body (verbatim)</summary>

## Current state

Open and blocked by #141, with no linked implementation pull request. The current `main` branch still has one shared `connect-signals` topic and the literal `kafka-signal` group in the connector template and Kafka ACLs. A signal topic is a Kafka stream carrying Debezium control commands; a consumer group stores a consumer's progress bookmark. The proposed per-tenant topics and groups are not implemented or verified.

## Context

This is the control path for incremental snapshots, where an operator sends a command to one tenant's Debezium connector. SQL Server CDC records committed database changes in CDC tables. Debezium reads those records and publishes events to Kafka, while its signal consumer reads the control command; that signal consumer must not let one tenant advance another tenant's command bookmark.

## Why this matters

Separate topic and group state prevents a running tenant connector from skipping a command intended for a stopped tenant. The issue remains blocked until #141 releases the connector path it owns.

## Historical evidence

The text below is retained from the original issue as historical evidence and planning context. For open work, unchecked acceptance items and unmerged plans are not evidence of completion.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Short answer

Give every tenant's Debezium connector its own Kafka signal topic and its own
signal consumer group.

An operator writes a command such as `execute-snapshot` to the tenant's signal
topic. A Kafka consumer inside Debezium reads that command. The consumer-group
ID is the name of Debezium's bookmark in Kafka's `__consumer_offsets` internal
topic. The bookmark tells that connector which signal command to read next
after a restart.

The current configuration gives all tenant connectors one shared topic,
`connect-signals`, and does not set `signal.kafka.groupId`. Debezium therefore
uses its default group ID, `kafka-signal`, for every connector. The connectors
filter commands by Kafka message key, but they still share the same committed
bookmark. One connector can move that bookmark past a command that another,
stopped connector has not seen.

This ticket removes that shared state. A tenant's commands and signal bookmark
must be independent of every other tenant.

## Who uses the signal path

| Component | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Platform operator or operations script | Writes an `execute-snapshot`, `stop-snapshot`, `pause-snapshot`, or `resume-snapshot` command to the selected tenant's signal topic. |
| Debezium inside Kafka Connect | Runs one Kafka signal consumer for each tenant connector and acts only on messages whose key matches that connector's `topic.prefix`. |
| Kafka group coordinator | Stores each signal consumer's committed topic position under its `signal.kafka.groupId` in `__consumer_offsets`. |
| SQL Server signaling table | Stores the OPEN and CLOSE watermarks Debezium needs while an incremental snapshot is running. The Kafka signal starts the work; the SQL table controls snapshot-window deduplication. |
| Downstream application consumer | Does not read the signal topic. Its consumer group and output-topic offsets are unrelated to Debezium's signal consumer. |

The signal topic is a connector control path. It is not a way to reset or
resynchronize a new downstream Kafka consumer group. A downstream group replays
retained Kafka events by starting at the earliest retained offset or by having
its own offsets reset.

## Current failure example

```text
1. Tenant A's connector is stopped.
2. An operator writes a Tenant A snapshot command at offset 20 of connect-signals.
3. Tenant B's connector reads offset 20.
4. Tenant B ignores the command because the key belongs to Tenant A.
5. Tenant B commits the shared kafka-signal group position as offset 21.
6. Tenant A restarts from the shared position, offset 21.
7. Tenant A never reads its command at offset 20.
```

Debezium 3.6.1.Final creates a Kafka consumer for the signal channel, defaults
its group ID to `kafka-signal`, enables automatic offset commits, and skips a
record when its key does not match the connector's logical name. Those
behaviors are useful when each connector has a separate topic or bookmark. The
current combination of one shared topic and one shared bookmark is the defect.

References:

- [Debezium 3.6 SQL Server signal configuration](https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/3.6/connectors/sqlserver.html)
- [Debezium 3.6 signaling channels](https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/3.6/configuration/signalling.html)
- [Debezium 3.6.1.Final Kafka signal consumer implementation](https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/v3.6.1.Final/debezium-connector-common/src/main/java/io/debezium/pipeline/signal/channels/KafkaSignalChannel.java)
- [Apache Kafka consumer offset tracking](https://kafka.apache.org/43/implementation/distribution/)

## Target design

The three build-scale tenants get these independent resources:

| Tenant | Signal topic | Debezium signal group | Required Kafka message key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lexfield-001` | `connect-signals-lexfield-001` | `kafka-signal-lexfield-001` | `tenant-lexfield-001` |
| `lexfield-002` | `connect-signals-lexfield-002` | `kafka-signal-lexfield-002` | `tenant-lexfield-002` |
| `lexfield-003` | `connect-signals-lexfield-003` | `kafka-signal-lexfield-003` | `tenant-lexfield-003` |

The three names have different jobs:

- `signal.kafka.topic` selects the Kafka topic that holds this tenant's commands.
- `signal.kafka.groupId` gives this connector an independent command bookmark.
- The Kafka message key remains the connector's `topic.prefix`; Debezium rejects a different key even when the command was written to the correct topic.

For example, the generated connector configuration for `lexfield-002` must
contain:

```json
{
  "topic.prefix": "tenant-lexfield-002",
  "signal.kafka.topic": "connect-signals-lexfield-002",
  "signal.kafka.groupId": "kafka-signal-lexfield-002"
}
```

The operator must write the command to `connect-signals-lexfield-002` with the
Kafka key `tenant-lexfield-002`.

## Behavior

When this ticket merges:

1. The connector generator derives a unique signal topic and signal group from
   every manifest tenant ID.
2. The disposable Kafka chart creates one single-partition signal topic for
   each of the three build-scale tenants and no shared `connect-signals` topic.
3. The Connect Kafka identity can read the `connect-signals-` topic prefix and
   the `kafka-signal-` group prefix.
4. The operations Kafka identity can write the `connect-signals-` topic prefix.
5. A signal queued while one tenant connector is stopped remains available to
   that connector even when another tenant processes its own signals.
6. Documentation tells a first-time operator how to select the topic and key,
   and how to distinguish the signal offset from the connector's SQL LSN in
   `connect-offsets`.

## Blocked by

- [x] #141
- [x] #172

Issue #141 owns `connect/connectors/` while it removes the obsolete custom SMT.
It must close before this ticket edits the connector template and golden files.

Issue #172 also edits `docs/specs/01-wire-format.md`, which this ticket declares,
in a disjoint region: #172 edits the event-envelope section near the top of the
file, while this ticket edits the signal-topic and offset text near the end. The
edge records that #172 merges first and this ticket then rebases its
wire-format edits onto the result, resolving any textual conflict at that point.
Added 2026-08-28 at Hari's direction (session s2); see the overlap note on #172.

## Paths

- `.github/workflows/gitops-kind.yml` (expected topic names only)
- `connect/connectors/connector-template.json`
- `connect/connectors/tests/connector-configs.golden`
- `connect/connectors/Lexfield.ConnectorGenerator.Tests/ConnectorGeneratorTests.cs`
- `connect/connectors/README.md`
- `infra/disposable/kafka/topics.yaml`
- `infra/disposable/kafka/users.yaml`
- `infra/disposable/kafka/README.md`
- `tests/Lexfield.Connect.Tests/Snapshots/IncrementalSnapshotFixture.cs`
- `tests/Lexfield.Connect.Tests/Snapshots/IncrementalSnapshotTests.cs`
- `docs/specs/01-wire-format.md` (signal topics and offset explanation only)
- `docs/specs/30-connect.md` (signal configuration and verification row only)

## Verification

Method: containers

Run the connector-generator tests:

```text
dotnet test connect/connectors/Lexfield.ConnectorGenerator.Tests/Lexfield.ConnectorGenerator.Tests.csproj
```

The golden output and focused assertions must prove that all three generated
connectors have different `signal.kafka.topic` and `signal.kafka.groupId`
values derived from their tenant IDs.

Run the incremental-snapshot container tests:

```text
dotnet test tests/Lexfield.Connect.Tests/Lexfield.Connect.Tests.csproj --filter FullyQualifiedName~Snapshots
```

The container test must run two tenant connectors. Stop Tenant A's connector,
write a command to Tenant A's topic, let Tenant B process a command from Tenant
B's topic, and then restart Tenant A. Tenant A must process its queued command.
Tenant B must not re-snapshot because of Tenant A's command.

The `gitops-kind` workflow must reconcile exactly three signal topics and must
verify the updated topic and group ACL declarations without Azure.

Run the repository ASCII and documentation checks over the changed docs.

## Acceptance checklist

- [ ] Every generated tenant connector has `signal.kafka.topic=connect-signals-{tenantId}`
- [ ] Every generated tenant connector has `signal.kafka.groupId=kafka-signal-{tenantId}`
- [ ] The signal Kafka message key remains exactly equal to `topic.prefix`
- [ ] The three build-scale signal topics exist with one partition each
- [ ] The shared `connect-signals` topic and literal `kafka-signal` group ACL are removed
- [ ] Connect has read access to the per-tenant signal topic and group prefixes
- [ ] Operations has write access to the per-tenant signal topic prefix
- [ ] Generator tests fail if two tenant configurations share a signal topic or signal group
- [ ] A two-tenant container test proves one connector cannot consume or skip another tenant's command
- [ ] A command written while Tenant A is stopped is processed after Tenant A restarts, even after Tenant B processes another command
- [ ] The existing incremental snapshot still re-emits the expected Outbox row through the normal transform chain
- [ ] Operator documentation gives the exact topic, message key, and JSON command for one concrete tenant
- [ ] Documentation separates the signal bookmark in `__consumer_offsets` from the Debezium SQL LSN and snapshot state in `connect-offsets`
- [ ] Documentation states that the signal topic does not reset a downstream consumer group
- [ ] No deploy-time generated connector file, tenant manifest, secret, connection string, or environment ID is committed

## Out of scope

- Changing the SQL Server `dbo.DebeziumSignal` watermark table or its grants
- Resetting or renaming downstream application consumer groups
- Changing `__consumer_offsets` directly
- Automating Kafka topic creation beyond the three build-scale tenants; fleet automation beyond n=3 is deferred from v1
- Migrating commands that are already pending on the old shared topic
- Changing Kafka authentication; #129 owns the separate Entra OAuth planning decision
- Running Terraform apply, Terraform destroy, or a live Azure test

## Size forecast

Implementation and verification PR: 10 files and at most 500 changed lines.

Contract documentation PR: 2 files and at most 180 changed lines. Open this PR
before the implementation PR merges, link both PRs, and keep both under this
ticket so the documented operator path lands with the behavior it describes.

---

Area: `connect/` and `infra/disposable` | Verification: containers | No `ready-for-agent` label requested.

</details>

items.body:
## Current context

**Current state:** GitHub records this issue as closed.

**Context:** Azure SQL change data capture (CDC) records row changes for Debezium, the connector that reads SQL Server changes into Kafka. Kafka is the event log used by the platform. This issue covers the self-hosted CI runner, database permissions, and the security boundary for the capture path. **Why it matters:** the runner and grants determine whether the container checks can exercise the same tenant onboarding and CDC path used by the platform.

**Outcome:** PRs #160, #161, and #163 merged on 2026-08-25. They delivered the runner foundation and tenant database grants. Follow-on issue #68 was implemented in merged PRs #183, #186, and #187: the onboarding and connector path now carry the SQL Server signaling-table behavior and a Kafka Connect Filter, a record transform that drops signaling-table rows from the business event stream, needed for incremental snapshots. Current `main` at `fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f` is not one consistent public contract. `docs/blueprint.md` and `docs/specs/11-infra-disposable.md` still contain Outbox-only and read-only wording, while `tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql` and `connect/connectors/connector-template.json` contain the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` CDC and Filter path. The documentation correction remains an explicit follow-on boundary.

**Repository evidence:** [PR #160](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/160), [PR #161](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/161), and [PR #163](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/163) (merged 2026-08-25); [PR #183](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/183), [PR #186](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/186), and [PR #187](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/187) (merged 2026-08-27). The current source files are [tenant-onboarding.sql](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql) and [connector-template.json](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/connect/connectors/connector-template.json).

## Unknowns

The current code and public documentation disagree about whether SQL Server CDC includes `dbo.DebeziumSignal` and whether the connector has a write grant on that table. The repository does not claim live Azure snapshot behavior or production-scale proof here.

## Historical evidence

The original issue body is retained below unchanged. It preserves the original behavior, blockers, paths, verification method, acceptance checklist, scope boundaries, size forecast, dates, and links.

<details>
<summary>Original issue body</summary>

## Behavior

An onboarding runner reads the tenant manifest and applies, per tenant database: the tenant schema including the Outbox table with its TraceParent column and the DebeziumSignal watermarking table, CDC on `dbo.Outbox` only, Change Tracking on `dbo.WorkflowTask` only, `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` on the database, and the TenantInfo claim row. Running it twice changes nothing and throws nothing. This T-SQL is the canonical definition of the tenant schema for the whole repository.

## Blocked by

- #31 (D3)

## Paths

- `tools/onboarding/`
- `tests/Lexfield.TestSupport/`
- `tests/Lexfield.Onboarding.Tests/`

## Verification

Method: containers

Run the runner against a Testcontainers SQL Server. Assert tables exist, including `dbo.DebeziumSignal`; `sys.databases.is_cdc_enabled`; a capture instance on `dbo.Outbox` and none on `dbo.WorkflowTask`; `sys.change_tracking_tables` contains `WorkflowTask` and nothing else; `sys.databases.snapshot_isolation_state` is on; the `TenantInfo` row holds the expected tenantId. Then run the whole thing a second time and assert nothing changed and nothing threw, which is the actual idempotency claim.

## Acceptance checklist

- [ ] `dbo.Outbox` is created with the nullable `TraceParent` column
- [ ] `dbo.DebeziumSignal` is created per tenant database for incremental-snapshot watermarking
- [ ] CDC is enabled on `dbo.Outbox` and on no other table
- [ ] Change Tracking is enabled on `dbo.WorkflowTask` and on no other table
- [ ] `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` is enabled on each tenant database
- [ ] The grant of INSERT and SELECT on `dbo.DebeziumSignal` only, to the connector identity, is authored in the canonical onboarding T-SQL; business and CDC tables stay read-only. Its execution against a real Entra user is verified in the live user-creation ticket
- [ ] The `TenantInfo` row holds the tenantId from the manifest
- [ ] A second run of the whole runner changes nothing and throws nothing, asserted rather than argued
- [ ] TestSupport switched to execute the canonical onboarding scripts; provisional DDL deleted

## Out of scope

- `CREATE USER FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER` and the execution of its grants (including the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` grant), which need a real Entra-backed server and are a separate live ticket. The grant T-SQL is authored here as part of the canonical scripts; only its execution is out of scope
- Connector registration, which is the connect area
- Any change to the schema contract itself; this ticket implements the contract, it does not redesign it

## Size forecast

8 files, 420 lines

---

Area: `infra/disposable` | Wave 2 | Plan id `D4` | Generated from `docs/specs/` by /to-tickets.

</details>
