items.title: Spike: conversational agent app (tacit) — Slack connector, assertion store, external MCP as first integration

labels.name: wontfix
labels.description: This will not be worked on

items.body:
## What

A demo app in this repo: an agent that lives in the company's chat tool, answers questions grounded in a business model it maintains, and asks questions to fill the gaps in that model.

This spike builds the thinnest end-to-end slice: **Slack in → agent loop → external MCP → answer with provenance**, plus the storage shape the model will need.

The first test tenant is a small internal team with an existing MCP endpoint — near-zero friction and real tools to hit. That validates the plumbing, **not** the business-modelling thesis: a handful of people have no tacit-knowledge problem and nobody there wonders who approves what. The thesis gets tested later, at a customer with enough headcount for the question to be real.

## Placement decisions (already made, don't relitigate in the spike)

- **App, not kernel.** Lives alongside `ticket0`. Two apps is not enough evidence to extract a channel abstraction into the kernel. Revisit when a second app has used the adapter without needing a special case.
- **Slack is a connector**, not app code. The connector owns transport, credentials, per-tenant install and webhook ingress. The app owns conversation semantics and rendering.
- **Identity mapping does not live in the app.** Slack workspace → tenant belongs to the connector. Slack user → Substrat identity belongs in AuthHero as an upstream IdP link. Email matching is not acceptable — it breaks on guest accounts and shared mailboxes, and every lookup must run as the user.
- **Model-agnostic runtime.** The agent loop uses the platform's default model abstraction. No vendor hardcoded in the app.

## Scope

### 1. Slack connector

- [ ] App manifest checked into the repo
- [ ] HMAC-SHA256 request verification (`v0:timestamp:body`, WebCrypto — no Bolt)
- [ ] Webhook ingress: tenant resolution from `team_id` **before** tenant context exists (this is the piece that cannot live in an app)
- [ ] Idempotency on retries (`X-Slack-Retry-Num`)
- [ ] Fast ack within 3s, async execution, `chat.update` to replace the placeholder
- [ ] OAuth install flow, credentials stored per tenant

**What the connector contract has today, and what this adds.** The registration in `apps/control-plane/src/connectors.ts` already carries a webhook ingress (`callback`, #96 — Scrive uses it) and a browser consent round (`consent`, the Fortnox connect flow), so neither ingress nor OAuth install is new in kind. But the ingress that exists is the wrong **shape** for Slack, in three ways, and each one is a contract change rather than a connector implementation:

1. **Routing.** Today's ingress is authenticated by a per-connection token minted into the URL (`route` is a `:param` pattern; the handler gets only `c.req.param()`). Slack has one Request URL per app, and the tenant is in the *body* (`team_id`). The handler needs the raw body and the headers, and resolves the connection itself.
2. **Verification.** The signature is over the raw body with a provider-wide signing secret, not a URL token. The contract needs a way to hand the handler the unparsed bytes before anything JSON-parses them.
3. **Response.** The worker awaits `handle()` and answers a fixed `{ ok: true }`. Slack needs the handler's own response (the `url_verification` challenge echo; a 200 within 3s) and the work continued via `waitUntil`. Today's shape — verify, then run the whole reconcile inline — is right for Scrive and would time out here.

So the spike adds a second ingress shape beside `callback`, not a replacement: provider-global route, raw request in, response out, deferred execution. The payments connector that comes later wants the same three things, so this is the right change to make anyway.

### 2. Agent runtime (in the app, for now)

- [ ] Normalise inbound to an internal message (tenant, user, conversation, thread ref, text)
- [ ] Tool registry + agent loop, running on the platform default model
- [ ] Neutral render primitives — keep to five: text, key/value facts, choice buttons, form, link-with-source. Do not build a universal card abstraction covering both Block Kit and Adaptive Cards.
- [ ] Every answer echoes the exact call it made (target, metric, interval) — provenance is not a later feature

**Note on the model abstraction:** the runtime stays model-agnostic, but tool-selection quality varies sharply between models and an agent loop with a dozen tools is where the weak ones fall apart. Pin a specific model for the evaluation below so the numbers are reproducible, and record which one. If the default model can't hold the loop, that's a finding about the platform default, not about this app.

### 3. Storage

- [ ] **Assertion table**, append-only: subject, predicate, object, who said it, when, source, supersedes. Never overwrite. Contradictions are the finding; overwriting destroys them, and append-only is also what makes "delete everything person X said" possible.
- [ ] **Entity registry**: canonical id + external ids per system, with provenance on each mapping. Without this a second source collapses the whole thing into string matching.
- [ ] Naive projection over the assertions. Always regenerable — change the conflict rules, recompute from the log.
- [ ] Visibility class per assertion, filtered at query time by role. Derived assertions do **not** inherit source permissions.

D1 / SQLite per tenant. Not a graph database — the graph is small and traversals are shallow, recursive CTEs are enough.

### 4. First MCP integration

- [ ] MCP client, **read-only**, no write tools
- [ ] Where the target system holds a large end-user table: lookups in DM only, never in a channel; masked by default, full details on explicit request, every lookup logged on our side. Slack retention is an untracked export path and this has to be closed before the pattern is reused anywhere.

## Out of scope

Teams. Additional source systems. Vector search (start with FTS5). Assertion expiry. Write tools. The elicitation/question-asking mode — this spike is answering only.

## Prerequisite

Point the target MCP at an off-the-shelf agent client and run 20 real questions before writing any of this. Unclear tool descriptions, overlapping tools and wrong-target selection all survive into our own runtime and are far more expensive to find there. This also validates that the MCP surface works for external agents, which is a separate product requirement.

## Acceptance

Not "does it work". Measure:

- tool selection accuracy over 20 real questions, on a named model
- does it abstain when it should
- does it guess date ranges
- **does anyone other than the author use it in week 3**

## Naming

`tacit` is the name — it names the thesis (the knowledge that matters is the unwritten kind), it is a real word that works in Swedish and English, and in lowercase it sits beside `ticket0` without forcing the product-vs-module naming question the suite currently leaves open. `Ora` was the working name and is dropped. Connectors stay functional (`slack`, `teams`, `google-drive`).

## Related

- #96 — the webhook ingress this extends
- #112 / #131 — the Substrat-side MCP surface (this spike is a *client* of an external MCP, the inverse direction)

items.title: Connector pollers create a DB scope and load config for every tenant every tick, including tenants with no config row
items.body:
## Summary

Every connector polling service, on every tick, fans out over **all** tenants and — for each one — creates a DI scope, sets the tenant, resolves `NocturneDbContext`, and calls `LoadForTenantAsync` (a database round trip). Only *after* that does it check `config.Enabled` and whether the sync interval has elapsed.

The result is a fixed per-minute database load proportional to `tenants × connector types`, almost all of it for tenants that have no configuration for that connector at all.

## Measured

On a deployment with 66 active tenants and 13 connector polling services:

| | |
|---|---|
| `connector_configurations` load calls | **858/min** (66 × 13) |
| `connector_configurations` rows that actually exist | **100** |
| Wasted loads | **~758/min — 8.6×** |

The supporting scope churn, from `pg_stat_statements`:

- `RESET app.current_tenant_id` — **9,423/min (157/s)**
- `DISCARD ALL` — **9,409/min**
- 4× `set_config(...)` per scope

`PollInterval` is 1 minute (`ConnectorBackgroundService.cs:142`), and all pollers share `StartupDelay = 5s`, so they converge on the same second — 22 sync-starts in a single second is observable in logs.

The disabled path is the worst case: it returns **without recording anything**, so a tenant with no config row for a given connector pays a full scope plus config load every tick, forever, and never becomes cheaper.

## Why the obvious fix does not work

Fanning out only over tenants that have a config row for the connector is blocked by row-level security:

```
 relname                  | relrowsecurity | relforcerowsecurity
 connector_configurations | t              | t
 tenants                  | f              | f
```

`tenant_isolation` is `tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id'), '')::uuid`. The polling loop's lookup context is leased with `TenantId = Guid.Empty`, which resolves to NULL and therefore matches zero rows. The existing tenant enumeration only works because `tenants` has RLS disabled.

The sanctioned cross-tenant pattern, `CreateTenantPinnedContextAsync(tenantId)`, is strictly per-tenant — there is no batch read path that can answer "which tenants have a row for connector X" in one query.

## Possible directions

Each of these touches tenant isolation, so none should be picked without discussion:

1. **A non-RLS enrollment projection** — a small table listing `(tenant_id, connector_name)` with RLS off, maintained on the write path. Needs a migration and write-path consistency guarantees.
2. **A narrow RLS policy exception** for a read-only enrollment query.
3. **A shared pinned-context strategy** usable across independent hosted services.

A purely in-memory next-due cache was considered and rejected: it saves roughly 80 of the 858, because it cannot skip *unconfigured* tenants, which are the bulk of the waste.

Note also that `RequestImmediateSync` is wired only to realtime push events — nothing nudges a poller when a user saves a connector config in the UI. Any backoff-based approach would therefore regress enable latency unless that is addressed too.

## Caveat on impact

The 8.6× figure is a **load** reduction, not a demonstrated reduction in connection residency. It is the leading hypothesis for why a single API instance sits at ~88 pooled connections against 2 concurrent active queries, but that causal link is unmeasured. Instrumenting per-tenant sync duration and a connection high-water mark should come first — no connector currently logs its own duration, so the timings available today are whole-tick spans.

Found while auditing database CPU and connection usage; not triggered by any incident.

items.body:
## Source research

- Beszel research and information architecture: ncosentino/pitcrew#20
- Runner-host resilience umbrella: ncosentino/pitcrew#8

## Status

**Completed and released in [Dashboard v0.6.0](https://github.com/ncosentino/pitcrew-dashboard/releases/tag/v0.6.0).**

Delivered sequence:

1. #42 — current contract-12 manager operation, subsystem-health, and capacity-deficit projection.
2. #39 — atomic, bounded historical telemetry/events with measured retention, durable identity, hourly rollups, provenance floors, and accessible history views.
3. #40 — restart-safe debounced incidents, acknowledgement, resolution, bounded immutable history, tenant isolation, and direct evidence links.

## Delivered guarantees

- SQLite and the existing tenant/auth model remain the only control-plane storage and authorization boundary.
- Connectors remain outbound-only; container mode remains read-only.
- Current and historical evidence preserve unknown, stale, unavailable, expired, incomplete, and truncated semantics.
- Alert pending timers survive restart.
- Stale or unavailable evidence cannot create a specific diagnosis or falsely prove recovery.
- Incidents never trigger automatic recovery.
- Autoscaled capacity below configured maximum is not itself unhealthy.
- Historical and incident storage are bounded by age and deterministic per-profile/node/database or per-tenant ceilings.

items.body:
## Summary

A dashboard whose connector is down does not go to an error — every widget sits on its skeleton for 30 s (60 s for the second half of a 12-widget dashboard), and while it waits the rest of the app freezes: clicking **Connections** in the sidebar took **52.8 s** to navigate, and the Connections page then shows every connector stuck with nothing visibly happening.

Found on `release/1.5` during a live demo, with two connections whose Neo4j hosts are unreachable.

## Root causes (three, stacked)

**1. The Neo4j driver retries a dead host for 30 s.** `Neo4jConnectionModule._runCypherQuery` runs through `session.executeRead` / `executeWrite`. Managed transactions retry `ServiceUnavailable` / `SessionExpired` for `maxTransactionRetryTime`, which `Neo4jAuthenticationModule.createDriver` never sets, so the driver default of 30 000 ms applies (`neo4j-driver-core/lib/internal/transaction-executor.js`, `DEFAULT_MAX_RETRY_TIME_MS`). `checkConnection` uses a plain `session.run`, which does not retry — that is why, against the same dead host, measured in the same session:

| call | route | time to fail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| connection test | `POST /api/connections/:id/test` | **100 ms** |
| widget query | `POST /api/query` | **30 888 ms** (→ 502 `CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE`) |

The connect failure is instant; the 30 s is pure retry backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s) against a host that was never going to answer. #1678 pinned `connectionAcquisitionTimeout` for the same reason and missed this one.

**2. Widget queries are never aborted.** `use-widget-query.ts` and `use-seed-query.ts` call `fetch("/api/query")` without TanStack Query's `signal`, so unmounting a dashboard leaves its requests in flight. Browsers allow 6 connections per origin over HTTP/1.1: six hung queries own the whole pool, and the next page's RSC payload, `/api/connections` and the six connection tests queue behind them. Measured: `/connections?_rsc=…` `duration: 52 852 ms`, then every test finishing in <100 ms the instant the pool freed.

**3. A fresh page load knows nothing.** #1678's `connection-status-store` flags a dead connection after the first failure so siblings paint "Connector unavailable" at once — but it is per-tab memory. Every reload, every other user and every auto-refresh cycle pays the full wait again. When the host black-holes packets (firewall, VPN down) rather than refusing them, that wait is the 30 s connect timeout and (1) does not help.

## Proposed fix

1. `connection/` — `maxTransactionRetryTime: 0` in `createDriver`. A dead host then fails a query as fast as it fails the connection test. Cost: a transient cluster error (leader switch, deadlock on a form write) surfaces instead of being retried by the driver; the widget recovers on the next refresh, and `noteQueryOutcome` already clears the flag on the first success.
2. `app/` — pass `signal` from the `queryFn` context into both `fetch` calls, so leaving a dashboard frees the connection pool.
3. `app/` — server-side short-TTL memo in the query route: after a `CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE` failure, answer that `connectionId` with the same 502 immediately for the next 30 s instead of dialling again. A successful connection test clears it. In-memory and per-process on purpose.

## Required tests

- **Integration (`connection/`, Testcontainers)** — a query through `runQuery` against a closed port fails in well under 5 s with a `ConnectorError`. Must fail (≈30 s) before the fix.
- **Unit (`connection/`)** — `createDriver` passes `maxTransactionRetryTime: 0`.
- **Unit (`app/`)** — `useWidgetQuery` and `useSeedQuery`: `fetch` receives the query's `AbortSignal`, and unmounting / `cancelQueries` aborts it.
- **Unit (`app/`)** — query route: after one `CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE` for a connection, the next request for it returns 502 with the same `reason` **without** calling `executeQuery`; after the TTL it dials again; a different connection is unaffected; the memo is keyed per tenant + connection; a query that reaches the database (rows or a syntax error) never sets it.
- **Unit (`app/`)** — a successful `POST /api/connections/:id/test` clears the memo.
- **E2E** — a dashboard on a connection pointing at a closed port shows "Connector unavailable" on every widget within 5 s, and clicking **Connections** mid-load navigates within 2 s. Assert the positive end state (#1748).

## Acceptance criteria

- Widgets on an unreachable Neo4j connector show "Connector unavailable" with the classifier's hint in < 2 s when the port is refused.
- Within the TTL, a reload of that dashboard shows the error immediately, including for a black-holed host.
- Navigating away from a loading dashboard is never blocked by its queries.
- Healthy connectors are unaffected; PostgreSQL behaviour is unchanged except for (2) and (3).
- A recovered connector is usable again within one TTL, or immediately after a successful test.

items.title: feat(hosting): Managed Mention deployments for organizations and communities
items.body:
## Product goal

Create **Managed Mention**: a paid hosting and operations offering for organizations, communities and institutions that want their own dedicated Mention deployment, custom domain and federated presence without having to run the infrastructure themselves.

The customer pays for:

- infrastructure
- isolation
- operations
- backups
- upgrades
- observability
- support
- optional custom-domain / enterprise integration work

The customer does **not** pay for privileged reach into the public Mention network, hidden access to user data, ranking advantages or moderation influence.

> Managed Mention sells infrastructure and operational responsibility, not attention.

## Important architectural stance

Do not turn the existing public Mention deployment into a loosely isolated multi-tenant SaaS simply because managed hosting needs customers.

The preferred initial model is **dedicated deployment per managed tenant/customer**, built from the same Mention codebase and configuration contracts.

This gives a much cleaner boundary for:

- data isolation
- backups/restores
- custom domains
- regional placement
- customer-specific scaling
- operational incidents
- export/exit

A future shared-control-plane optimization can be considered later, but the product contract should not depend on weak logical tenancy inside one database.

## Example customers

Managed Mention should fit cases such as:

- a university running `social.university.example`
- a municipality/public body running an official community network
- a nonprofit or cooperative running its own social instance
- a company running an internal/external community
- a publication running a branded social space
- a large creator/community needing dedicated capacity

The exact commercial/exemption policy is separate from the technical product. Organizations that qualify for Oxy licensing exemptions may still pay for optional hosting/operations if desired; licensing fee and managed-service fee are different concepts.

## Product surface

### Dedicated deployment

Each Managed Mention tenant receives a distinct deployment identity, including at minimum:

- canonical tenant id
- primary domain
- deployment region
- release channel/version
- database/data-plane resources
- object/media storage boundary
- cache/queue boundary where feasible
- federation identity/domain
- operational status

Do not use customer display name as an infrastructure identifier.

### Custom domain

Support customer domains such as:

- `social.example.org`
- `community.example.com`

Managed setup should include:

- DNS verification
- TLS certificate issuance/renewal
- canonical host configuration
- ActivityPub/WebFinger host correctness
- redirect/canonical policy
- email/domain ownership validation where needed

Domain ownership must be re-verified on sensitive changes.

## Branding

Allow limited customer branding without forking the product:

- instance/community name
- logo
- favicon/app icon where packaging supports it
- accent/theme tokens
- about text
- terms/contact links
- optional home/landing copy

Do not create a proprietary white-label fork path.

Breathe attribution requirements remain intact. A managed customer may have its own brand prominently displayed, while Mention/Oxy attribution remains available in the reachable location required by the license.

## Identity

### V1

Prefer keeping Oxy identity/session infrastructure as the canonical account/authorization layer so Managed Mention does not invent a second identity system.

The tenant config should define:

- which Oxy account(s) administer the managed deployment
- allowed signup policy
- optional domain/email restrictions
- invitation policy
- tenant-level roles/capabilities where they are truly deployment administration rather than ordinary social account authority

### Enterprise SSO later

If SAML/OIDC enterprise SSO is added, integrate it through Oxy identity rather than teaching every Managed Mention deployment to become its own identity provider/client stack.

Avoid tenant-local passwords if Oxy can remain the identity authority.

## Public vs private deployments

Managed Mention should support explicit deployment modes.

### Public federated

- publicly reachable
- normal ActivityPub federation according to policy
- public profile/post surfaces where author visibility permits
- optional public registration

### Public but restricted signup

- public reading/federation
- signup by invite/domain/admin approval

### Private/community deployment

Potential future mode:

- authenticated access required for most content
- federation disabled or tightly scoped
- not discoverable as a normal public instance

Do not treat `private` as a UI toggle only. It changes indexing, federation, media, caches, robots, previews and API authorization and needs its own security review.

## Federation

Federation is a core reason to offer Managed Mention.

Every public managed deployment should be capable of interoperating with:

- Mention's public service
- other Managed Mention deployments
- Mastodon / compatible ActivityPub servers
- wider Fediverse according to existing connector behaviour

Tenant/customer commercial status must have **zero effect** on federation ranking or reach inside the public Mention service.

A managed instance is another federated participant, not a preferred advertiser.

### Federation policy

Tenant administrators may need configurable federation controls:

- allow/block instances
- media proxy policy
- discovery visibility
- federation enable/disable where supported
- moderation policy hooks

Do not let tenant admins override another instance's moderation decisions outside normal federation semantics.

## Data isolation

This is a hard requirement.

For dedicated deployments:

- [ ] Separate PostgreSQL database/cluster or clearly dedicated database boundary per tenant.
- [ ] Separate media/object-storage prefix/bucket policy with tenant-scoped credentials.
- [ ] Separate cache namespaces/instances with no unkeyed cross-tenant access.
- [ ] Separate secrets.
- [ ] Separate backup artifacts and encryption context where practical.
- [ ] Tenant id/domain must never be inferred from untrusted client headers without an authenticated routing boundary.

If any infrastructure is shared, document exactly what is shared and prove tenant scoping in tests/policy.

## Control plane vs data plane

Introduce a clear conceptual separation.

### Managed control plane

Owns operational metadata only:

- tenant/deployment id
- customer/admin Oxy account
- plan/capacity
- region
- desired Mention version/release channel
- domain verification state
- infrastructure status
- backup policy
- billing entitlement
- support/SLA metadata

### Tenant data plane

Owns the social product data:

- posts
- feeds
- engagement
- notifications
- federation state
- local Mention tables
- media references

The control plane should not casually ingest raw tenant social content.

Support staff access to tenant data must be exceptional, auditable and scoped to explicit support/security needs.

## Provisioning

A new Managed Mention deployment should be provisionable from a deterministic config rather than manual SSH work.

Suggested flow:

1. customer/admin chooses deployment name, domain and region
2. billing/entitlement established
3. control plane creates deployment record
4. infrastructure is provisioned
5. database migrations run
6. Mention backend/frontend/MCP components deploy
7. health checks pass
8. domain is verified and attached
9. federation/WebFinger smoke tests pass
10. deployment becomes active

Provisioning should be idempotent and resumable after partial failure.

## Deployment configuration contract

Create a typed config surface for Managed Mention rather than patching source files per customer.

Possible categories:

```ts
type ManagedMentionConfig = {
  tenantId: string;
  publicBaseUrl: string;
  apiBaseUrl: string;
  federationDomain: string;
  region: string;
  signupPolicy: 'open' | 'invite' | 'approval' | 'domain_restricted';
  branding: ManagedBranding;
  federation: ManagedFederationPolicy;
  limits: ManagedCapacityLimits;
};
```

Secrets must not live in this public/non-secret config object.

## Upgrades

Managed Mention should sell the fact that the customer does not need to operate upgrades themselves.

Need release channels such as:

- stable
- delayed/stable-plus-N-days
- optionally preview for test tenants

Upgrade process:

- preflight checks
- backup/snapshot before destructive migrations where appropriate
- migration
- deploy
- health/E2E checks
- rollback policy when schema allows
- clear handling for irreversible migrations

Do not let customer deployments drift indefinitely into unsupported forks.

## Source availability and customer modifications

Managed Mention is based on a source-available codebase whose commercial terms still require corresponding source/attribution.

Therefore:

- provide a reachable way for users/customers to identify the deployed Mention version/source
- customer-specific modifications deployed by Oxy must remain publishable under the applicable license obligations
- no `enterprise secret fork` architecture
- prefer configuration, plugins and documented public interfaces over one-off source divergence

If a customer requires custom functionality, first ask whether it belongs in upstream Mention, a reusable extension point or an external integration.

## Backups

Managed service must define actual backup semantics.

At minimum:

- automated database backups
- media/object-storage durability strategy
- retention schedule
- encrypted backups
- restore testing
- documented RPO/RTO targets per plan if sold

A backup that has never been restore-tested is not sufficient for a paid managed offering.

### Restore

Support:

- full tenant restore
- restore to replacement infrastructure
- operator-visible restore status
- prevention of accidental federation duplicate emissions after disaster recovery

The federation/idempotency implications of restoring an older database snapshot need explicit testing.

## Export and exit

Avoid lock-in as a business model.

Customers should be able to leave Managed Mention.

Provide a documented export/offboarding path including, where technically and legally applicable:

- database export
- media export
- source/version/config needed to redeploy
- domain migration guidance
- federation identity/migration considerations
- account/content export using Mention/MTN portability

Do not deliberately make self-hosting harder to protect hosting revenue.

## Observability

Per deployment collect operational telemetry such as:

- health
- request/error rates
- latency
- queue depth
- DB resource pressure
- federation delivery failures
- storage use
- backup success/failure
- deployment version

Operational telemetry must not become a backdoor behavioural analytics product.

Do not centralize raw post bodies or private user activity merely because monitoring is easier that way.

## Privacy / support access

Define a support-access model before selling the service.

Recommended rules:

- default support has infrastructure visibility, not unrestricted social-data access
- content/data access requires an explicit elevated support workflow
- elevated access is time-bounded
- reason/ticket/customer context recorded
- access is auditable
- customer-visible audit where feasible
- never use tenant content to build advertising/marketing profiles

## Security

Managed hosting materially increases responsibility.

Need:

- tenant-scoped secrets
- automatic secret rotation support
- least-privilege service credentials
- patch management
- vulnerability response process
- DDoS/rate-limit strategy
- abuse handling
- audit logs for deployment-admin actions
- disaster-recovery runbook
- incident communication path

Tenant administrators must not receive cloud credentials that allow them to escape into another tenant/control plane.

## Capacity / plans

Commercial tiers may vary on infrastructure/service properties, for example:

- storage quota
- media bandwidth
- active users/capacity guidance
- dedicated compute size
- backup retention
- support response target
- region availability
- custom domain count

Plans must **not** vary:

- feed ranking priority in public Mention
- federation priority for commercial customers
- moderation outcome
- credibility/verification status
- access to unrelated user data

## Billing

Managed Mention can be recurring infrastructure/service billing.

Billing entitlement controls whether Oxy continues providing the managed service, not whether the customer's posts rank.

Non-payment flow must be humane and reversible:

1. payment failure notification
2. grace period
3. restrict administrative provisioning changes first where possible
4. eventual suspension according to contract
5. data retention/export window
6. deletion only after documented retention period

Do not instantly destroy customer data on a failed renewal.

## Moderation responsibilities

Managed deployments introduce an important policy split.

Document who is responsible for:

- local community rules
- illegal-content response
- federation blocklists
- reports by local users
- CrowdSource integration if enabled
- Oxy-level platform abuse/security rules

A customer may administer its own community rules without acquiring the ability to alter moderation on the public Mention service.

## MCP / AI

Each deployment may expose the Mention MCP surface if enabled.

Requirements:

- correct resource audience/base URL per deployment
- Oxy central authorization remains account/deployment scoped
- tokens for one Managed Mention deployment cannot be replayed against another
- capability catalog version must match deployed Mention version
- revocation remains live

Do not share one ambiguous MCP audience across managed tenants.

## Mobile apps

V1 does **not** need a separately branded App Store/Play Store binary for every customer.

Prefer:

- web/PWA/custom domain first
- universal Mention mobile client capable of opening/following managed/federated accounts where architecture allows

Per-customer native binaries are operationally expensive and should be a separate enterprise feature/issue if ever required.

## Infrastructure placement

The application changes belong in Mention, but provisioning modules may ultimately live in `oxy-infra` or the appropriate infrastructure repository.

This issue should define the product/application contract and then split infrastructure implementation into linked issues once the boundary is agreed.

Do not bury customer-specific shell scripts in the Mention repository as the final provisioning system.

## Implemented foundation evidence (2026-10-28)

Checked implementation items below identify source/configuration and regression coverage; they do **not** claim customer provisioning or operational acceptance. Acceptance criteria remain open until demonstrated end to end. Commercial terms and activation remain deferred.

- [Application foundation](https://github.com/OxyHQ/Mention/commit/0287aeafff788313f8aafbfe9c2f64e326aad268): typed manifest, canonical origins, branding/admission/discovery and distinct-domain tests. Live WebFinger/ActivityPub interoperability is still a separate gate.
- [API/worker lifecycle](https://github.com/OxyHQ/Mention/pull/1647): split roles, strict Redis startup/readiness and idempotent drain. Public Mention still uses its combined default.
- Infrastructure [data plane](https://github.com/OxyHQ/oxy-infra/pull/406), [backup policy](https://github.com/OxyHQ/oxy-infra/pull/407), [runtime services](https://github.com/OxyHQ/oxy-infra/pull/408), and [database bootstrap](https://github.com/OxyHQ/oxy-infra/pull/409) are merged, with mock Terraform plans and 23 local PostgreSQL 17/TLS/AWS-boundary tests for bootstrap. No customer resources were applied. Backup declarations are not restore evidence.
- [Canonical Oxy registration](https://github.com/OxyHQ/oxy/pull/2012) is merged: transactional operator-only owner/origin/workload bindings, drift/revocation guards and durable metadata. This does not provision a customer or grant blanket cross-tenant Files access.

Still required: complete provisioning orchestration and constrained operator authority; live DNS/federation; two-tenant media/data isolation; real backup/restore/export; release/monitoring/support workflows; and the deferred commercial lifecycle. Activation order is empty database bootstrap → privileged PostGIS setup → application migrations. Do not install PostGIS before the empty-database ownership handoff.

## Implementation slices

### Phase A — make Mention deployment-configurable

- [x] typed non-secret deployment config
- [x] arbitrary canonical domain support
- [ ] ActivityPub/WebFinger correctness off non-`mention.earth` domains
- [x] branding config
- [x] signup-policy config
- [x] deployment/version/source-info surface
- [x] tests with at least two distinct domains

### Phase B — dedicated tenant provisioning

- [x] infrastructure template/module
- [ ] tenant-specific Postgres
- [ ] tenant-specific media storage boundary
- [ ] secrets
- [x] deployment health checks
- [ ] automated migrations
- [ ] provisioning state machine

### Phase C — custom domains + federation

- [ ] domain verification
- [ ] TLS automation
- [ ] canonical host setup
- [ ] WebFinger/ActivityPub integration tests
- [ ] federation smoke test against public Mention / external AP instance

### Phase D — operations

- [ ] backups
- [ ] restore automation/test
- [ ] monitoring/alerts
- [ ] release channels
- [ ] upgrade/rollback workflow
- [ ] support-access audit flow

### Phase E — commercial lifecycle

- [ ] managed-service entitlement
- [ ] grace/suspension/retention state machine
- [ ] plan/capacity limits
- [ ] customer/admin dashboard
- [ ] export/offboarding

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two Managed Mention deployments can run simultaneously on distinct domains without sharing social data.
- [ ] Each has its own database/data boundary and secrets.
- [ ] ActivityPub/WebFinger identities use the tenant's canonical domain correctly.
- [ ] A managed instance can federate with public Mention without receiving preferential ranking.
- [ ] Customer branding is configuration-driven and does not require a source fork.
- [ ] Oxy attribution/source requirements remain reachable.
- [ ] Provisioning is automated, idempotent and recoverable from partial failure.
- [ ] A deployment can be upgraded through a documented release workflow.
- [ ] Automated backups exist and a restore is tested.
- [ ] Support access is scoped/auditable rather than permanent unrestricted database access.
- [ ] A customer can export/offboard without Oxy deliberately withholding their data/source/config.
- [ ] Non-payment follows grace/retention policy rather than immediate destruction.
- [ ] Managed plan/billing state is absent from public Mention feed/search/recommendation ranking.

## Non-goals

- selling priority federation delivery
- selling feed/search ranking
- giving customers access to unrelated Mention user data
- proprietary closed-source enterprise forks
- mandatory per-customer native mobile binaries in v1
- a social-media-management dashboard for third-party networks
- using monitoring as behavioural ad analytics

## Open decisions

- First supported deployment modes: public federated only, or restricted-signup at launch too?
- First infrastructure regions.
- Dedicated DB instance vs dedicated DB on shared cluster for lower plans.
- Whether Managed Mention customers get optional dedicated MCP hostnames from day one.
- SLA/RPO/RTO tiers.
- Where the managed control plane lives: Oxy Console, separate service or another existing Oxy administrative surface.
- How much tenant-level moderation policy is configurable in v1.

items.title: [P0] Enforce authenticated tenant ownership for ZAIcoder workspaces and billable API
items.body:
## Severity: P0 — caller-controlled workspace ownership and unauthenticated billable API

### Verified Main evidence

Current Main: `caa20794c1763470aa3d21bd80ef04396b1be340`.

Read-only inspection found:

- `apps/zaicoder/web/server/http.mjs` (blob `7aa7d41f8020633bf7e06b2c2ced118b5df1eea8`) has no user authentication/session middleware before `POST /api/workspaces`, `GET /api/workspaces/:id`, `POST /api/chat`, `POST /api/chat/stream`, or `POST /api/files`.
- `tenantOwner(request)` takes the caller-supplied `X-Tenant-Id` header as the owner.
- Workspace creation uses `owner: tenantOwner(request) || input.owner`, so a caller without the header can choose `input.owner` in the JSON body.
- Workspace reads and file linking use the caller-supplied header as the ownership assertion.
- `apps/zaicoder/web/server/workspace-store.mjs` (blob `dd040a4a59d4fa8ebad572250e26e1fe5770dc68`) skips owner comparison when no owner is supplied (`assertOwner` returns when owner is absent); `ensure()` accepts caller-supplied owner and defaults missing owner to `local`.
- The chat/file proxy uses the server-side `Z_PLATFORM_SERVICE_TOKEN`; that authenticates the app to the AI Gateway, not the end user. No user auth gate prevents unauthorized AI spend or file upload.

The server defaults to loopback, and this source finding does not assert that it is currently public. It is not safe for multi-tenant exposure behind a proxy until the identity boundary is implemented and direct-origin access is controlled.

### Required remediation

1. Authenticate every non-health route using the selected ZIDP OIDC/session integration or a cryptographically verified trusted-edge assertion.
2. Derive tenant and subject from the verified principal. Never accept `X-Tenant-Id` or `input.owner` as authority. Reject mismatches rather than silently trusting caller data.
3. Require an authenticated owner on every workspace read, create, update, delete, file-link and cleanup operation. Remove the unauthenticated `local` owner fallback from network-facing paths.
4. Enforce tenant ownership in the metadata service/database itself, not only in the HTTP adapter. Make owner predicates part of atomic reads/writes and prevent TOCTOU ownership changes.
5. Protect chat, streaming and file upload before invoking the AI Gateway. Add per-tenant/user rate limits, request budgets, upload quotas, timeouts and idempotent file-linking.
6. Add negative tests for missing/invalid/expired identity, forged `X-Tenant-Id`, forged body `owner`, known workspace ID from another tenant, cross-tenant file linking, direct-origin access, and unauthenticated AI-provider calls.
7. Audit logs must record verified subject/tenant and request ID without prompts, tokens or uploaded content.

### Acceptance gates

- Tenant A cannot create/read/update/link files into Tenant B's workspace by changing a header or body field.
- Missing/invalid identity fails before disk/metadata writes, file upload or billable AI calls.
- Exact-head integration/security tests pass; independent review and signed provenance are verified.
- Effective Main protection requires independent approval and required checks.

### Safety

Use synthetic tenants and mocked AI/file providers only. Do not enable public traffic, call paid providers, or deploy this change to production from the issue. No user files, prompts or credentials are included here.

items.title: AEX- OVERVIEW
items.body:
# AEX Web — Developer Onboarding Guide

> This README is a practical, code-verified guide to the `aex-web` codebase (npm package name `bigfixaex`). Every claim below is backed by an exact file path (and line number where useful). Anything that could not be verified from the code is called out explicitly in [Unknowns / Areas Requiring Further Investigation](#unknowns--areas-requiring-further-investigation) instead of being guessed.

---

## Project Overview

**What this project does.** AEX Web is HCL's "Agent Experience" platform: a multi-tenant conversational-AI / chatbot + live-agent-assist web application. A single Node.js/Express server hosts:

- A server-rendered chat widget / bot UI (Handlebars views).
- An **admin/configuration console** (Vue 3 SPA, `src/`) — GenAI agent builder, workflow automation, RBAC, self-heal, learning console, live-agent-console admin, channel configuration, etc.
- A **live-agent console** (Vue 3 SPA, `src-agent/`) — the human-agent chat/dashboard UI used for live chat hand-off.
- A large library of **GenAI/LLM integrations** (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI cloud, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex/Gemini, custom LLM endpoints) plus an **A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol** server/client.
- A **Microsoft Bot Framework** connector layer (Teams, Slack, Telegram, Facebook, SMS, email, IVR/Twilio, Google Chat).
- ~50 pluggable **"tool" connectors** (Slack, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Jira, AWS/Azure/GCP services, databases, etc.) that GenAI agents can call as functions.
- Real-time features (live chat, agent transfer, workflow monitoring) over **Socket.IO**.

**Main purpose.** Let enterprise customers (tenants) configure and run AI-powered chatbots and live-agent-assist workflows across many channels, backed by a common admin console, RBAC, and a large set of external-system connectors.

**Main technologies/frameworks:**
- **Backend:** Node.js 24 (pinned in `package.json:205`, enforced at runtime in `app.js:5-8`), Express 4, Express-Handlebars, Socket.IO 4, Passport (LDAP/SAML/OIDC/IBM AppID), Redis (`redis`/`@redis/client`, standalone or cluster), MongoDB / IBM Cloudant / DynamoDB (pluggable via a "Dispatcher" abstraction), `botbuilder` (MS Bot Framework), `@a2a-js/sdk`.
- **Frontend:** Vue 3 + Vue Router + Pinia, built with Vite; two separate SPAs (`src/`, `src-agent/`) plus legacy jQuery/Materialize-based assets under `public/`.
- **Cloud SDKs:** AWS (`@aws-sdk/*`), Azure (`@azure/*`), IBM Cloud (`ibm-cos-sdk`, `@ibm-cloud/cloudant`, `ibmcloud-appid`).
- **Testing:** Vitest.
- **CI/CD:** Azure DevOps pipelines under `DevOps/` (SonarQube, Mend SCA, AppScan SAST, container security, image signing) — see `DevOps/README.md`.

---

## Project Structure

| Path | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `app.js` | The entire Express/Socket.IO app bootstrap (see [Application Startup Flow](#application-startup-flow)). |
| `dev.js` / `config-back.js` | `dev.js` hardcodes the local-dev tenant subdomain (`devplayground`). `config-back.js` is a **legacy/unused** Cloudant+Memcache config module, not read by current startup code. |
| `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js` | Loads all configuration and secrets (per-`AEX_ENV`), and creates the global `redisClient`. |
| `lib/corearchitecture.js` | Base class (`CoreArchitecture`) for per-session conversation handling; the canonical example of the `GLOBAL.Dispatcher` service-locator pattern. |
| `lib/scripts/dispatchers/` | The pluggable-backend abstraction layer: DB (`dbServices/`), GenAI (`cognitiveServices/`), object storage (`objectStorageServices/`), key vault, third-party/channel-dependent services. |
| `lib/scripts/` (everything else) | Business-logic modules: live-agent transfer/queueing, bot connectors, A2A protocol, GenAI prompting, workflows, notifications, LDAP client/sync, translation, etc. See [Core Modules](#core-modules). |
| `lib/socket/` | Socket.IO event handlers: `chat.js` (entry point), `liveAgentv2.js` (live-agent broker events), `notification.js`, `workflowMonitor.js`. |
| `routes/` | All HTTP routes, split into `unauthroutes.js` → `naclroutes.js` → `aclroutes.js` (mounted in that order — see [Application Architecture](#application-architecture)), plus ~40 feature subfolders (`genAI/`, `liveAgentConsole/`, `rbac/`, `lums/`, `channels/`, `workflows/`, etc.). |
| `middleware/` | `ldapRoleRefresh.js` (background LDAP role sync) and `rbac/` (permission middleware, static role/permission matrix, user-operation guards). |
| `models/` | Data-access classes. Either extend `models/base/index.js` (`BaseModel`, wraps the Dispatcher), call the Dispatcher directly (legacy prototype style, e.g. `models/customer.js`), or are pure-Redis models (e.g. `models/webNotifications.js`). |
| `tools/` | ~50 self-contained connector plugins (Slack, ServiceNow, AWS, databases, etc.) with a uniform `{name, fields, functions[]}` shape, invocable as LLM function-calling tools. |
| `src/` | Vue 3 SPA — the **admin/configuration console**, served at `/admin`. |
| `src-agent/` | Vue 3 SPA — the **live-agent console** (chat + live dashboard), served at `/agents`. |
| `views/` | Handlebars templates — legacy/auth pages, the server-rendered chat widget, login/SSO/OIDC pages. |
| `public/` | Static assets, including the legacy embeddable chat-widget bundle (built by `buildEngine/bundle.js`). |
| `buildEngine/` | Build/post-build tooling: `uiCacher.js` (Brotli-compresses & uploads `dist/` to object storage/CDN after `vite build`), `bundle.js` (legacy chat-widget bundler). |
| `config/` | Only `config/actions.js` exists in this checkout (a small action-name registry). `config/config.js` (the local/dev default config) is referenced by code but **not present** in this checkout — see [Unknowns](#unknowns--areas-requiring-further-investigation). |
| `migrate/` | **Tenant provisioning** scripts (`core.js`, `manage.js`) — not a schema-migration framework; seeds new-tenant data (users, views, default groups, console catalog). |
| `tests/` | Vitest test suite, mirrors `routes/`, `lib/`, `models/`, `middleware/` structure. |
| `tools*/DevOps/deployment` config | `Dockerfile` (root), `deployment/{dev,ibm,onprem}/` (per-environment Dockerfiles/build scripts), `DevOps/` (CI pipeline YAMLs + its own README). |

---

## Application Architecture

```
                                   ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                                   │   Browser / External Client │
                                   └───────────────┬─────────────┘
                                                    │ HTTPS
                     ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┐
                     │                              │                              │
             GET /admin (SPA)               GET /agents (SPA)              GET / , /login, bots,
             src/ (Vue3, Pinia)             src-agent/ (Vue3, Pinia)       channels, APIs, webhooks
                     │                              │                              │
                     └──────────────┬───────────────┴───────────────┬──────────────┘
                                    ▼                                ▼
                    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                     Express app (app.js)                  │
                    │  session (connect-redis) → tenant/subdomain resolve →     │
                    │  unauthroutes.js → naclroutes.js → aclroutes.js → 404     │
                    │  RBAC: middleware/rbac/*  |  LDAP refresh: ldapRoleRefresh │
                    └───────────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                    │                        │
                     ┌──────────────▼───────────┐   ┌────────▼─────────────────┐
                     │   Socket.IO (default ns)  │   │  GLOBAL.Dispatcher       │
                     │  chat.js → liveAgentv2.js,│   │  (service locator)       │
                     │  workflowMonitor.js,       │   │  .DB   → Mongo/Cloudant/ │
                     │  notification.js           │   │          DynamoDB       │
                     │  (@socket.io/redis-adapter │   │  .CGS  → GenAI providers│
                     │   for multi-instance pub/  │   │  .OSS  → object storage │
                     │   sub via redisClient)      │   │  .KP,.TPA,.CDS → more   │
                     └──────────────┬───────────┘   └────────┬─────────────────┘
                                    │                         │
                     ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐  ┌───────▼────────────────────┐
                     │  lib/scripts/* business logic│  │  models/* (BaseModel or    │
                     │  agentManager, queueManager, │  │  direct Dispatcher calls)  │
                     │  transferManager, agentTransfer,│└───────┬────────────────────┘
                     │  connectorBots (Bot Framework),│         │
                     │  a2aServer/a2aClient, workflows,│         ▼
                     │  ldapClient/ldapSync, gptPrompter│  MongoDB / Cloudant / DynamoDB
                     └──────────────┬──────────────┘   (system of record, per DB_TYPE)
                                    │
                     ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
                     │        tools/* (~50)         │
                     │  Slack, ServiceNow, AWS, DBs, │
                     │  webhooks... invoked as LLM   │
                     │  function-calling tools        │
                     └───────────────────────────────┘

                     Redis (global `redisClient`, standalone or cluster):
                     sessions (connect-redis) · caching (lib/helper/caching.js) ·
                     rate limiting · Socket.IO adapter pub/sub · agent/queue/transfer
                     state · LDAP connection-pool invalidation · A2A context cache
```

Key architectural traits:
- **Single global service locator** (`GLOBAL.Dispatcher`, set once in `app.js:181`) hides which physical backend (Mongo/Cloudant/DynamoDB, which GenAI provider, which object-storage vendor) answers a given call — see [Database / Storage](#database--storage).
- **Global singletons via bare `GLOBAL`/`config`/`redisClient`/`passport` variables** (declared `writable` via ESLint globals in `.eslintrc.cjs:13-20`), not passed through constructors/DI — an important non-obvious convention for new contributors.
- **Three route "tiers"** (`unauthroutes.js` → `naclroutes.js` → `aclroutes.js`) implement a coarse-grained "must be logged in" / "no ACL" / "ACL + RBAC" split, layered with a finer-grained RBAC v2 permission system (`middleware/rbac/`).
- **Two independent Vue SPAs** (`src/` admin console, `src-agent/` agent console) are built as **separate Vite entry points** (`vite.config.js:27-40`: `index.html` → `main`, `agent.html` → `agent`) and served from the same Express server at `/admin` and `/agents` respectively.
- **Redis is load-bearing infrastructure**, not just a cache: sessions, Socket.IO horizontal scaling (via `@socket.io/redis-adapter`), live-agent queue/transfer state, rate limiting, and LDAP pool coordination all depend on it.

---

## Application Startup Flow

Entry point: `npm start` → `node app.js` (`package.json:12`).

1. **Node version gate** — `app.js:5-8` exits immediately if the running Node isn't v24.x.
2. **`require('module-alias/register')`** (`app.js:9`) activates the `_moduleAliases` map from `package.json:209-219` (`@root`, `@models`, `@lib`, `@libscr`, `@libhlp`, `@helpers`, `@routes`, `@tools`, `@middleware`) so every subsequent `require('@lib/...')`-style import resolves correctly.
3. **`initEnv()`** — `require('@libhlp/envConfiguration').init` (i.e. `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js`) is awaited **before anything else runs**. This:
   - Builds the global `config` object from `process.env.AEX_ENV` (`aks` | `eks` | `onprem` | default) — see [Configuration](#configuration).
   - In production, fetches secrets from the environment's secret store (Azure Key Vault for `aks`, AWS Secrets Manager/IAM for `eks`, OpenBao for `onprem`).
   - Creates the global `redisClient` — a Redis Cluster client (`@redis/client` `createCluster`) or standalone client (`createClient`) depending on `config.IS_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE`, connects it, and PINGs it before returning.
4. Inside the `.then(async () => {...})` callback (the rest of `app.js`):
   - Express app + `http.createServer(app)` + Socket.IO server (`new IOServer(server, {pingTimeout:15000, serveClient:false})`) are created (`app.js:12-26`).
   - Handlebars view engine registered with custom `json`/`checkif` helpers (`app.js:34-52`).
   - **Session store**: `connect-redis`'s `RedisStore` wraps `redisClient` (`app.js:54-56`); cookie name `app`; secure/`sameSite:'none'`/`partitioned` cookies in production.
   - Body parsers, `passport.initialize()/session()`, `connect-flash`, `lusca` security headers (nosniff, HSTS, CSP, referrer-policy), `morgan` logging (`app.js:99-149`).
   - **`GLOBAL` wiring** (`init()`, `app.js:179-198`): `GLOBAL.TEMP_PATH`, `GLOBAL.Dispatcher = new (require('./lib/scripts/dispatchers'))()`, `GLOBAL.SplitIntent`, and `require('./lib/scripts/translationAgent').translationInit()`.
   - **Tenant/subdomain resolution middleware** (`app.js:202-235`): from `config.SUB_DOMAIN` for on-prem/aks/eks, or parsed from `req.hostname` for multi-tenant SaaS (session destroyed on subdomain mismatch); `dev.js`'s hardcoded subdomain is used outside production.
   - **`@socket.io/redis-adapter` wiring** (`app.js:164-171`): duplicates `redisClient` into a `sub` client, then `io.adapter(createAdapter(redisClient, sub, {...}))` — this is what lets Socket.IO events fan out across multiple app instances.
   - **Route mounting**, strictly in this order (`app.js:238-243`): `unauthroutes.js` → `naclroutes.js` → `aclroutes.js` → 404 handler.
   - **`startServer(port, address)`** (`app.js:268-277`) polls `vectorDBs('checkConnection')` every second and only calls `server.listen(...)` once the vector DB connection is confirmed. Production listens on `process.env.PORT` at `0.0.0.0`; non-production hardcodes port `3000` on `localhost`.
   - Graceful-shutdown handlers (`SIGINT`/`SIGTERM`/etc., production only) decrement Redis-backed agent-queue counters and close Redis/vector-DB connections before `process.exit`.
   - Finally, `lib/socket/chat.js` and `lib/socket/notification.js` are initialized with `io` and the duplicated `sub` Redis client (`app.js:334-335`) — this is where the single `io.on('connection', ...)` handler actually lives (see [Request/API Flow](#requestapi-flow)).

---

## Request/API Flow

### HTTP request path
```
Client
  → app.js middleware chain (cookies, session/RedisStore, tenant-subdomain resolve,
     body parsers, passport, lusca security headers, morgan)
  → routes/unauthroutes.js   (public: assets, /login, /logout, captcha, webhooks, bot inbound...)
       → ends with a login gate: if !req.session.username → redirect to '/' (unless XHR/API)
  → routes/naclroutes.js     (must be logged in; ldapRoleRefresh middleware; e.g. /agent, /notify, /user_info)
  → routes/aclroutes.js      (admin/management; re-validates customer_credentials; legacy v1 ACL check;
                               RBAC v2 via routes/permissionWrappers.js + middleware/rbac/permissionMiddleware.js)
  → route handler (routes/**/index.js)
       → models/* (BaseModel-backed, legacy-prototype, or pure-Redis)
            → GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.DB, serviceKeys) → Mongo/Cloudant/DynamoDB
       → and/or lib/scripts/* business logic (agentTransfer, workflows, gptPrompter, connectorBots...)
       → and/or redisClient directly (cache, queue counters, rate limiting)
  → res.json(...) / res.render(...) / res.send(...)   (no centralized error-formatting helper — see Error Handling)
```

### Real example — `GET /admin/agentassist/desk/:title` (fetch a live-agent "desk")
1. `app.js:243` mounts `aclroutes.js`.
2. `routes/aclroutes.js:62` — `router.use('/admin', csrfLoginCheck, require('./admin.js'))`.
3. `routes/admin.js:85` — `router.use(adminLogger)` (writes an `AdminLog` audit record for every admin request).
4. `routes/admin.js:113` — `registerRouteWithPermission(router, '/agentassist', require('./liveAgentConsole'))` (from `routes/permissionWrappers.js`) inserts `hasPermission('agentAssist','view')` before mounting.
5. `routes/liveAgentConsole/index.js:11` — `router.use('/desk', require('./desks'))`.
6. `routes/liveAgentConsole/desks/index.js:18-21` — `router.get('/:title', isUserAdmin, async (req,res) => { ... })`; `isUserAdmin` (`desks/index.js:62-69`) restricts to `Admin`/`Viewer` roles via `@libhlp/agentUtility`.
7. Handler calls `new Desk(req.session).get(req.params.title)` (a `BaseModel`-backed model) and responds `res.json({deskDetails})`.

### Real example — `GET /notify/fetchNotifications`
1. `app.js:240` mounts `naclroutes.js`; `naclroutes.js:98` — `router.use('/notify', require('./pushNotification.js').auth)`.
2. `routes/pushNotification.js:40-47` — `router.get('/fetchNotifications', ...)` builds a range key from `req.session.username`, instantiates `new Notification({}, req.session)` (`models/pushNotification.js`), and returns raw DB docs via `res.send(data)`.

### Socket.IO event path (live agent chat)
```
Client socket connects (query.agent=true from src-agent/) 
  → lib/socket/chat.js: single io.on('connection', ...) handler (app.js:334 wires this in)
       → chat.js:492 detects query.agent and skips end-user chatbot listeners
       → chat.js:523 calls AgentTransferSocketEvents(socket)  (== lib/socket/liveAgentv2.js's init())
            → liveAgentv2.js registers 'Transfer Broker' / 'Agent Broker' / 'Peer Broker' / 'disconnect'
            → each Broker event's payload carries an internal `event` name dispatched via switch
            → handlers use QueueManager / AgentManager / TransferManager (all backed by redisClient)
              and lib/scripts/agentTransfer (desk queueing, transfer orchestration, models/agentAssist/*)
```

---

## Core Modules

### Dispatchers (`lib/scripts/dispatchers/`)
- **Purpose**: single abstraction point ("service locator") that hides which concrete backend (database, GenAI provider, object storage, key vault, third-party API) answers a call.
- **Key files**: `index.js` (the `dispatcher` class — maps short keys `DB`/`CGS`/`OSS`/`KP`/`TPA`/`CDS` to sub-modules; `.service(name, keys)` instantiates the right handler), `dbServices/index.js` (DB backend selection), `cognitiveServices/index.js` (GenAI backend selection), `objectStorageServices/`, `keyVaultServices/`, `thirdPartyAPIServices/`, `channelDependentServices/`.
- **Important functions/classes**: `dispatcher.prototype.service(serviceName, keys, type)` (`dispatchers/index.js:40-42`); `dbDispatcher` methods `find/findById/update/updateById/insert/destroy/searchByMR/bulk/...` (`dbServices/index.js:13-88`).
- **Dependencies**: `mongodb`, `@ibm-cloud/cloudant`, `@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb`.
- **Connects to**: instantiated once as `GLOBAL.Dispatcher` (`app.js:181`); called from almost every model and many `lib/scripts/*` modules.

### Live-agent chat backend (`lib/scripts/agentManager`, `queueManager`, `transferManager`, `agentTransfer`, `liveAgentTransfer`)
- **Purpose**: manage human-agent availability, chat queueing, and transferring a conversation from bot to human agent.
- **Key files/classes**: `agentManager/index.js` (`AgentManager` — Redis-backed online/offline/socket-id/active-chats state), `queueManager/index.js` (`QueueManager` — desk queue counters), `transferManager/index.js` (`TransferManager` — per-transfer Redis state), `agentTransfer/index.js` (the orchestrator: `registerTransfer`, `publishToUser/Agent`, `quitUserFromTransfer`, scheduled transfers), `agentTransfer/activeChatsManager.js` (`ActiveChatsManager`, Redis-Set atomic active-chat tracking), `liveAgentTransfer/index.js` (an older, separate rule-driven live-chat bridge used by bot connectors, not the desk/queue system).
- **Dependencies**: global `redisClient`, `models/agentAssist/*` (Desk, DeskSettings, AgentTransfer, AgentConversations), `@libscr/notifications`, `@lib/scheduler`.
- **Connects to**: instantiated throughout `lib/socket/liveAgentv2.js`; `agentTransfer` calls `GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers.transferAgentMessage` (from `connectorBots`) to reach bot-channel users.

### Bot Framework connectors (`lib/scripts/connectorBots/`)
- **Purpose**: integrate with Microsoft Teams, Slack, Telegram, Facebook, SMS, email, IVR/Twilio, Google Chat via the Microsoft Bot Framework SDK.
- **Key files**: `index.js` (current, `CloudAdapter`-based, builds/caches per-channel connectors, publishes `GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers`), `indexV1.js` (legacy `BotFrameworkAdapter`-based), `botbuilder-redis-storage/` (Redis-backed Bot Framework `Storage` implementation for conversation/user state).
- **Dependencies**: `botbuilder`, `botframework-connector`, global `redisClient`.
- **Connects to**: `routes/connector_bots.js`; `GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers` is called by `agentTransfer`, `notifications`, `chatMessages`.

### A2A protocol (`lib/scripts/a2aServer/`, `lib/scripts/a2aClient/`)
- **Purpose**: expose AEX GenAI agents as Agent-to-Agent (A2A) servers, and let AEX call out to external A2A agents.
- **Key files**: `a2aServer/index.js` (AgentCard building, channel resolution), `a2aServer/executor.js` (`runCGSTurn` — wraps the CGS conversation pipeline in a Promise with a timeout), `a2aServer/taskStore.js` (`ChannelTaskStore`), `a2aServer/contextCache.js` (Redis-backed conversation context, 15-minute TTL), `a2aClient/index.js` (`sendMessage`, `sendMessageStream`, auth-header building for API key/Basic/Bearer/OAuth2).
- **Dependencies**: `@a2a-js/sdk`, `models/externalAgents`, global `redisClient`.
- **Connects to**: `routes/external/a2a.js`, `routes/a2aClient/index.js`, `routes/connector_bots.js`, `lib/scripts/dispatchers/cognitiveServices/openai/externalAgentTool/`.

### GenAI / cognitive services (`lib/scripts/dispatchers/cognitiveServices/openai/`)
- **Purpose**: unify multiple LLM providers behind one interface (the "openai" dispatcher key is used as an umbrella name for all providers).
- **Key files**: `openai.js` (Azure OpenAI), `openaicloud.js` (OpenAI public cloud), `bedrock.js` (AWS Bedrock, Titan/Nova), `vertex.js` (Google Vertex/Gemini), `customllm.js` (customer-configured LLM via a workflow), `gptCaller.js` (unifying caller), `agents.js` (agentic tool-calling loop — this is what actually calls `tools/*`), `guardrail.js`, `callMCP.js` (Model Context Protocol client), `contextManagement/` (planning, sliding-window context, user-preference injection).
- **Dependencies**: `@azure/identity`, `jsonwebtoken` (for GCP service-account JWTs), AWS SigV4 signing (`crypto`).
- **Connects to**: `routes/genAI/*`, `lib/scripts/gptPrompter`, `tools/*` (function-calling), `a2aClient` (external-agent-as-tool).

### GenAI prompting & language utilities (`lib/scripts/gptPrompter`, `interpreters`, `translationAgent`)
- **`gptPrompter/index.js`**: `prompt({...})` — generic one-off LLM question helper with named prompt templates per "console"/use-case (`ucd/`, `ow/`, `translator/`, `functions/`, `pg/`). Called by `routes/genAI/index.js`.
- **`interpreters/slack/index.js`**: converts internal "MCT" markup + Markdown into Slack Block Kit.
- **`translationAgent/index.js`**: dispatch table for translation providers (`watson`, `openwhisk`, `google`, `microsoft`) plus spell-check via a configurable endpoint.

### Workflows, notifications, PWA (`lib/scripts/workflows`, `notifications`, `pwaSubscription`, `chatMessages`)
- **`workflows/index.js`**: `traverseFlow`/`initiateWorkflow` — walks a workflow node graph (`models/workflow`), injects per-node-type credentials (e.g. ServiceNow), integrates with the external scheduler service (`config.SCHEDULER_API`).
- **`notifications/index.js`**: `sendNotifications({channel,...})` — routes to web push (`models/webNotifications`), channel bots (`GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers.proactiveMessage`), or email.
- **`pwaSubscription/index.js`**: Web Push (VAPID) subscription management.
- **`chatMessages/index.js`**: a generic "chat message mode" bridge (separate feature from live-agent transfer), used by `connectorBots`.

### LDAP integration (`lib/scripts/ldapClient`, `lib/scripts/ldapSync`, `middleware/ldapRoleRefresh.js`)
- **`ldapClient/index.js`**: low-level LDAP connectivity (`ldapts`), a **per-tenant connection pool** (size 5) with Redis pub/sub pool-invalidation (`aex:ldap:pool-invalidate`), RFC-4515 filter escaping, configurable search/attribute/lockout policy.
- **`ldapSync/index.js`**: `resolveGroups` maps a user's LDAP group DNs to AEX `AccessGroup` roles; upserts LDAP profile fields; invalidates the Redis role-TTL cache (`aex:role_ttl`).
- **`middleware/ldapRoleRefresh.js`**: applied globally in `naclroutes.js:28`; non-blocking background role refresh keyed off a Redis TTL per user.

### Tool connectors (`tools/`)
- **Purpose**: ~50 pluggable integrations (Slack, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Jira, AWS/Azure/GCP services, databases, webhooks, etc.) that GenAI agents can invoke as function-calling tools.
- **Key files**: `tools/index.js` (`getAllToolFunctions()` flattens every tool's `functions[]` into one registry keyed by function name; `getToolDescription(toolName)`), `tools/example.tools.js` (the template every tool follows).
- **Plugin shape** (every `tools/<name>/index.js`): `{ name, fields: { secrets, config }, functions: [{ name, description, parameters, function }] }`.
- **Invocation path**: `cognitiveServices/openai/agents.js` loads the registry once, presents `functions[].parameters` (OpenAI-function-calling JSON Schema) to the LLM, and on a tool call executes `TOOLS[toolName].function(toolArgs)`.

### Frontend apps (`src/`, `src-agent/`)
- **`src/`** — admin/configuration console (Vue 3 + Pinia + Vue Router, `createWebHashHistory('/admin#')`). Pages: GenAI agent builder, workflows, RBAC, self-heal, learning console, live-agent-console admin views, master config, UI management, channel configuration.
- **`src-agent/`** — live-agent console (`Home.vue`, `Chat.vue`, `LiveDashboard.vue`). Connects to `lib/socket/liveAgentv2.js` via `socket.io-client` with `query: { agent: true }` (`src-agent/helpers/chat/socket-events.js:59`).
- Both call the backend via plain `axios` on **relative, same-origin paths** (no central API client) — a CSRF token from `GET /user_info` is applied globally to `axios.defaults.headers.common['x-aex-ad-client']`.

## Database / Storage

**Primary databases** — selectable per tenant via `config.DB_TYPE` / a tenant's `service_keys`, all accessed through the Dispatcher (`lib/scripts/dispatchers/dbServices/index.js:1-9`):
- **MongoDB** (`mongodbHandler/mongoDBHandler.js`) — lazily opens/pools a `MongoClient` per host on first use, connection string from `config.MONGO_URL`.
- **IBM Cloudant** (`cloudantHandler/cloudantHandlerV3.js`) — **the default backend** when `DB_TYPE` is unset.
- **DynamoDB** (`dynamodbHandler/`) — an alternative backend.
- **Cosmos DB** handler exists on disk (`dbServices/cosmosHandler/`) but is **not wired into the backend-selection map** — effectively dead code (unverified intent).

**Dispatcher methods** available on a DB handle: `find`, `findById`, `update`, `updateById`, `updateWithoutQuery`, `insert`, `destroy`, `searchByMR`, `searchByMRKeys`, `searchByMRQuery`, `searchByMRWithKeys`, `bulk`, `getAllMR`, `addMR`, `editMR`, `publishDefaultMR`, `updateDefaultMR`, `deleteMR`, `bulkFetchByKeys` (`dbServices/index.js:13-88`). No `.aggregate` — this is a CouchDB/Cloudant-style "map-reduce view" API, not native Mongo aggregation.

**Models** (`models/`) follow three different patterns:
1. **`BaseModel` subclasses** (`models/base/index.js`) — constructor binds `this.dbHandler = GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.DB, session.customer_credentials.service_keys)`, i.e. **per-session, per-tenant DB handle**. No schema — thin Promise wrapper over the Dispatcher's document/view API. Example: `models/channel.js`.
2. **Legacy standalone prototype objects** that call `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.DB, null)` directly per method, always using the default/system DB connection (not per-tenant). Example: `models/customer.js`.
3. **Pure-Redis models** with no Dispatcher involvement at all. Example: `models/webNotifications.js` (explicitly commented "All data is stored in redis").

**Redis** (global `redisClient`, `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js:458-524`) is used for: sessions (`connect-redis`), read-through caching (`lib/helper/caching.js`), rate limiting (`lib/scripts/rateLimiter`), live-agent queue/transfer/active-chat state, Socket.IO cross-instance pub/sub (`@socket.io/redis-adapter`), LDAP connection-pool invalidation, and A2A conversation-context caching (15-minute TTL). It supports both **standalone** and **cluster mode**, gated by `config.IS_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE` — see the note in [Unknowns](#unknowns--areas-requiring-further-investigation) about a gap in the `onprem` config branch.

**Vector DB** (`lib/scripts/vectorDB/index.js`) — a **separate** connection from the main app DB, selecting Mongo Atlas Vector Search or pgvector based on `config.VECTOR_DB.TYPE`, used by GenAI search/RAG features (`cognitiveServices/openai/searcher.js`).

**Other DB drivers under `tools/`** (`mssql`, `postgres`, `mongodb`, `cloudant`, `clickhouse`, `databricks`) are **tool connectors** — per-invocation connections to a *customer's own external* database for bot/agent actions, unrelated to the app's own storage.

### Read/write flow example — `lib/helper/caching.js`
1. `cacheData(cacheTerm, callback)` first checks Redis: `redisClient.get('${cacheTerm}_cached')`.
2. On a miss, `reCache()` calls `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.DB, null).searchByMR('customer_configuration', {key: cacheTerm}, ...)` — this constructs a fresh DB handle (opening/reusing a pooled Mongo client, or a Cloudant client, depending on `DB_TYPE`) and runs the equivalent of a map-reduce view query.
3. The result is written back to Redis with a 1-hour TTL (`redisClient.setEx(...)`) before being returned via callback.

This **read-through cache pattern** (Redis fast path, Mongo/Cloudant/DynamoDB system of record via the Dispatcher) is used throughout the app.

## Error Handling

- **No centralized Express error-handling middleware exists** — a repo-wide search found no `(err, req, res, next)`-style middleware and no `app.use((err,...) => ...)` in `app.js`.
- **404 handler** (`app.js:245-266`) is the only terminal fallback, content-negotiated (HTML/JSON/text) — it is *not* an error handler (takes 2 args, not 4).
- **Process-level safety net**: `process.on('uncaughtException', alert.exceptionalert)` (`app.js:316`) → `lib/alertnotificationhandler.js` logs the stack, emails `lucydevelopers@hcl.com`, then `process.exit(1)` (crash-and-restart, presumably under a process manager/orchestrator restart policy — not verified which one).
- **Per-route convention**: ad-hoc `try/catch` with `console.error(...)` and manually shaped responses. Response shapes are **inconsistent across the codebase** (`{status:false,message}`, `{error:'...'}`, `{success:false,error}`, plain-text `res.send(...)`) — there is no shared error/response helper module.
- Some files define local error constants (e.g. `const ERROR = {error: 'Something went wrong!'}` in `routes/liveAgentConsole/desks/index.js:1`), but these are not shared infrastructure.

### Session handling
`connect-redis` + global `redisClient` (`app.js:54-56`). Session is blanked (`req.session = {}`) for bearer-token/bot-channel API calls (`app.js:103-109`). Tenant subdomain is injected/validated per request (`app.js:202-235`), destroying the session on mismatch. Common session fields: `username`, `displayName`, `groups`, `customer_credentials` (full tenant config), `ums_version`, `ums_acl_info`, `effectiveRoles`, plus various flow-control flags (`opt_required`, `change_password_check`, CSRF token, etc.).

### Authorization (RBAC)
Two models coexist, gated by `session.ums_version`:
- **v1 (legacy)**: `routes/aclroutes.js:13-18` → `lucyACLcheck.acl_check()` (`routes/lums/acl.js`), backed by `models/ums_groups.js` and `models/routes_access.js` (per-access-level route allowlists).
- **v2 (current)**: `lib/helper/getUserRoles.js` resolves a user's roles (Redis-cached, falling back to `models/userProfile.js`), then `roleHasPermission(roles, module, action)` checks a static matrix in `middleware/rbac/rolesPermission.js`. Route-level enforcement is `hasPermission(module, action)` (`middleware/rbac/permissionMiddleware.js:69-123`), wired per mount-path by `routes/permissionWrappers.js`'s `registerRouteWithPermission()` using static `MODULE_PATHS`/`METHOD_TO_ACTION`/`CUSTOM_ACTIONS` tables.
- `middleware/rbac/userOperationMiddleware.js` adds a second layer for user-mutation endpoints (blocks self-modification, protects Admin/Superadmin accounts from lower roles).
- `middleware/ldapRoleRefresh.js` keeps LDAP-derived roles fresh in the background (non-blocking, Redis-TTL-gated).

## Important Business Logic

**1. Bot-to-human live agent hand-off.**
A chat message from an end-user, when a hand-off condition is met (`lib/scripts/liveAgentTransfer.shouldTransfer` or the desk/queue system), is registered against a "desk" (`agentTransfer.registerTransfer` → checks desk availability/queue limits via `QueueManager` and `models/agentAssist/{Desk,DeskSetting}`), broadcast to available agents over Socket.IO (`liveAgentv2.js` Broker events), and once an agent accepts, subsequent messages are relayed both ways (`publishToUser`/`publishToAgent`), with per-transfer state (language, inactivity timers) tracked in Redis (`TransferManager`) and active-chat sets per agent (`ActiveChatsManager`, Redis SADD/SREM for race-free updates).

**2. Multi-provider GenAI conversation turn.**
A conversation turn is normalized through `lib/corearchitecture.js`'s `CoreArchitecture.continueConversation()`, which enforces a recursion guard (max 5) and a trial-tenant message cap (500), then dispatches to `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.CGS, ...)` → the appropriate provider module (`openai.js`/`bedrock.js`/`vertex.js`/etc.) → optionally an agentic tool-calling loop (`cognitiveServices/openai/agents.js`) that can call any registered `tools/*` function or a configured external A2A agent.

**3. Multi-channel bot delivery.**
`connectorBots/index.js` builds and caches one Bot-Framework `CloudAdapter`-based connector per channel (Teams/Slack/Telegram/etc.), publishing a `GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers` object that other modules (`agentTransfer`, `notifications`, `chatMessages`) call into to actually deliver messages/proactive notifications/meeting invites back out to the channel, regardless of which channel it is.

**4. Tenant provisioning.**
New tenants are bootstrapped (not "migrated" in the schema sense) by `migrate/core.js`/`migrate/manage.js`: creating an initial admin user, publishing default Map-Reduce views, seeding a default Super Admin access group, and populating the tenant's enabled admin-console catalog (`migrate/manage.js`'s hardcoded ~18-entry console list).

## Data Flow

1. **Inbound chat message** → Socket.IO (`lib/socket/chat.js`) or channel webhook (`connectorBots`) → `CoreArchitecture.continueConversation()` → GenAI dispatcher → (optionally) tool calls / A2A calls → response streamed back over the same channel.
2. **Tenant configuration** → stored as documents in the primary DB (Mongo/Cloudant/DynamoDB, per tenant's `service_keys`) → read through `lib/helper/caching.js`'s 1-hour Redis cache → consumed by nearly every request (`customer_credentials` in session).
3. **Live-agent transfer state** → written directly to Redis (queue counters, active-chat sets, per-transfer metadata) for low-latency real-time coordination, with the durable transfer/conversation record persisted via `models/agentAssist/*` (Dispatcher-backed).
4. **User roles/permissions** → computed once from LDAP groups or UMS group membership, cached in Redis with a TTL, refreshed in the background (`ldapRoleRefresh`), and re-derived into a permission map served to the frontend via `/user_info`.
5. **Built frontend assets** → `vite build` → `dist/` → `buildEngine/uiCacher.js` Brotli-compresses and uploads to object storage/CDN (`config.cosui.bucketpath`) → served to browsers from the CDN, with only `dist/index.html`/`dist/agent.html` read from local disk by the Express app.
